verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's editorial parenthesis is devastating in its precision: Judas did not care about the poor; he was a thief who helped himself to the common fund. The righteous-sounding objection — sell it for the poor — is moral laundering. This is the pattern of false discipleship: using the language of the gospel's values (care for the poor) to serve personal interest. It is particularly dangerous because it is indistinguishable from genuine concern without the diagnostic knowledge John here provides. The Lord who knows what is in man (2:25) knows the difference between the Judases and the Marys, even when their language overlaps.

The sum is worth converting. Three hundred denarii is roughly a year's wages for a labourer — a denarius was a day's pay, and once sabbaths and feasts are taken out, three hundred working days is about a year.

So the question is not trivial and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. A year's income has just been poured onto somebody's feet and cannot be recovered. Judas's arithmetic is correct, and if his motive had been what he said it was, his objection would have been a good one.

Which is precisely why John supplies the parenthesis, and it is worth noticing how much he knows. Judas kept the glossokomon — the box, originally a case for the mouthpieces of flutes, then any small chest — and he used to help himself, in the imperfect tense: not once, habitually, over a long period.

Two things follow that are worth stating plainly.

The first is that Jesus knew and appointed him treasurer anyway. Nothing suggests the theft was undetected by the one who knew what was in man (2:25). He let a thief carry the bag for the best part of three years.

The second is about the shape of the objection, because it is a permanent shape. Judas does not argue for theft. He argues for the poor. The cover story is not merely respectable — it is more obviously righteous than what Mary has just done, and anybody in that room who had not read John's parenthesis would have found him the more spiritual man at the table.

Which is the warning. A concern for the poor can be perfectly genuine and can also be the most effective possible disguise, and the two are not distinguishable from outside. The only person in the room who could tell was the one being anointed.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: Judas had the moneybag

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave her alone: Jesus defends Mary against Judas with a directness that is itself an act of protective love. Her action, which she may not have fully understood, has a meaning he does name: she has anointed him for burial. The fragrant ointment will linger in the house; the crucified body will receive its burial ointment from Nicodemus (19:39-40). But what Mary has done cannot be taken back. The poor you always have with you: not an indifference to poverty but a calibration of the unique and unrepeatable moment. There will be opportunities to serve the poor; there is only one moment to anoint the Son of God for his sacrificial death.

Now the guard, because the second half of verse 8 has done more damage than almost any sentence Jesus ever spoke.

The poor you always have with you is quoted, regularly and confidently, as a reason not to bother — a shrug from Christ himself, proof that poverty is permanent and efforts against it are naive. It has been used to justify indifference from pulpits and dinner tables for centuries.

The sentence is a quotation, and the whole trouble is that the second half is left off.

He is citing Deuteronomy 15:11, and here is what it actually says: For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.

The permanence of poverty is not the conclusion. It is the premise — and the conclusion drawn from it, in the same breath, is a command to open your hand. Every Jew at that table would have known the rest of the verse; the first half brings the second with it, the way half a proverb does.

So the sentence means the opposite of the way it is used. He is not saying the poor can wait. He is quoting a command to give to them continually, and adding that there is exactly one week in human history in which a woman can anoint him for burial.

The chapter before this is worth remembering too. Judas, the man who raised the objection, had every day of those three years to open his hand and used the box to fill his own.

Then the phrase in verse 7, which is genuinely difficult in Greek: leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. The ointment is already poured out; there is nothing left to keep. The best sense is probably that she had been keeping it — that this jar had been put by, perhaps for her own burial or for a wedding — and Jesus is saying that she has, without fully knowing it, spent it on the right day.

Because in six days he will die, and be taken down in a hurry, and buried in a new tomb before sunset. Nicodemus will bring spices (19:39-40), but to a body already dead. Mary does it six days early, and she does it while he can still smell it.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd comes for two reasons: Jesus and Lazarus — the performer of miracles and the evidence of miracles. Living evidence is more compelling than testimony about past events. And so the institutional response to living evidence is to destroy it: the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus to eliminate the testimony. This is the logical endpoint of institutional unbelief: when the evidence cannot be answered, eliminate the evidence. The resurrection that was meant to produce faith has produced a murder plot against the resurrected man. The powers of death always try to reclaim what the power of life has liberated.

The faith spreading through the Lazarus testimony is the immediate cause of the intensification of the plot.

Verse 10 is one of the darkest sentences in the New Testament and it is nearly comic in its futility.

So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well.

They are proposing to kill a man who has already been killed once — or rather, who has already been dead once, and got up. Whatever they thought they had learned from the events at Bethany, it was not that the man was hard to bury.

And the reasoning is stated flatly: on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus. The problem is not that Lazarus is preaching. There is not a word recorded from him anywhere in this Gospel — he says nothing, before or after. The problem is that he exists.

That is the position a certain kind of witness occupies, and it is worth naming for anybody who feels they have nothing to say about their faith. Lazarus's entire testimony is that he is alive and people can see him at dinner. It was enough to empty the temple's constituency and enough to get him a death sentence.

And note what the crowd came for: not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus. They wanted to look at the evidence. Which is a very human and entirely reasonable thing to want, and it is why the council's solution was the one it was. When testimony cannot be refuted, the remaining option is to remove the witness — and every persecuting authority since has arrived at the same conclusion by the same route.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd that has come to Jerusalem for Passover hears that Jesus is coming: word travels fast in a city full of pilgrims who have been asking about him (11:56). The convergence of the Passover festival (thousands of pilgrims) and the raising of Lazarus (the most dramatic sign yet) creates the conditions for the public entry. Everything is moving toward the appointed moment — the hour that Jesus has been saying had not yet come is now very nearly here.

Palm branches were symbols of Jewish nationalism and victory — used at the rededication of the temple (Maccabees) and at the Festival of Tabernacles. The crowd greets Jesus as a conquering king: Hosanna (Save now!), Blessed is he who comes (Ps. 118:26), King of Israel. They are right about the title and wrong about the method. Jesus' response is to find not a warhorse but a donkey — the fulfillment of Zechariah 9:9, the prophet's vision of the humble king who makes peace. He accepts the acclamation but corrects the expectation through the animal he chooses.

Two details in what the crowd does are more pointed than they look.

The first is the palms. John is the only evangelist who mentions them, and they were not a general festive decoration — they were a political symbol. When Simon Maccabaeus retook the citadel in Jerusalem the people entered with praise and palm branches (1 Macc. 13:51), and palms were struck on Jewish coins during both revolts against Rome. Waving them at a man entering the capital is roughly what waving a national flag at a returning general would be.

The second is what they shout. Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord is Psalm 118:25-26 — and Psalm 118 was the last of the Hallel psalms, sung at Passover, so every pilgrim there had it by heart. Hosanna is Hebrew for save now: originally a cry for help that had worn down into an acclamation, the way God save the King has.

And then they add five words that are not in the psalm: even the King of Israel.

That is the crowd's own contribution, and it is the whole misunderstanding in a phrase. The psalm is about pilgrims arriving at the temple. They have turned it into a coronation, and they have supplied the title themselves.

Which is why the donkey matters, and why John gives it no explanation. Jesus does not silence them. He does not correct the psalm or refuse the shouting. He finds an animal and sits on it — and the animal is the argument. A king coming to a city on a warhorse is coming to take it; a king on a donkey has come in peace, and every one of them knew Zechariah well enough to feel the difference.

Matthew mentions a donkey and her colt (Matt 21:2–7), while Mark, Luke and John mention one animal. Matthew names both because Zechariah’s prophecy names both; the others mention only the colt Jesus rode. To mention more is not to contradict.

He lets them crown him and quietly declines the kingdom they have in mind.
verseByVerse.note: Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration. “Hosanna” means “save, we pray.”

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
branches of palm trees at the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples did not understand these things at first: the honest admission that accompanies every major event in John's gospel. The triumphal entry made no sense to the disciples while it was happening — they did not grasp the donkey's significance or the prophecy's fulfillment. When Jesus was glorified: the resurrection and ascension were the hermeneutical event that made the past intelligible. Pentecost illuminated Passover; the resurrection decoded the entry. Christian memory is always retrospective: we understand what we participated in after the Spirit opens our eyes. This is why the church can say more about the Trinity than the disciples could say during Jesus' ministry.

There is a small alteration in the quotation worth noticing. Zechariah 9:9 begins Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! John writes Fear not, daughter of Zion.

He has swapped the opening for a phrase that runs through Isaiah and Zephaniah — fear not, do not be afraid, the standard word to a frightened Israel. Which changes the register of the whole entry. The crowd is exultant and does not need telling to rejoice; they are already doing it, loudly, and about the wrong thing. What they will need in five days is the other sentence.

Then verse 16, which is one of the most quietly generous admissions in the Gospel: his disciples did not understand these things at first.

They were in the procession. They had presumably fetched the animal — the other Gospels say Jesus sent two of them for it — and they walked into Jerusalem in the middle of the noise, and John says plainly that none of it meant anything to them at the time.

Only afterwards, when Jesus was glorified, did they remember and see it.

Here is the comfort, and it is for anyone who has looked back at a stretch of their life and only then seen what was happening. The men closest to Jesus, physically present at the fulfilment of a prophecy, understood nothing on the day. Understanding was not a condition of being in the procession. It came later, and it came as memory — the same events, sitting still, suddenly legible.

Which is worth saying to the person in the middle of something they cannot read. The disciples' incomprehension did not stop the donkey being the right donkey.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey
fear not, O Zion

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The testimony about Lazarus is the engine driving the crowd. Two groups converge: those who witnessed the resurrection directly and continued to testify, and those who heard their testimony and came to see for themselves. This is the apostolic pattern: eyewitnesses testify, hearers believe, believers become witnesses. The chain of testimony from the tomb to the Passover crowd to the entire Mediterranean world to our generation is unbroken. We believe on the basis of testimony that originated with those who were there when the stone rolled away and Lazarus walked out.

The tense in verse 17 is doing work: the crowd continued to bear witness — imperfect, an ongoing action. They had not stopped talking about it. Weeks after the event, the people who had stood outside that cave were still telling anyone who would listen.

And verse 18 gives the mechanism of the entry, which is not what a reader assumes. The crowd did not come out because a famous teacher was approaching. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.

So the palm branches are downstream of Lazarus. The whole triumphal entry — the shouting, the psalm, the coronation the crowd improvised — was generated by a resurrection in a village two miles away.

Which ties the chapter together and explains the council's panic in the next verse. They had already worked out that Lazarus was the problem (v. 10). Here is the demonstration: one man alive at a dinner table produced a crowd large enough to fill the road into Jerusalem.

There is also a chain being described here that has not stopped running. Verse 17 is the people who were there; verse 18 is the people who heard them and came.

Nobody in verse 18 saw anything. They acted on the word of witnesses, and they were right to, and they made up the bulk of the crowd on the road. That is the ordinary mechanism by which almost every Christian who has ever lived came to faith — not by seeing, but by believing people who did, and the first link in the chain was a crowd standing outside a cave in Bethany who could not stop talking about it.

Which is exactly what Jesus will say to Thomas at the end of the book: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (20:29).

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world has gone after him: the Pharisees' despairing complaint is ironic prophecy — in trying to suppress Jesus, they are witnessing the beginning of the world-mission that the cross and resurrection will unleash.

This is the shortest entry in the commentary and the verse deserves considerably more, because it is one of the most finely built ironies in the Gospel — and it depends entirely on what happens in the next sentence.

Take the complaint first. You see that you are gaining nothing. It is said by Pharisees to one another, which means it is an internal recrimination. Somebody at that meeting is being blamed. They have had a warrant out for days (11:57), they have taken a formal decision to kill him (11:53), they have added Lazarus to the list (12:10), and a crowd has just carried him into the city shouting a coronation psalm. The policy is not working and they are turning on each other.

Now the sentence that does the work: Look, the world has gone after him.

They mean it as hyperbole and despair — everybody, the whole town, we have lost the room. It is the sort of thing people say when a thing has got away from them.

And John, who has been waiting for this, opens the very next verse: now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks.

The world. Not the crowd from Bethany, not the Passover pilgrims from Galilee. Gentiles — outsiders to the covenant, come up to worship at the feast, standing somewhere in the outer court where the notice warned them not to go further. They ask to see him, and the moment their request reaches him he says the hour has come.

So the Pharisees, complaining bitterly and using the biggest word they can find, have accidentally announced the programme. The world has gone after him — not yet, but it is beginning at the end of this sentence, and it will not stop. John has done this to them before: Caiaphas said one man should die for the people and prophesied the atonement (11:50-51), and the soldiers will shortly nail a title to a cross in three languages so that nobody can miss it.

His enemies keep saying true things in the wrong tone.

And there is a second irony sitting underneath. The Pharisees think the crowd's enthusiasm is their defeat. In five days that same crowd will be shouting for a crucifixion, and the Pharisees will have won everything they wanted — and the world will go after him anyway, by exactly the route they arranged.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–50 — The Hour Has Come: Lifting Up the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Greeks come seeking Jesus, prompting the announcement that 'the hour has come.' Jesus speaks of the grain of wheat, the lifting up that will draw all people, the voice from heaven, and the crisis that his presence creates. The section concludes with a sustained reflection on unbelief and the light that has come into the world, closing out the public ministry.

The join at v. 19. The Pharisees complain the world has gone after him, meaning it as hyperbole and despair — and John opens the very next verse with some Greeks. Gentiles, come up to worship, standing in the outer court beyond which stone notices in Greek and Latin promised death to any foreigner who passed. The world arrives at the door in the next sentence, and the hour strikes. His enemies keep saying true things in the wrong tone.

The hour (vv. 22-23). Three times John has told us it had not come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). The clock running under this book since the second chapter stops here — and what stops it is not the arrest or the plot but a handful of foreigners asking to see him, because the only way they get in is through what is about to happen. Note that Philip hesitates and fetches Andrew: there was no procedure for Gentiles, and he does not know if it is allowed.

Hating your life (v. 25). Hate here means to love less, as in hating father and mother (Lk. 14:26). It is not a licence for self-loathing, which devout people have taken it to be with miserable results. It is about ranking, and it is a way of holding things.

John's Gethsemane (vv. 26-27). This Gospel has no garden agony — no prayer that the cup pass, no sweat, no sleeping disciples — and readers have concluded that its Jesus is too serene to struggle. He is not. The struggle is here, in public, four days early. Now is my soul troubled uses the word John used of him at the tomb (11:33) and will use again at the supper (13:21). And what shall I say? "Father, save me from this hour"? is Gethsemane compressed: a genuine recoil and a genuine refusal to act on it, said out loud in front of a crowd with no attempt at a settled face.

The only voice (vv. 28-29). Matthew, Mark and Luke each record two heavenly voices, at the baptism and the transfiguration. John records neither, and this is the one occasion in the fourth Gospel on which the Father speaks aloud. And nobody in the crowd reports hearing words: some said thunder, others an angel. That is not a comment on their hearing but on what happens when God speaks into a room not listening for him — the commonest response to God is not denial but reclassification.

The ruler cast out (vv. 30-31). Two enormous claims in one verse. Now is the judgement of this world — the trial in which the world condemns Jesus is the trial in which the world is condemned. And cast out is the exorcist's word, applied to the chief of them. Something was defeated at Calvary, not only forgiven (Heb. 2:14-15; Col. 2:15).

Draw all (vv. 32-33). The third and last lifted up saying, and the only one John stops to explain. All people cannot mean every individual without contradicting 6:66, 8:24 and 12:48 in the same book. It means all kinds: the barrier is down, and Greeks have just asked for him. Note where the magnet is — not the teaching, not the signs, but a man being executed.

The objection nobody answers (vv. 34-35). The Christ remains forever is right, and they can cite it (Ps. 89:36; Isa. 9:7; Ezek. 37:25; Dan. 7:14). A Messiah who dies fails the one test they can name. Jesus does not resolve it — the last exchange of his public ministry leaves a fair theological difficulty standing — and speaks instead about the four days of daylight remaining.

Isaiah saw his glory (vv. 36-41). Seven words end the public ministry: he departed and hid himself from them. Then John's own verdict on three years — though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe — which disposes of the notion that unbelief is a failure of evidence. He explains it from Isaiah 53:1, the opening of the suffering servant song, and Isaiah 6:10, the hardening commission. And then, in a subordinate clause, one of the largest christological claims in the New Testament: Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory. The figure on the throne, high and lifted up, with the seraphim covering their faces, was the pre-incarnate Son — and lifted up is the same verb John has just told us describes the manner of his death.

The secret believers (vv. 42-43). John's full construction: these are believers. And the diagnosis is doxa, which means both glory and reputation — the same charge as 5:44. It is about which currency a man is paid in rather than courage in general. But note who else John puts in this category and what became of them: Nicodemus came at night and ends up at the cross with seventy-five pounds of spices (19:39), and Joseph of Arimathea is called a secret disciple in John's own words (19:38) and is the man who went in to Pilate for the body when the twelve had scattered. A concealed faith is a dangerous condition and not a settled verdict.

The closing summary (vv. 44-50). Jesus cried out — a shout — and the position of these verses after he has hidden himself suggests John has gathered up the case and restated it. What it contains is not a doctrine but a redirection: whoever believes in me believes not in me but in him who sent me. Faith in Jesus is a transparency, not a terminus. Verse 47 restates 3:17 at the far end of the ministry, and verse 48 shows how it fits: he does not judge, the word does — so the standard on the last day is a set of sentences spoken publicly and available ever since. And the final claim of the public ministry is that none of it was his own, and that its content is life.
verseByVerse.theology: The hour is the theological center of John's gospel — referenced as 'not yet come' repeatedly throughout the narrative (2:4; 7:30; 8:20), now announced as arrived (v. 23). The hour is the cross-resurrection-ascension event, the moment when the Son of Man is simultaneously lifted up in humiliation and glorified in triumph. The cross is not the Father's defeat but his decisive victory; it is not the Son's shame but his glory. This is the theology that has to be maintained against every attempt to split the crucifixion from the resurrection: both are the one event called 'the hour.'
verseByVerse.examples: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. This is the law of the kingdom: life through death, fruitfulness through sacrifice. Jesus applies it first to himself and then to his disciples. The disciple who 'hates his life in this world' — who does not cling to temporal existence at the cost of eternal loyalty — will find life preserved in ways that the self-preserver never can. The call to follow him is a call to follow him even into death.

verseByVerse.quote: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We wish to see Jesus: the request of every genuinely seeking soul in every generation. The Greeks — Gentile god-fearers who have come to Jerusalem for Passover — represent the world that exists outside the covenant community but has been drawn toward the God of Israel. They approach Philip, the disciple with a Greek name from the bilingual city of Bethsaida. Their request will prompt Jesus' announcement of the hour — the universal scope of the Gentile mission is the occasion for the disclosure of the cross. Seeing Jesus costs more than they know they are asking for; but what it costs is what it gives.

Who these men were is worth getting right. John calls them Greeks — Gentiles by birth, not Greek-speaking Jews up for the feast. They are outsiders.

They had come to worship at the feast, which places them among the God-fearers: Gentiles who had attached themselves to the God of Israel without becoming proselytes, who kept the moral law and came to the festivals. Cornelius in Acts 10 is the type.

And there was a wall for them. The temple's outer court was as far as a Gentile could go, and stone notices in Greek and Latin warned that any foreigner passing the barrier had himself to blame for the death that followed. Two of those inscriptions have been dug up. So these men have travelled to a feast at a temple they are forbidden to enter, to worship a God who has told them, in writing, where to stop.

That is the position from which they ask their question.

And they take it to Philip — who has a Greek name, and who comes from Bethsaida in Galilee, a mixed border town where Greek would have been spoken daily. They picked the man most likely to understand them, which suggests they had thought about it.

Their sentence has ended up on more pulpits than almost any in the Gospel, usually carved on the inside of one where only the preacher can see it: Sir, we wish to see Jesus.

It is worth taking at face value first. They are not asking for a doctrine or a decision. They want to look at him — which is the least sophisticated request in the chapter and, as it turns out, the only one that gets an answer.
verseByVerse.note: These Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, like the centurion Cornelius. Philip had a Greek name.

parallels.desc: other sheep

verseByVerse.quote: Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hour has come: the announcement the entire gospel has been building toward. The arrival of the Greeks — representatives of 'the world' that has 'gone after him' — signals the moment. The Son of Man is to be glorified: not the national Davidic king the crowd wanted, but the lifted-up Son of Man of Daniel 7 whose dominion extends to all peoples, nations, and languages. The glorification Jesus announces is the cross seen from the perspective of heaven: the moment when love's ultimate act is performed and the Father's saving purpose is accomplished. The hour that was 'not yet' is now.

Watch what Philip does, because it is oddly hesitant and it is characteristic. He does not take them to Jesus. He goes and tells Andrew, and then the two of them go together.

Philip is the man who did the arithmetic on the loaves and concluded it could not be done (6:7). Andrew is the man who brought the boy with the lunch anyway (6:8-9), and who brought his brother Peter in the first place (1:41). It is the same pair doing the same thing: Philip hesitates, Andrew brings people.

Why the hesitation? Almost certainly because they were Gentiles, and there was no procedure for this. Jesus had said he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel (Matt. 15:24); nobody had yet worked out what to do when the nations turned up asking. Philip is not being obstructive. He does not know if it is allowed.

And then the answer, which does not mention the Greeks at all and is the pivot of the entire Gospel.

The hour has come.

Three times John has told us it had not. At Cana: my hour has not yet come (2:4). At the feast: no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (7:30). In the treasury: the same sentence again (8:20). The clock has been running under this book since the second chapter, and it has just stopped.

And what stopped it was not the arrest, or the plot, or the entry into Jerusalem. It was a handful of foreigners asking to see him. The moment the world arrives at the door, the hour strikes — because the only way the world gets in is through what is about to happen, and he says so in the next breath with a picture of a seed going into the ground.

Note also the title: the Son of Man, from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man is given a dominion of all peoples, nations, and languages (Dan. 7:14). Greeks ask for him, and he answers with the title that has the nations written into it.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grain of wheat parable is Jesus' own interpretation of his coming death. Alone versus much fruit: the choice is between preservation that leads to barrenness and sacrifice that leads to multiplication. The same law applies to disciples: the one who clings to temporal life loses it; the one who releases it for Christ's sake receives it back in a way that cannot be taken. This is not masochism but kingdom economics: the currency of the new creation is not accumulation but sacrifice, not self-preservation but self-giving. Jesus models what he commands; he is himself the grain of wheat.

He answers a request from Gentiles with a fact about agriculture, and it takes a moment to see why it is the answer.

They want to see him. He tells them what it will cost to be seen — and it is not a rebuff but an explanation of the mechanism. A seed kept in a jar stays exactly what it is. It remains alone, which is the word he uses, and it is an odd word for a seed and the right word for him. The only way that one grain becomes many is by being buried and destroyed as a grain.

So there is no route by which those Greeks get in except the one he is about to take. Not by his teaching more clearly, not by his living longer, not by a change of policy about the outer court. The wall comes down because the seed goes into the ground.

And the picture is not a metaphor he reached for. It is what happens in a field: the seed must genuinely be lost, must stop being retrievable, before anything comes up. He is telling them plainly that he is going to die, in the gentlest available image, four days before it happens.

Then verse 25, and it needs a guard, because whoever hates his life has done harm when read flat.

It is an idiom, and Scripture uses it elsewhere in ways that make it unmistakable — Jesus says a disciple must hate his father and mother (Lk. 14:26), and Malachi has God saying Esau I have hated where the sense is plainly preference and rejection rather than malice. To hate in this sense is to love less, to set second, to be willing to let go of.

So this is not a licence for self-loathing, and it is not an instruction to despise one's own existence, which some devout people have taken it to be with miserable results. It is about ranking. The man who holds his life as the thing that must be preserved at all costs will find that it was not preservable; the man who holds it loosely, because something matters more, gets it back.

Note also that it is not a single act of renunciation performed once at a conversion, but a way of holding things.

Here is the test, and it is a plain one. Ask what you would be unable to obey God about, if he asked. Not what you would find hard — what is genuinely not on the table. Whatever that is, it is the part of your life you are still loving in the sense this verse means.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone serves me, he must follow me: discipleship is not admiration from a distance but the path of the grain of wheat — death and fruitfulness, suffering and resurrection. Where I am, there will my servant be also: the servant shares the master's path, including the path of the cross and, through it, the path of resurrection glory. Now is my soul troubled: the Gethsemane-like realism of the moment — Jesus is not stoically indifferent to what approaches. But for this purpose I have come to this hour: the trouble does not produce retreat. The hour is not intrusion but fulfillment.

This is John's Gethsemane, and it should be labelled as such, because it is easy to miss that he has one.

John records no garden agony. There is no sweating, no let this cup pass, no sleeping disciples — by the time we reach the garden in chapter 18 he walks out to meet the soldiers and asks who they want. Readers have sometimes concluded that John's Jesus is too serene to struggle.

He is not. The struggle is here, in public, four days early.

Now is my soul troubled. The verb is tarasso, and John has used it twice already for exactly this kind of disturbance — of Jesus at the tomb, where he troubled himself (11:33), and it will come again at the supper when he is troubled in spirit and names his betrayer (13:21). It is a strong word: agitation, churning, the state of water that has been stirred up.

Then the sentence that is the whole of Gethsemane compressed: and what shall I say? "Father, save me from this hour"?

The Greek can be punctuated two ways and translations differ. It can be a question he asks and rejects — shall I say, save me from this hour? No; for this purpose I came. Or it can be a real prayer, prayed and then answered by himself in the next clause. Either way the content is identical to the garden: a genuine recoil, and a genuine refusal to act on it.

What is worth having is that he does not hide it. He is standing among Greeks, disciples and a crowd, and he says out loud that his soul is in turmoil. There is no attempt to present a settled face.

Which is worth a great deal to anyone who has assumed that faith means equanimity, or that being troubled about something God has clearly appointed is itself a failure. Here is the Son of God, entirely certain of the Father's will, entirely committed to it, and churned up about it — and the trouble does not weaken the obedience by so much as a syllable.

And note the two things he says about servants just before it. Where I am, there will my servant be also — which sounds like a promise about heaven and, in this context, is first of all a promise about the road. The place he is going in four days is a cross. And then: if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. The honour comes from the Father, which is precisely the currency verse 43 will say the authorities preferred not to be paid in.

parallels.desc: Gethsemane

verseByVerse.quote: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, "An angel has spoken to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Father, glorify your name: the prayer is not for rescue from the hour but for the Father's name to be glorified through it. The Father's answer comes from heaven — the third direct divine voice in Jesus' ministry (baptism, transfiguration, here) — affirming that the glorification has already begun (in Jesus' ministry) and will be completed (in the cross and resurrection). The crowd cannot agree on what they heard: thunder or angel? The voice of God sounds different depending on the spiritual condition of the listener. Those who are the Father's hear it as address; those who are not hear it as weather.

The prayer is four words and it is the answer to the question he has just asked himself: Father, glorify your name.

Not save me. Not give me strength, which is what any of us would have asked for. He has just said his soul is churning, and the request he settles on has nothing about himself in it at all.

And the voice that answers is the only one in this Gospel. Matthew, Mark and Luke each record two — at the baptism and at the transfiguration — and John records neither. He has no baptism scene and no transfiguration. This is the single occasion in the fourth Gospel on which the Father speaks aloud, and it is worth registering that John saved it for here.

I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again. Past and future, and nothing in the present — which is exactly right, since the present is the hour itself. The Father is saying: everything up to now, and everything about to happen, and both are the same work.

Then the crowd, and verse 29 is one of the shrewdest observations in the New Testament.

Some said it thundered. Others said an angel had spoken. Nobody in the crowd reports hearing words.

Which is not a comment on their hearing but on what happens when God speaks into a room of people who are not listening for him. The sound was real — everybody agreed something had happened, and nobody thought they had imagined it. What they could not do was receive it as address. So it became weather, or at best a phenomenon: something impressive, safely categorised, requiring nothing.

That is still the commonest response to God, and it is not usually denial. It is reclassification. Something happens that does not fit, and the mind finds a heading for it — coincidence, psychology, atmosphere — and the heading does the work that unbelief used to have to do openly.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment of this world and the casting out of its ruler happen not at the final judgment but at the cross. The death of Jesus is simultaneously the condemnation of the world-system that operates under the devil's influence and the decisive defeat of the devil himself. Hebrews 2:14-15 explains it: through death Jesus destroyed the one who had the power of death. The cross appears to be the enemy's victory — he has arranged the execution of the Son of God — but it is in fact his defeat, the moment when the power of death is broken by the one who dies and rises. The hour of apparent defeat is the hour of actual triumph.

The first sentence is a kindness worth noticing: this voice has come for your sake, not mine.

He did not need it. The Son does not require audible reassurance from the Father, and had just said as much at the tomb — I knew that you always hear me (11:42). The voice was for the people standing in the road, which is the same reason he gave for praying aloud at Bethany. Twice in two chapters he tells a crowd that the visible piety is being staged for their benefit, and both times he says so openly rather than letting them think they are overhearing something private.

Then two of the largest claims in the Gospel, dropped into one verse.

Now is the judgment of this world. Not at the end of history — now. The judgement of the world happens at the cross, which is a strange thing to say about an execution, and it means that the trial in which the world condemns Jesus is the trial in which the world is condemned. Both verdicts are handed down in the same week.

And now will the ruler of this world be cast out. The verb is ekballo — the ordinary word for throwing something out, and the word used all through the Gospels for casting out demons. The exorcist's word, applied to the chief of them.

Which is worth putting plainly, because it is easy to keep the cross entirely in the register of forgiveness and miss the other half. Something was defeated at Calvary. Hebrews says it flatly: through death he destroyed the one who had the power of death, and freed those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb. 2:14-15). Paul says the rulers and authorities were disarmed and made a public spectacle (Col. 2:15).

The enemy arranged that execution. He entered Judas, and he got exactly what he wanted, and it turned out to be the mechanism of his eviction. It is the oldest pattern in Scripture — the thing meant for harm becoming the thing that saves — and here it is at full scale.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I am lifted up: the ambiguity of crucifixion (lifted up on a cross) and exaltation (lifted up to glory) is deliberate — both are the same event seen from different angles. Will draw all people to myself: the universal scope of the atonement's drawing power. Not all without exception will respond, but the cross's magnetic force reaches across every boundary — ethnic, cultural, historical — drawing those the Father gives to the Son from every tribe and language and people and nation. The cross does not merely make salvation possible; it actively draws. The drawing is the Spirit's work through the proclamation of the crucified and risen Lord.

This is the third and last of the lifted up sayings — 3:14 to Nicodemus, 8:28 in the temple, and here — and it is the only one where John stops to explain: he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.

Which settles the ambiguity by refusing to settle it. Lifted up is used in Scripture for exalting someone to honour (Isa. 52:13). It is also, brutally and literally, what happened to him: a man raised off the ground on a beam. John tells us the second meaning is intended and never withdraws the first. The exaltation and the execution are one motion.

Then I will draw all people to myself, and the guard is needed in two directions.

The verb is helkyo, the same one from chapter 6 — no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (6:44). It is a strong word, used of hauling a net (21:6) and drawing a sword (18:10), and it is the same drawing, now attributed to the cross.

And all people is, in the Greek, simply all — the word people is supplied by translators. Some have read it as a promise that every individual will finally be saved. It will not carry that: the same Gospel that records this sentence records that many walked away (6:66), that some die in their sins (8:24), and that the word spoken will judge on the last day (12:48), and a book does not contradict itself a few verses apart.

What the all means is made obvious by the situation it was spoken in. Greeks have just asked to see him. He has said the hour has come. All here is all kinds — the barrier is down, the outer court no longer marks the limit, and the drawing now runs to every nation on earth. It is the same promise as the other sheep of chapter 10 and the one flock.

And note where the magnet is. Not in his teaching, which they had had for three years, and not in his miracles, which the council conceded and used against him. In the cross. The thing that draws is a man being executed, and it is precisely at his most powerless that he says he will pull the world in.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: So the crowd answered him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?" So Jesus said to them, "The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd's theological objection is real: if the Messiah remains forever, how can he be lifted up in death? They understand the finality of death but not the reality of resurrection — or the way that the 'being lifted up' is the pathway to the eternal reign, not its contradiction. Jesus does not resolve the paradox with argument; he responds with urgency: the light is present now; walk in it while you have it. The time for deliberation is running out. The darkness that follows the departure of the Light is disorienting in a way that those who have always lived in the dark cannot anticipate.

Their objection is a serious one and deserves the respect of being stated properly. We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever.

They are right, and they can cite it. The promise to David was of a throne established forever (Ps. 89:36); Isaiah's child would reign from this time forth and forevermore (Isa. 9:7); Ezekiel's David would be prince forever (Ezek. 37:25); and Daniel's son of man received a dominion that shall not pass away (Dan. 7:14). By the Law they mean the Scriptures generally, and the Scriptures are unanimous.

So the difficulty is genuine: a Messiah who is lifted up and dies has failed the one test they can name. It is exactly the objection Paul would meet for the rest of his life — a crucified Christ, a stumbling block to Jews.

And the last question is the honest one: who is this Son of Man? They have noticed that he has quietly substituted a title. They said the Christ; he said the Son of Man; and they want to know whether these are the same person.

He does not answer either question. That is worth sitting with, because it is the last exchange of his public ministry and he lets a fair theological difficulty go unresolved.

What he says instead is about time: the light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light.

The little while is about four days. He is not refusing to answer out of impatience; he is telling them that the season for standing about asking questions is nearly over, and that the light will shortly go out of the street. The urgent thing is not to resolve the paradox. It is to walk while there is enough to see by.

Which is not anti-intellectualism, and it should not be used as one. He answered questions for three years, and this Gospel records a great many of them. It is a statement about a particular moment, and about the fact that understanding can always be postponed and daylight cannot.

parallels.desc: his offspring shall endure forever

verseByVerse.quote: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light." When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sons of light: the goal of believing in the Light is not merely receiving illumination but being transformed into children of light — those who bear the family resemblance of the Father of lights. Jesus departs and hides: the withdrawal of the light creates darkness, which is itself a judgment on those who refused the light while it was available. They still did not believe — after the signs, after the teaching, after the raising of Lazarus. The inability to believe is not the excuse of insufficient evidence but the verdict of hearts that have hardened against the evidence they have received.

Seven words end the public ministry: he departed and hid himself from them.

That is the last thing Jesus does in front of a crowd in this Gospel. Everything after it is private — the supper, the disciples, the arrest, the trials. He has been teaching in public for three years, and it stops here, in the middle of a street, with a warning about walking while the light lasts, and then he is gone.

John has used that sentence before, at the end of chapter 8, and both times it follows a moment when the light has been offered and refused. There is nothing dramatic about the exit. He simply stops being available.

Then verse 37, which is John's own verdict on three years: though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him.

It is a devastating sentence to write about the ministry of the Son of God, and John writes it flatly, without excuse. Water into wine, an official's son at twenty miles, a man off a mat after thirty-eight years, five thousand fed, a walk on the sea, a beggar born blind, and a man four days dead walking out of a cave. And the verdict on the whole series is they still did not believe.

Which disposes, permanently, of the notion that the failure of people to believe is a failure of evidence or presentation. Nobody has ever had better material to work with, and the material was not the problem.

And note the phrase in verse 36 that he leaves them with: that you may become sons of light. Not merely be illuminated — become children of it, take the family likeness. It echoes chapter 1, where those who received him were given the right to become children of God. The offer standing at the close of the public ministry is exactly the one made in the prologue.

parallels.desc: walk as children of light

verseByVerse.quote: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 53:1 — the suffering servant chapter — is cited to explain mass unbelief: who has believed our report? The question presupposes that many will not. The prophets anticipated the rejection; the rejection fulfills the prophecy. Therefore they could not believe: the inability is judicial, not mechanical — God has confirmed them in the hardness they have chosen. The arm of the Lord revealed is the gospel of the crucified servant; those who receive it are those to whom the Father has given eyes to see. The sovereignty of God in salvation and in hardening operates through the free choices of human beings without eliminating those choices.

John reaches for Isaiah twice to explain what he has just reported, and it matters which parts of Isaiah he takes.

The first is Isaiah 53:1 — the opening line of the suffering servant song, the chapter about the man despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions, led like a lamb to the slaughter. Lord, who has believed what he heard from us?

That is a question with an answer built into it: almost nobody. The prophet who was given the fullest description of the cross in the Old Testament opens it by asking who will accept the report — and the answer, seven centuries later, is a rejected Messiah walking away from a crowd.

So the unbelief is not a surprise, and it is not a defeat. It was written into the passage that describes the whole operation.

Then the phrase that troubles readers: therefore they could not believe.

Not would not — could not. It is the hardest formulation in the chapter and it should not be softened, but it should be read in sequence. Verse 37 says they did not believe though they had seen everything. Verse 39 says that at a certain point they could not. The inability follows the refusal; it does not precede it.

That is the consistent biblical pattern and it is worth having, because it is easy to hear these verses as though God prevented people who were trying. Pharaoh hardened his own heart through five plagues before Exodus says God hardened it. Romans 1 says three times that God gave them up — to what they had already chosen. The judgement is that a man is finally given what he has been insisting on.

Which is a fearful doctrine and not a mechanical one. Nobody in Scripture is ever recorded as wanting to come to God and being refused.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them." Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 6:9-10 — the commission scene where Isaiah is told that his preaching will harden — is applied to the Jews' rejection of Jesus. He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart: the divine hardening is the judicial confirmation of a direction already chosen. God does not harden those who would otherwise have softened; he confirms the hardness of those who have repeatedly refused the light. Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory: the glory Isaiah saw in the temple (Isa. 6:1-4) was the pre-incarnate glory of the Son. The prophets testify about Christ even when they do not know they are doing so.

The second quotation is from Isaiah 6, and it is the passage every reader of the Old Testament knows: the year King Uzziah died, the throne, the train filling the temple, the seraphim, holy, holy, holy, the coal from the altar. It is the great vision of the glory of God.

And the commission Isaiah receives out of it is the bleakest given to any prophet — go and preach, and the preaching will close their eyes.

Then John does something that ought to stop a reader cold. He adds: Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.

Whose glory? The him in the sentence is Jesus. John is saying that the figure Isaiah saw on the throne, high and lifted up, with the seraphim covering their faces, was the pre-incarnate Son.

That is one of the largest christological claims in the New Testament and it is made in a subordinate clause. Isaiah 6 says the prophet saw the King, the LORD of hosts (Isa. 6:5) — the covenant name, the God of Israel. John says he saw Christ. There is no way to hold both except the one the church eventually put into the creeds.

And there is something further in it. Isaiah saw him high and lifted up (Isa. 6:1) — and lifted up is the very word Jesus has used of himself three times in this Gospel, most recently nine verses ago, with John's note attached that it meant the manner of his death.

But does God harden people who would otherwise believe? Some read hardening only as God giving people over to the unbelief they have already chosen, as with Pharaoh. Others, with Romans 9:17–24, see God’s sovereign purpose behind the hardening itself. Scripture holds both: God hardens, and those hardened are responsible, for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God (v. 43). He never hardens a heart that is seeking him.

The throne Isaiah saw and the cross John is walking toward are described with the same verb. The glory the seraphim could not look at is the glory of a man on a Roman gibbet outside a city wall, and this Gospel has been saying so since the prologue: we have seen his glory.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah saw the Lord’s glory in the temple; John says that glory was Christ’s.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull
I saw the Lord, high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many of the authorities believed but would not confess: the faith that does not produce confession is a faith at risk. They loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God — the precise diagnosis Jesus gave in 5:44. Covert discipleship, while not impossible (Joseph of Arimathea will eventually act publicly), is spiritually dangerous: the pressures that prevent confession also prevent growth, and the faith that cannot be named publicly is faith that has not yet been fully tested. Nicodemus comes by night; eventually he stands by the cross. The trajectory of authentic faith is always toward greater openness, not greater concealment.

These two verses are the most uncomfortable in the chapter for the ordinary reader, and they need handling with some care, because there is a way of preaching them that produces despair in exactly the wrong people.

Take the facts first. Many even of the authorities believed in him — and the construction is John's full one, believed into him. He is not describing shallow admiration; by his own vocabulary these are believers. And they would not say so, because the synagogue ban of 9:22 was hanging over them and they had more to lose than a beggar did.

Then the diagnosis, which is the sharpest sentence in the chapter: they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.

Glory here means reputation — praise, standing, the good opinion of others. Jesus had put the same charge in almost the same words earlier: how can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? (5:44).

So this is not primarily about cowardice. It is about which currency a man is being paid in. The authorities were not lacking courage in general — some of them were formidable people. They had simply arranged their lives around a form of approval that Jesus was about to cost them.

Now the pastoral half, because there will be a reader who has not told his family, or his colleagues, and who has just read that he loves human praise more than God.

Notice who John names elsewhere in this category. Nicodemus came at night, and is named here in the same book that puts him at the cross with seventy-five pounds of spices (19:39). Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews — in John's own words (19:38) — and it was he who went in to Pilate and asked for the body when the twelve had scattered.

Both men are in this verse's category. Both came through. John records the failure and then records what became of them, which is his way of saying that a concealed faith is a dangerous condition and not a settled verdict.

Here is the test, and it is more useful than resolving to be braver. Ask what specifically would be lost — name it, precisely, not people might think less of me but the actual thing: the promotion, the friendship, the family dinner, the standing in a particular room. Then ask what it is worth, and whose opinion is being purchased with it. The men in verse 42 never did that arithmetic out loud. That is why the verse can describe them as believers and still be about their loss.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final public proclamation of Jesus' ministry (before the farewell discourse) is a summary of everything he has been saying: to believe in him is to believe in the Father; to see him is to see the Father. Jesus is not an alternative to the Father but the Father's self-revelation in human form. This is the heart of the incarnation's meaning: the God who could not be seen (1:18) has made himself visible in the Son. Faith in Jesus is not a human projection onto a religious figure but the response to God's own self-giving. The one who receives Jesus receives the Father who sent him.

The verb should be heard: Jesus cried out. It is a shout — the same register as the shout at the tomb and the shout on the last day of the feast. These are not quiet closing remarks. The last public words of the ministry are delivered at volume.

And their position is odd. He hid himself in verse 36; John gave his verdict in verses 37-43; and now, without any indication of a new scene, Jesus speaks again. Most readers take these seven verses as John's own summary — the case for the prosecution and the defence, gathered up and restated at the end of the public ministry, with the words placed where they belong rather than where they were said.

Which makes what they contain significant, because a summary shows what the author thinks the whole thing was about.

And what it contains is not a doctrine. It is a redirection. Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me.

Read flatly that is nearly a denial, and it is the opposite. He is saying that nobody who comes to him stops at him — that faith in Jesus is not a terminus but a transparency. Look at him and what you are looking at is the Father. Whoever sees me sees him who sent me.

Which answers a suspicion that has followed Christianity from the beginning: that Christians have got attached to a figure and lost God somewhere behind him. The prologue said no one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known (1:18). Here is the same claim in the first person, at the end, as the door closes on the public ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have come as light: the declaration of the Prologue (1:4-5, 9) is now spoken in first person by the Light himself as his public ministry closes. The purpose is salvation, not condemnation: I did not come to judge but to save. This is the first movement of the gospel — the Son came in love, not in judicial wrath. The judgment comes, but it comes as consequence, not as primary purpose. The one who hears and does not keep is not judged by Jesus directly; he is judged by the word itself on the last day. The gospel is simultaneously the most gracious offer and the most solemn warning in human history.

I have come into the world as light.

The prologue said it about him — the true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world (1:9). Chapter 8 had him say it in a temple courtyard beside the extinguished lamps of Tabernacles. Chapter 9 had him prove it with mud. And here, in the last thing he says in public, he says it about himself one more time, and adds what it is for: so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness.

Note the verb: not may escape the darkness but may not remain in it. It assumes where everybody starts.

Then verse 47, which needs holding together with what follows or it will be read as a contradiction. I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.

That is 3:17 again, almost word for word, and it stands at both ends of the public ministry like a pair of brackets. Whatever else is said about judgement in between — and a good deal is, including for judgment I came into this world three chapters ago — the stated purpose of the visit never changes.

The way the two fit is in the next verse, and it is the thing to carry away. He does not judge. The word does. A man who hears and refuses is not sentenced by a personal act of Christ; he is measured against what he was told, and the measuring happens on the last day, and the standard is a sentence he has already heard.

Which means the gospel is never neutral once it has been heard. It arrives as an offer and it stays as a standard, and there is no third condition in which a person has heard it and it is doing nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day: the words of Jesus are not merely historical utterances but active agents of eschatological judgment. The Sermon on the Mount, the bread of life discourse, the I AM sayings — all will stand as evidence on the last day. And the authority of these words is the Father's own authority: Jesus has spoken only what the Father commanded. Rejecting Jesus' words is rejecting the Father's words; the final Judge is the same one who offered himself in the Son. Mercy refused becomes the standard of judgment.

There is something worth sitting with in the idea that a word is the judge.

It sounds like a legal fiction until you notice what it does to the picture. Nobody stands before a judge who has private information about them, or hidden criteria, or a temper. The standard on the last day is a set of sentences that were spoken publicly, in Galilee and Jerusalem, in front of crowds, and written down, and have been available ever since in any language a person can read.

There will be no surprises about the criteria. That is the point of saying the word will judge.

And then he grounds the authority of those words where he has grounded everything: I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak.

The two verbs are slightly different: what to say and what to speak, roughly the content and the delivery. He is claiming that neither the substance nor the manner was his own invention.

Which is a strange thing to be the last claim of the public ministry. A teacher's closing statement is usually about what he has taught. His is that none of it was his.

And it makes the rejection in verse 48 a different offence from the one it appears to be. To refuse his words is not to disagree with a Galilean rabbi. It is to have been handed, by the Father, through the Son, a commandment whose content is eternal life — and to have set it down.

One further note on the phrase the one who rejects me. It means setting aside, disregarding — not arguing against.

Which fits the chapter. Nobody in John 12 has refuted Jesus. The council conceded the signs, the crowd could not answer the donkey, and the authorities in verse 42 actually believed. What the chapter describes is not defeat by argument but a decision to set the whole thing aside and get on with things.

That is how most rejection of Christ actually happens, then and now. Not a conclusion reached. A subject dropped.

parallels.desc: I will put my words in his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His commandment is eternal life: the Father's instruction to the Son — the mission, the message, the words — has as its content and goal the eternal life of those who receive it. What Jesus says is what the Father says; the word of the Son is the word of the Father. The public ministry closes with this reminder: everything Jesus has said, every sign, every teaching, every confrontation, every promise — all of it is the Father's eternal life reaching toward humanity in the person of the Son. The gospel is not the Son's independent project; it is the eternal purpose of the Trinity expressed in the Son's mission to the world.

The last sentence of the public ministry has a phrase in it that repays a long look: his commandment is eternal life.

Not his commandment leads to eternal life, which is what one expects and what most of us would write. The commandment is it. What the Father told the Son to say is not a set of instructions with life attached at the far end as a reward. The words are the thing itself, which is what he said in Capernaum when the crowd was leaving: the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life (6:63).

And so the public ministry ends where the prologue began. In him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4). Twelve chapters later, in a street, at a shout, with the light about to go out and the crowd about to disperse: I know that his commandment is eternal life.

Nothing further will be said to the world in this Gospel. From the next verse he is alone with the twelve in a room with a basin of water, and the only people who will hear him speak again in public are Annas, Caiaphas, Pilate and a soldier.

He talked to anybody for three years. Crowds who wanted bread, a woman at a well at noon, a teacher who came at night, men who picked up stones twice, a beggar nobody had ever addressed by name. He answered questions from people arguing in bad faith and from people who did not understand a word of what he said, and he went on doing it until four days before he died.

And the last thing he says to all of them, at the top of his voice, is that the message was never his own, and that its content is life.
