13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the night of his arrest, knowing that his hour has come and that he will return to the Father, Jesus takes a towel and basin and washes his disciples' feet — including Judas'. The enacted parable of servanthood precedes the verbal commandment of love. He who is Lord and Teacher makes himself the servant of all.

His own (v. 1). Having loved his own who were in the world uses the word from the prologue's saddest sentence: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11). There he had his own and was turned away; here, on the last night, he has his own again, and this time the sentence ends differently.

The towel and the cross (vv. 3-4). He laid aside his garments, as he had said he would lay down his life: the good shepherd lays down his life… I lay it down of my own accord (10:11, 18). And in verse 12 he puts them on again. The foot-washing is the crucifixion in miniature, acted out at a table. Note also the sequence: John gives him the largest possible credentials — all things in his hands, come from God, going to God — and the next thing those hands do is pick up a towel. Nobody still trying to establish his position can afford the towel.

How far down this was (v. 5). Modern readers hear foot-washing as a quaint courtesy. The rabbinic material is explicit that a Jewish slave could not be required to do it; it was work for a Gentile slave, a wife, or a child. The basin had been in that room all evening and nobody had touched it — and Luke tells us what the twelve were doing over supper: arguing about which of them was greatest (Lk. 22:24).

Peter's two errors (vv. 6-9). His objection is not false modesty — Lord, do you wash my feet? He is registering that the universe is upside down, and he is right, which is what makes him wrong. His difficulty at the basin and his difficulty at the cross are one difficulty. Then you shall never wash my feet — he is not hesitating, he is forbidding — and the answer is you have no share with me. Peter thinks he is defending his master's dignity and is refusing his own salvation, and the two look identical from inside.

One bath, many foot-washings (v. 10). Two different verbs: to bathe the whole body, and to wash a part. A man bathed at home before dinner and only his feet needed attention on arrival. That is the doctrine of assurance and daily confession in a household image — what happened at the beginning does not need repeating, and the walking still soils. (Some early manuscripts lack except for his feet; the sense is carried by the two verbs either way.)

Example, obligation, and the question of an ordinance (vv. 12-17). He takes the titles Teacher and Lord without a flicker — there is no self-deprecation anywhere in this passage. Whether verse 14 institutes a rite is a fair question: some churches wash feet, and they are obeying the surface of the text. The weight of the evidence is against it — the epistles regulate baptism and the Supper in detail and never mention this — and verse 15 calls it an example, a pattern. But the churches that do not wash feet are under exactly the same obligation and have a harder time discharging it, since a service can be got through in twenty minutes and this has no fixed occasion. And verse 17 puts the blessing on the far side of a gap: knowing is assumed, doing is not.

The heel and the Name (vv. 18-20). Psalm 41:9 is quoted with one clause dropped. The psalm says my close friend in whom I trusted; Jesus leaves that out, because he had known from the beginning (6:64). He was betrayed by someone he had never trusted and had kept beside him for three years anyway. And the reason he tells them in advance is protective: without warning, a betrayal by his own treasurer would prove he had been taken in. He gives them the true reading before the event — you may believe that I am he, the words of 8:24 and 8:28 again.
verseByVerse.theology: The foot washing is simultaneously a moral example (do as I have done) and a picture of the cleansing only Christ gives (you need to have your feet washed to have a part in me). Peter's characteristic resistance — then misunderstanding, then over-correction — clarifies both aspects: the washing Jesus gives is not merely a lesson in humility but the cleansing that makes fellowship with him possible. The once-washed disciple needs only the cleaning of feet — the ongoing renewal of those already justified, not re-justification. This is the distinction between initial cleansing (bath) and ongoing renewal (feet-washing): the one already clean needs only this.
verseByVerse.examples: You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am (v. 13). The authority of the foot-washing is its own argument. Jesus does not wash feet because he has forgotten who he is; he washes feet because he knows exactly who he is (v. 3-4). The servant heart flows from the secure identity: those who are anxious about their position never serve freely; those who know their position in Christ serve without self-protection. Genuine servanthood is not self-abasement but the overflow of a heart that has been secured by the Father's love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He loved them to the end: the Greek eis telos can mean 'to the end' (of his life) and 'to the uttermost' (completeness of love). Both are true: the cross is the temporal end of his earthly life and the absolute limit of love's self-giving. The Passover Feast: the lamb is about to be slaughtered; the true Passover Lamb is hosting his final meal. And already Judas has received the devil's suggestion — the darkness at the table, the night in the disciple's heart. Jesus knows it all and washes Judas' feet anyway. This is love to the end: unwavering even toward the betrayer.

Two questions arise as this chapter opens, and both are the kind a reader notices and then cannot un-notice. The first is the date. John says this happened before the Feast of the Passover, later says the authorities avoided the praetorium so that they might eat the Passover (18:28), and calls the day of the crucifixion the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14). Matthew, Mark and Luke, by contrast, present the Last Supper plainly as the Passover meal itself. So did Jesus die on the day the lambs were killed, or the day after eating the lamb with his disciples?

The tension is real, but it is smaller than it looks, and most of it dissolves in the wording. The word rendered Preparation is the ordinary Greek term for Friday — it is still the word for Friday in Greek today — so the day of Preparation of the Passover most naturally means the Friday of Passover week, not the day before the meal. And Passover was used loosely for the whole seven-day festival, so to eat the Passover at 18:28 can easily mean the festival meals that followed, particularly the one on the first full day. Read that way John and the others agree: the supper was the Passover meal, and Jesus was crucified on the Friday of the feast. A second solution has also long been offered, that different groups reckoned the feast a day apart, so that two observances ran back to back and both accounts are exactly right about different suppers. Either resolution serves; what should not be said is that John invented a date to make a point. He did not need to. Jesus really did die at Passover, and John's great theme — behold the Lamb of God — was handed to him by the calendar, not the other way round.

The second question is more surprising once seen. Where is the bread and the cup? All three of the other Gospels record the institution of the Lord's Supper at this table, and Paul had already written it down for the Corinthians. John gives us a basin and a towel instead, and never mentions the words over the bread at all. The most likely reason is the one that explains much else in this Gospel: John writes last, with the other accounts long in circulation and the church keeping the Supper every week for sixty years. He does not repeat what everyone has; he supplies what is missing. And he had already given the meaning of that meal, at length, in chapter 6 — the bread that came down from heaven, the flesh given for the life of the world. Having taught what the Supper means, he gives us here what the Supper requires: the Lord of glory on the floor with a towel round his waist, washing the feet of the man who was about to sell him.

One phrase in verse 1 reaches all the way back to the prologue and is easy to walk past: having loved his own who were in the world.

The word is idios, and John used it in his opening paragraph, twice in one sentence, in the saddest verse of the Gospel: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11).

There he had his own and they turned him away. Here, twelve chapters later, on the last night, he has his own again — eleven men in a room, and one who is leaving — and this time the sentence ends differently. He loved them to the end.

And the end of that love is the point of to the end, which will not decide between duration and degree because both are true. To the last minute, and to the last inch.

Then verse 2, which sets the temperature of the room. The devil had already put it into the heart of Judas. The decision has been taken. Whatever conversation happened with the chief priests has already happened, and the money is presumably already agreed.

So the man whose feet are about to be washed has, at that moment, an arrangement in place. He is not being tempted; he is executing.

Which is the fact that makes everything in the next ten verses what it is. John does not tell us about Judas afterwards, as an explanation of how things went wrong. He tells us at the top, before the basin comes out, so that the reader watches the whole washing knowing.
verseByVerse.note: John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17). “Simon’s son” is a different Simon from Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands: the sequence is crucial — because Jesus knows his authority and security, he can serve without self-protection. The servant heart flows from the secure identity; those who are uncertain of their status cannot truly serve because service threatens what they are still trying to establish. He rises, lays aside his outer garment, ties a towel — each action a voluntary divesting of dignity, anticipating the stripping that will occur at Calvary. The incarnation is itself the ultimate laying aside: the eternal Word divesting himself of divine prerogatives to take the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7).

The sentence is built to make one contrast and it is worth slowing down for.

Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands — and the next thing those hands do is pick up a towel.

John gives him the largest possible credentials in the same breath: everything handed over, come from God, going to God. Total authority, known origin, certain destination. And then a man gets up from supper and starts undressing.

The verb in verse 4 is the one to catch. He laid aside his outer garments — tithemi — and it is the identical word he used five times in chapter 10 about his life: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep… I lay it down of my own accord (10:11, 15, 17, 18).

He lays aside his clothes as he will lay down his life, and in verse 12 he will put them on again, as he will take his life up again. The foot-washing is the crucifixion in miniature, acted out at a supper table hours before it happens.

And the towel. He took a towel, tied it around his waist — what he is doing is dressing as a slave. He is now, visibly, in the costume of the lowest person in the household.

Which is the answer to a question people ask about service and never quite resolve: where does the freedom to do a demeaning job come from? Not from thinking little of yourself. The man in this verse knows exactly who he is — John has just told us in the most extravagant terms available — and that is given as the reason he can kneel. Nobody who is still trying to establish his position can afford to take the towel. Only someone whose position is beyond question has nothing to lose by it.
verseByVerse.note: Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave; roads were dusty and people wore sandals.

parallels.desc: I am among you as the one who serves

verseByVerse.quote: Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, do you wash my feet? — the question is theologically accurate: this is Lord, and it is inconceivable that Lord should wash feet. Peter's objection is not false modesty but genuine christological instinct: something is wrong with this picture. And he is right — except that the wrongness of the picture is precisely the point. The one who should be served serves. The one whose feet should be washed washes. The incarnation and atonement are both versions of the same reversal: the greatest becomes the least, the Lord becomes the servant, the one who deserves worship gives himself as ransom.

It has to be said how far down this was, because modern readers hear foot-washing as a quaint courtesy rather than the thing it was.

Roads were dust or mud; people wore open sandals; the same streets carried animals. Feet arriving at a house were genuinely filthy, and washing them was the job at the bottom of the household list. The rabbinic material is explicit that a Jewish slave could not be required to do it — it was work for a Gentile slave, or a wife, or a child. There were rabbis who said a disciple should do anything for his teacher except loose his sandal.

So there was a basin and a jug in that room, and there had been all evening, and nobody had touched them. Luke tells us what the twelve had been doing over supper: arguing about which of them was the greatest (Lk. 22:24). Thirteen men, one basin, and a dispute about rank.

Then Peter, and his objection is not false modesty. The pronouns in the Greek are emphatic and shoved up against each other: Lord, you — my feet? He is not being humble. He is registering that the universe is the wrong way up.

And he is right, which is what makes him wrong. Everything Peter's instinct is protecting is true: this is the Lord, and lords do not wash feet. What he cannot yet accommodate is a Lord who does — and within a day he will have to accommodate a Lord who is executed, which is the same problem at full scale. Peter's difficulty at the basin and his difficulty at the cross are one difficulty.

And there is a question the text leaves open that is worth asking anyway: in what order did he go round?

John does not say, and Peter's objection comes partway through — he came to Simon Peter, which implies others first. Whatever the sequence, at some point in that circuit he knelt in front of Judas, and Judas put his feet in the water, and neither of them said anything that John thought worth recording.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand." Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I do not wash you, you have no share with me: the washing is not merely ceremonial humility but the condition of fellowship. Peter's refusal, however pious-sounding, is a refusal of the grace that makes union with Christ possible. The foot-washing is a parable of the atonement: only what Jesus does — the unilateral cleansing from sin's defilement — creates the possibility of abiding with him. You cannot participate in Christ while refusing what he gives. The pattern holds across every form of false humility that refuses grace: 'I'm not worthy' can be a deeper refusal than 'I don't need it.'

Two things here, and the first is a promise worth keeping for a dark stretch: what I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.

He does not explain. He could have — the explanation comes ten verses later — and instead he asks Peter to let him proceed without it. The understanding is promised, and it is promised for later.

Which is the position a good deal of the Christian life is lived from. Something is being done that does not make sense while it is happening, and the assurance offered is not an account of it but a person's word that it will make sense in retrospect. John himself is the proof: he is writing this sixty years afterwards, and the afterward arrived.

Then Peter's refusal, and the Greek is as absolute as English can make it — a double negative with an eternal future: “you shall never, to eternity, wash my feet.” He is not hesitating. He is forbidding.

And the answer is the sharpest sentence in the chapter: if I do not wash you, you have no share with me. The word is meros — a portion, a part, an allotted share, the word used in the Greek Old Testament for a tribe's inheritance in the land. No part in me. No inheritance.

Which turns the whole exchange. Peter thinks he is defending his master's dignity; he is in fact refusing his own salvation, and the two look identical from inside.

Here is the test, and it catches a particular kind of good person. There is a refusal of grace that presents as humility — I couldn't ask that, others need it more, I'll manage — and it can be indistinguishable from reverence. The way to tell them apart is to ask what it protects. Reverence protects God's honour. This protects a self-image in which one does not need to be carried, and it will keep a man out of the kingdom while he is being admired for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus said to him, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter overcorrects: if some is good, more must be better. Jesus' answer distinguishes between the bath (initial justification, complete cleansing from sin's guilt) and the foot-washing (ongoing sanctification, the daily renewal needed as the justified walk through a world that soils the feet). The one already bathed does not need re-justification; he needs daily cleansing from the accumulated defilement of walking in a fallen world. You are clean, but not all of you: Judas is at the table, washed like the rest, but not truly cleansed — because the external washing has not been met with internal reception.

Peter swings to the opposite extreme in a single verse and it is entirely in character: if this is the condition, wash all of me.

He is wrong twice in ninety seconds, in opposite directions, and both times because he is trying to control the terms. First he will have none of it; then he will have more than is offered. What he never does is simply put his feet in the water.

And Jesus' answer turns on two different Greek verbs that English flattens into one. The one who has bathed — louo, to wash the whole body — does not need to wash — nipto, to wash a part.

The picture is ordinary domestic life. A man bathed at home before going out to dinner. He then walked to the house through the streets, and by the time he arrived only his feet needed attention. Nobody had a second bath at the door.

So: one bath, many foot-washings.

Which is the whole of the Christian doctrine of assurance and confession in a household image, and it is worth having plainly. What happened at the beginning does not need repeating. The justification is not renewed each time it is damaged, because it was never resting on the walking. And yet the walking does soil, daily and genuinely, and the feet do need washing, and pretending otherwise is not faith but grubbiness.

An honest note: some early manuscripts lack the words except for his feet, and a footnote may appear in a modern Bible. The shorter reading gives essentially the same sense — the bathed man does not need washing — and the distinction between the bath and the feet is carried by the two verbs regardless.

Then the sentence that darkens the room again: and you are clean, but not every one of you. Twelve pairs of feet have been washed. Eleven men are clean. The washing was identical and the outcome was not.
verseByVerse.note: Guests bathed before a banquet and needed only their feet washed on arrival.

parallels.desc: you are already clean

verseByVerse.quote: For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, "Not all of you are clean." When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, "Do you understand what I have done to you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He knew who was to betray him: Judas has received the foot-washing along with the eleven, but without the transformation it signifies. External participation in the means of grace — baptism, the Lord's Supper, the ministry of the word — does not automatically produce internal cleansing. This is the warning of the sacraments: they are genuine means of grace but not automatically effective apart from faith. When he had resumed his place, he asks the interpretive question: Do you understand what I have done? The teaching always follows the enacted parable; the Spirit always interprets the sign.

The two verbs of verse 12 close the loop that verse 4 opened. He put on his outer garments and resumed his place.

Laid aside, taken up. He has acted out the whole thing at the table: the descent from the place at the head of the meal to the floor, and the return.

And then, having done it, he asks a question rather than delivering a lesson: do you understand what I have done to you?

Note the order, because it is his method throughout this Gospel and it is the reverse of ours. The sign comes first and the explanation second. He turned water into wine before anyone knew what to make of it, fed five thousand before the discourse about bread, raised a man before he explained anything to the crowd. Here he washes twelve pairs of feet in silence, dresses, sits down, and then asks what they made of it.

Which is worth knowing about how God generally teaches. The experience arrives uninterpreted. The understanding is offered afterwards, and often has to be asked for.

And the answer to his question, at that moment, was almost certainly no. Verse 7 has already said so: you do not understand now. He asks anyway — not to expose them but to begin the explanation, which is the next thing he does.

Verse 11 is the one that should not be smoothed over: for he knew who was to betray him.

It is placed here, after the washing rather than before it, so that the reader is told twice — at verse 2 and again at verse 11 — that nothing about Judas was hidden. There is no possibility of reading this chapter as a story about a man who was fooled.

He washed the feet of a man he knew was at that moment under contract to sell him. The knowledge did not modify the service by one degree.

verseByVerse.quote: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are right, for so I am: Jesus does not modestly disclaim the titles Teacher and Lord; he affirms them. His servanthood does not diminish his authority; it expresses it in its highest form. Because I am Lord and Teacher and have washed your feet — the argument is from the greater to the lesser. If the one of greater dignity serves those of lesser dignity, how much more should the disciples serve one another? The foot-washing is both example and obligation: the way Jesus loves is the way his people are to love, characterized by the voluntary downward movement of serving those who cannot repay.

The order of the titles in verse 13 is worth noticing, because he reverses it in verse 14. They call him Teacher and Lord; he says your Lord and Teacher, putting the greater first for the argument he is about to make.

And he takes the titles without a flicker. You are right, for so I am. There is no self-deprecation anywhere in this passage — no oh, don't call me that. The man on the floor with the towel has just claimed both titles in front of twelve witnesses.

Now the question a reader is entitled to ask: is verse 14 an ordinance? Some churches have taken it literally and hold foot-washing services, and they are not being silly — the sentence says you also ought to wash one another's feet, and ought is a word of obligation, the language of a debt owed.

The case for taking it literally is that he says it plainly. The case against is that the New Testament never mentions the practice again — the epistles, which regulate baptism and the Lord's Supper in detail, say nothing about it — and that verse 15 calls it an example, a pattern, rather than a command to repeat the act.

The honest position is that the second reading is right and the first is not contemptible. Where a church washes feet, it is obeying the surface of the text and no harm is done. Where a church does not, it is under exactly the same obligation and has a harder time discharging it, because the substance is not a ritual with a towel but the willingness to do, for one another, the job nobody wants.

Which is the more searching form of the command. A foot-washing service can be got through in twenty minutes once a year. What he is describing has no fixed occasion and no end.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have given you an example: the word means a pattern or model to follow. The foot-washing is not a unique non-repeatable sacrament but a pattern of loving servanthood to be embodied in the community of disciples. A servant is not greater than his master: if the Master washes feet, the servants cannot consider themselves above it. The hierarchy of dignity that the world constructs is consistently inverted in the kingdom: the greatest serves, the first becomes last, the Lord takes the towel. This is not merely counter-cultural; it is counter-natural, requiring the Spirit's work in the community.

Two proverbs in verse 16, and both come back later in the farewell discourse with the comfort taken out of them.

A servant is not greater than his master. Here it means: if the master washes feet, no servant is above it. In chapter 15 the same sentence will mean something else entirely — if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (15:20). The proverb cuts twice: it puts a limit on how high a disciple can hold himself, and a floor under how much he can expect to be spared.

And nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him — the word for messenger is apostolos, an apostle. It is the only occurrence of the word in this Gospel, and it turns up in a sentence about not being above the job.

Then verse 15, which is the one that governs. I have given you an example — hupodeigma, a pattern, a specimen, the word for a model laid down to be copied.

And what is to be copied is stated more precisely than we usually notice: that you also should do just as I have done to you. Not something similar in spirit. The measure of the imitation is the original act, and the original act was performed by somebody with all things in his hands for people who were arguing about rank, including one who was selling him.

Which is why this cannot be reduced to a general disposition toward helpfulness. The pattern has specifications: it is voluntary, it is downward, it is done for people who will not repay it, and at least one of the recipients does not deserve it.

And there is a limit built into the second proverb that is easy to miss. Nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him cuts against a particular danger in Christian service: the servant who begins to think the work is his.

Everything an apostle has — the message, the authority, the commission — arrived from somewhere else. A man carrying a letter is not the author of it, and the moment he starts behaving as though he were, he has misunderstood his own position in a way that will eventually show.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you if you do them: the beatitude of enacted knowledge. It is not enough to understand the principle of servanthood; the blessing comes with the practice. I know whom I have chosen: the election of the twelve included Judas — not in ignorance but in sovereign purpose, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled. He who ate my bread: Psalm 41:9, the betrayal of a trusted companion, now fulfilled in the one who just received the foot-washing. The chosen betrayer and the Scripture's fulfillment are not in tension: God's sovereignty encompasses even the sin that will accomplish his purpose.

Verse 17 is one of the most exposed sentences in the Gospel: if you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

Two conditions, and the blessing hangs on the second. Knowing is assumed — he has just explained it, and they cannot claim ignorance. What is not assumed is the doing, and the blessing is attached there.

It is worth pausing on how uncomfortable that is for a commentary, and for anybody reading one. Every commentary ever written, this one included, is on the wrong side of that sentence. Knowledge about foot-washing is not the blessing. The verse specifically distinguishes between the two and places the happiness on the far side of the gap.

Then the quotation, and it is bitter. Psalm 41:9: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.

David wrote it about his own betrayal — the tradition connects it with Ahithophel, his counsellor, who went over to Absalom and hanged himself. Jesus quotes it about a man sitting at the table with bread in his hand.

And the phrase lifted his heel is a picture rather than an idiom: it is what a horse does before it kicks. Some hear also the shaking of dust from the sandal, the gesture of contempt for a place one is finished with.

Note what he leaves out of the quotation. The psalm says my close friend in whom I trusted, and Jesus drops that clause. He could not say it. He had known from the beginning (6:64).

Was Judas, then, chosen to be lost and so less guilty? Jesus chose him to be an apostle (6:70), not to be saved. Judas acted willingly, for money, and was fully responsible; Scripture foretold his act but did not force it (Acts 1:16). Jesus said it would have been better for that man not to have been born (Matt 26:24). God’s sovereignty and Judas’ guilt stand side by side, as they do at the cross itself (Acts 2:23).

Which is its own kind of loneliness, and it is worth naming. He was betrayed by someone he had not trusted, and had kept beside him anyway for three years, and had just washed.
verseByVerse.note: Lifting the heel against someone is a picture of treachery.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: "I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am telling you before it takes place: predictive prophecy in service of faith. When the betrayal happens, the disciples will not conclude that Jesus was surprised or defeated; they will remember that he announced it beforehand and believe more deeply. This is the function of prophecy in John's gospel: not to satisfy curiosity about the future but to produce faith in the past. And the apostolic commission: whoever receives my apostle receives me. The missionary church carries the delegated authority of the one who sent it — to receive the gospel messenger is to receive the gospel Lord.

The reason he tells them in advance is given plainly, and it is pastoral rather than predictive: that when it does take place you may believe that I am he.

Think about what the betrayal would otherwise have done to them. One of the twelve, hand-picked, sells him — and if that had come without warning, the obvious conclusion is that Jesus had been taken in. A man who cannot see through his own treasurer is not the Son of God.

So the announcement is a piece of protective work done in advance. When it happens, the disciples will have a choice between two readings, and he has given them the true one before the event, so that the thing which looks most like a failure of his judgement becomes evidence of the opposite.

And what he says they will believe is that I am he — the words of 8:24 and 8:28 again. The claim, laid down once more, at supper, attached to a warning about a friend.

Then verse 20, which looks like a change of subject and is not. Whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.

He has been talking about a man who was sent and went wrong. Now he tells the other eleven what it will mean when they are sent — that the chain runs unbroken from the Father through the Son to them, and that how people treat them is how they are treating him.

It is an extraordinary thing to say to eleven men who will all run away before the night is out.

And there is a real dignity conferred in verse 20 that should not be lost under the betrayal material surrounding it.

The chain he describes runs Father — Son — apostle, and it runs unbroken. What a person does with the messenger, he is doing with the one who sent him, all the way up.

Which is a startling weight to place on eleven fishermen and tradesmen, and it is placed on them the same night one of their number sells him and another denies him. He does not wait until they have proved reliable.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe that I am he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — The Betrayer Exposed and the New Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus announces that one of the twelve will betray him; the beloved disciple asks who; Jesus identifies Judas with a morsel of bread, who immediately goes out — and it is night. Jesus then announces the new commandment: love one another as I have loved you. Peter's confident declaration of loyalty is met with the prediction of triple denial.

Nobody could tell (vv. 21-22). This is the third time John uses tarasso of him — at the tomb (11:33), in the temple (12:27), and now. But verse 22 is the remarkable one: he says one of you will betray me, and eleven men look at each other with no idea who is meant. Judas had kept the bag for years and been stealing from it the whole time (12:6), and not one of the men who slept in the same rooms had a suspicion. Matthew adds that each of them asked is it I, Lord? — they looked inward rather than around the room, which is the healthier reflex and the one Judas never had.

In the bosom (v. 23). The ESV margin gives the phrase as in the bosom of Jesus, and John has used it once before, in the prologue's last sentence about the Son: God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known (1:18), where the Greek has in the bosom of the Father. The Gospel's opening picture is reproduced at the supper table with a man in the Son's place — and that man is the one who wrote it down. He tells us who Jesus is because he was lying against him when he found out. This is also the first appearance of the disciple whom Jesus loved, who never uses his own name and records about himself only that he was loved.

The seating plan (vv. 25-26). Guests reclined on their left elbows, so the man on Jesus' right leaned back against his chest — which is where the beloved disciple is. And Jesus hands the morsel to Judas without getting up, which puts Judas within arm's reach on the other side, in the place of highest honour. The two men closest to him at that supper were the disciple he loved and the man who had already sold him, one on each side. And the morsel is not an accusation but a courtesy — a host singling a guest out for favour — which is exactly why nobody understands what has happened when Judas leaves. All they saw was a kindness, and it was the last thing Jesus ever gave him.

Satan entered (v. 27). The only use of that name in the whole Gospel, and the timing is exact: after the morsel. Verse 2 said the devil had put the idea into his heart; verse 27 says he entered. Between the two lie a washing and a piece of bread, both received, neither opening anything. And do quickly is a release with the timing attached — Judas thinks he is running an operation, and the arrest happens on the night Jesus intends to die rather than any of the other nights available.

The cover story (v. 29). The disciples assume he has gone to buy for the feast or to give to the poor — the second being the very cause he had championed over Mary's ointment. Betrayal generally leaves a room not with a slammed door but with a plausible explanation nobody has reason to doubt.

Now is the Son of Man glorified (vv. 31-32). The pivot of the evening. Note the first three words: when he had gone out. The whole farewell discourse begins the moment the door shuts behind Judas, and none of it was said in his hearing. And Jesus greets the start of the worst night in history by announcing that his glory has begun — now, with the arrest hours away. The verb appears five times in two verses. The claim is not that God brought good out of a terrible thing afterwards; it is that the dying itself is the glory.

Little children (v. 33). Teknia, a diminutive, used only here in the Gospel — and seven times in John's first letter sixty years later, so he kept it. And where I am going you cannot come is the sentence he had used to the men who wanted him dead (7:34; 8:21), now turned to his friends, with the difference that for them it is temporary.

By this all people will know (v. 35). The most quoted verse in the chapter and it was not in the summary. Notice what he did not choose as the badge: not doctrine, not moral rigour, not miracles, not numbers. And the test is one an outsider can apply with no theological equipment at all — he hands the world a criterion and invites it to use it, which has been both the church's vindication and its humiliation. He knew what he was risking and said it anyway.
verseByVerse.theology: Love one another as I have loved you is the social ethics of the atonement made into community commandment. The 'as I have loved you' is the measure and the model: not abstract love or sentiment, but the costly, self-giving, foot-washing, cross-bearing love that Jesus has just demonstrated and is about to complete. This is a new commandment not because love was absent from the Mosaic law (Lev. 19:18) but because the standard is new: as I have loved you is qualitatively greater than 'as yourself.' The measure of Christian community love is the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The prediction of Peter's denial is embedded within Peter's most confident declaration. He will not only follow Jesus but lay down his life for him. Jesus accepts neither the protest nor the probability: Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you — the triple denial will come before morning. Jesus does not shame Peter but tells the truth that Peter needs to hear: his fidelity rests on a foundation Peter has not yet tested. The testing will come, the failure will happen, and the restoration that follows (ch. 21) will be built on a more honest foundation than confidence ever was.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, "Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was troubled in his spirit: the same word as at the tomb of Lazarus — genuine inner disturbance at the proximity of evil and death. The announcement — one of you — is devastating in its application. One of the twelve: the betrayer is not a stranger but a companion of the table. Uncertain of whom he spoke: the disciples cannot identify the traitor, which is itself a comment on the subtlety of Judas' performance. He has been indistinguishable from the rest in his outward discipleship. The traitor in the community is never obviously different until the betrayal occurs.

This is the third time John uses this verb of him, and the three occurrences map the whole approach of the cross.

At the tomb of Lazarus he was greatly troubled (11:33). In the temple courts, when the Greeks came: now is my soul troubled (12:27). And now, at the table: troubled in his spirit. Each time it is agitation, churning, and each time it is provoked by death: somebody else's, then his own, and now the man who will arrange it.

What is remarkable is verse 22 rather than verse 21. He says one of you will betray me, and eleven men look at each other with no idea who is meant.

Judas had been the treasurer for years. He had been stealing from the bag the whole time (12:6). He had gone to the chief priests, taken money, and come back to supper. And not one of the men who had lived on the road with him, slept in the same rooms, eaten every meal with him, had the faintest suspicion.

Matthew records that they each asked is it I, Lord? — which is the other half of the same fact. Nobody could point at Judas, and every one of them was uncertain enough about himself to ask.

That is worth having in both directions. A man can be indistinguishable from a disciple for years — not by clever acting, but by doing the same things and going to the same places — and be nothing of the kind. And the disciples' instinct, when told there was a traitor at the table, was to look inward rather than around the room. It is the healthier reflex, and the one Judas never had.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus' side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beloved disciple — John, typically understood — reclines closest to Jesus at the Passover posture, at his side. Peter, always the spokesman, uses his proximity through the beloved disciple: find out. The beloved disciple's position is both physical (next to Jesus) and relational (the model of the disciple who receives and believes). Peter, who will soon fail most visibly, organizes the inquiry; John, who will stand at the cross, is already in the place of intimate witness. Their roles at this supper anticipate their roles in the passion narrative.

The phrase John uses for where this disciple was sitting is worth having, because he has used it once before and only once.

Reclining at table at Jesus' side — the ESV margin gives the Greek as in the bosom of Jesus. The posture is ordinary enough at a formal meal: guests lay on their left elbows around a low table, so the man to Jesus' right had his head more or less at his chest, and could lean back to speak privately.

But the last time John wrote those words was in the prologue's final sentence, about the Son: God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known (1:18), where the Greek has in the bosom of the Father.

Same phrase. So the Gospel's opening picture of the Son against the Father's heart is reproduced at the supper table, with a man in the Son's place — and the man is the one who will write it all down. He tells us who Jesus is because he was lying against him when he found out.

This is also the first appearance of the disciple whom Jesus loved, a title that will recur and never be attached to a name. He is at the supper, at the cross (19:26), at the tomb (20:2), on the beach (21:7), and named at the end as the one who wrote these things (21:24). Early church tradition identified him as John, and nothing in the book contradicts it.

Note the modesty of the arrangement. He never uses his own name. What he does record about himself is that he was loved — which is either the most self-effacing or the most confident thing a writer could say, and probably both.

And Peter is doing what Peter does: he cannot get at the information himself, so he signals to the man who can. It is characteristic of the pair throughout this Gospel. Peter acts; John sees.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow; the one on the host’s right lay with his head near the host’s chest. The disciple “whom Jesus loved” is traditionally identified as John, the Gospel’s author.

verseByVerse.quote: So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, "Lord, who is it?" Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dipped morsel given to Judas is a gesture of honor — the host giving a choice piece to a guest — and simultaneously the identification of the betrayer. Jesus honors the one who will betray him with the gesture of distinction. Love to the end means that even the identification of the traitor is performed through an act of love, not contempt. Judas receives the morsel that names him and seals him; the sacramental gesture (bread given, bread received) is a bitter parody of what it could have been. Grace offered and refused becomes the occasion of judgment.

There is something in the seating plan that most readers never see, and it changes the scene.

At a formal meal the guests reclined on their left sides around a low three-sided table. The host was not at the head but at a defined position, and the place of highest honour was immediately to his left — close enough that the host could reach it without effort.

Now: the beloved disciple is on Jesus' right, since he leans back against his chest to ask the question. And Jesus hands the morsel to Judas without any indication of getting up or passing it along.

Which puts Judas within arm's reach on the other side — in the place of honour.

Whether or not that seating was deliberate, it means the two men closest to Jesus at that supper were the disciple he loved and the man who had already sold him, one on each side.

And the morsel itself is not a mark of guilt. Dipping a piece of bread in the common dish and handing it to a particular guest was a courtesy — a host singling somebody out for favour, the equivalent of serving him first. There are cultures where it is still done.

So the identification of the betrayer is made by an act of hospitality. Nobody else at the table registers it as an accusation, which is exactly why they do not understand what has happened when Judas leaves. All they saw was a kindness.

Consider what that gesture was. Jesus knew everything — the arrangement, the money, the hour — and what he does with the knowledge is offer the man the best piece of bread. There is no scene, no denunciation, no naming to the room. Eleven men go on eating.

Was Judas present for the Lord’s Supper? Luke places the warning about the betrayer after the cup (Luke 22:21), while Matthew and Mark place it before, and John has Judas leave right after the morsel. Luke often arranges events by topic rather than strict order, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the bread and cup were shared.

It is the last thing he ever gives him.
verseByVerse.note: Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan entered into him: the morsel accepted without faith becomes the moment of full satanic possession. Judas has been incrementally moving toward this since the complaint about the ointment (12:6); now the movement is complete. Jesus' command — do quickly — is not surrender but sovereignty: Jesus is not reacting to Judas's plan but directing its timing. The betrayal will happen on Jesus' schedule, not Judas's. The disciples' incomprehension (no one knew why) is part of the pattern: the cross is not understood until the Spirit interprets it through the lens of resurrection.

Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him.

It is the only time John uses that name in the whole Gospel, and the timing is exact: after the morsel. The last kindness offered was the point at which the door closed.

That is a solemn thing and it should not be softened. Grace refused does not leave a man where it found him. Verse 2 said the devil had already put the idea into his heart; verse 27 says he entered. Between those two is a washing and a piece of bread, both received, neither of them opening anything.

Then Jesus' one sentence to him, and it is worth hearing how strange it is: what you are going to do, do quickly.

Not don't. Not a plea, not a warning, not even a rebuke. A release — and a release with the timing attached.

Which is the sovereignty in this chapter and it runs under everything. Judas thinks he is running an operation. He has chosen his moment, kept his own counsel, and fooled eleven men. And the man he is selling tells him to get on with it, and he goes when he is told, and the arrest happens on the night Jesus intends to die rather than any of the several other nights available.

Nobody in the room understands. John says so twice — here and in the next verse — and it is characteristic: the most decisive moment of the evening passes in front of eleven witnesses and registers as nothing.

One more thing about the command. What you are going to do, do quickly is not permission, and it is not encouragement, and it should not be read as either.

It is the last word Jesus ever speaks to Judas, and it is a dismissal from the room — the point at which a man who has decided is allowed to go and do it. There is nothing in it of go ahead. There is a great deal in it of enough.

God does not compel anybody's betrayal. But there comes a moment when he stops preventing it, and this verse is what that sounds like.

verseByVerse.quote: Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, "Buy what we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it was night: three of the most ominous words in John's gospel. Judas walks out of the light into the darkness — literally (it is after sunset) and spiritually (he has left the presence of the Light of the world). The disciples' misreading — perhaps he's gone to buy food or give to the poor — is characteristic. The forces of darkness always have their cover story; the traitor always has a plausible explanation. Night falls when the betrayer exits; the darkness that John has been using as theological symbol throughout the gospel is now literal and personal. The ruler of darkness is about to have his hour.

The disciples' two guesses in verse 29 are worth pausing on, because they show how completely normal Judas seemed.

They assume he has gone to buy something for the feast, or to give something to the poor. Those are the two things the man with the bag would ordinarily be sent out to do — and one of them is the very cause he had championed so publicly over Mary's ointment (12:5).

Nobody thinks anything is wrong. The treasurer has been sent on an errand at night, which is odd but not sinister, and eleven men return to their supper.

Which is how betrayal generally leaves a room: not with a slammed door but with a plausible explanation that everybody accepts because they have no reason not to.

Then four words that are the darkest in the Gospel, and John puts them at the end of the sentence where they cannot be missed.

And it was night.

It is a statement of fact — it was after sundown, the meal was a night meal — and John does not write about darkness by accident. He opened the book with it: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5). Nicodemus came by night. Men loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (3:19). Jesus had said, on the way to Bethany, that the one who walks in the night stumbles, because the light is not in him (11:10).

And here a man gets up from a table where the Light of the world is sitting, walks to the door, and goes out into it.

Note that John does not say he went out into the night. He says: he went out, and it was night. The clause is left standing on its own, without comment, and it is the last thing said about Judas before the arrest.
verseByVerse.note: Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom.

parallels.desc: send portions to anyone who has nothing ready
the power of darkness

verseByVerse.quote: When he had gone out, Jesus said, "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now is the Son of Man glorified: the departure of Judas into the night is the beginning of the passion sequence, and Jesus greets it as the moment of glorification. The cross is glory — not despite its suffering but through it. The mutual glorification of Father and Son in the passion: the Son glorifies the Father by perfect obedience to the saving will; the Father glorifies the Son by resurrection and exaltation. And glorify him at once: not after a long delay but immediately — the resurrection is three days away. The certainty of the vindication is already present in the announcement.

The first three words matter: when he had gone out.

Not before. The great discourse of chapters 14 to 17 — the vine, the Spirit, the peace, the prayer — begins the moment the door shuts behind Judas. What follows is said to eleven men, and nothing in it was said in his hearing.

And what Jesus says at that moment is astonishing, because the situation has just become irreversible: the betrayer is on his way to the chief priests, and the machinery is running.

Now is the Son of Man glorified.

Now. Not on the third day, and not at the ascension — now, with the arrest a few hours off and the trial and the flogging and the nails between here and there. He greets the beginning of the worst night in history by announcing that his glory has started.

The verb appears five times in two verses, which is not accidental, and the movement in it is mutual: the Son is glorified, God is glorified in him, God will glorify the Son in himself, and at once. Father and Son passing glory back and forth across the cross.

Which is worth stating plainly because it is the thing most people find hardest to hold about the crucifixion. It is not that the cross was terrible and God brought good out of it afterwards, though that is true as far as it goes. The claim here is stronger: that the dying itself is the glory — that if you want to know what the weight and beauty of God look like, the answer is a man on a Roman cross taking what he did not owe.

Anywhere else, glory means the absence of humiliation. Here it is the same event.

verseByVerse.quote: "Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, 'Where I am going you cannot come.' A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children: the term of deep paternal affection, used only here in the gospel (though characteristic of 1 John). The farewell is coming. And then immediately: the new commandment. Love one another: not new in content (Lev. 19:18) but new in standard. As I have loved you — the foot-washing, the cross, the self-giving unto death — this is now the measure. The community of the Crucified One is called to embody cruciform love in its own common life. The new covenant community is defined not by ethnic identity or ritual observance but by the quality of love that mirrors the love of its Lord.

Little children. He has never called them that before, and he will not again in this Gospel — one occurrence, here, in the first sentence after Judas leaves. It is the sort of word an old man uses; and John himself will use it seven times in his first letter, sixty years later, evidently having kept it.

Then the hardest thing he has said to them: where I am going you cannot come — and he points out that he has said it before, to the men who wanted him dead (7:34; 8:21). The same sentence, now turned to his friends, with the difference that for them it is temporary.

And into that — the announcement of separation — comes the commandment.

The obvious question is what is new about it. Loving one another is not an innovation; Leviticus 19:18 had said you shall love your neighbor as yourself, and Jesus had already called it the second greatest commandment (Matt. 22:39).

The newness is in the standard, and it is in the words at the centre: just as I have loved you.

Leviticus gave a measure that everybody carries with them — as yourself. It is a real standard and a demanding one, and it has the advantage of being always available for comparison. What replaces it here is a measure outside the self altogether, and one that has just been demonstrated on the floor with a basin, and will be demonstrated again tomorrow afternoon.

Which raises the bar past anything achievable by effort. As yourself can be attempted. As I have loved you cannot be attempted at all in the ordinary sense; it can only be received first and then passed on, which is why the vine comes in chapter 15 and the Spirit in chapter 14. The commandment is impossible on purpose, and the rest of the discourse is the provision for it.
verseByVerse.note: Love of neighbour was old; the new standard is “as I have loved you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered him, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this all people will know: the public witness of the church is its love. Not its doctrine alone, not its correct theology, not its moral achievement — the love that mirrors the cross is the testimony that cannot be fabricated. The world can argue with theology; it has no argument against a community that genuinely loves the unlovable, forgives the unforgivable, serves the unworthy. You will follow afterward: Peter will eventually follow Jesus into death — tradition records his crucifixion in Rome. The 'not now' is not permanent exclusion but postponement; the cross that separates them now will be the path Peter himself eventually walks.

He names the badge, and it is worth noticing what he did not choose.

Not doctrine, though he cared enormously about truth and this Gospel is the most doctrinally dense of the four. Not moral rigour. Not miracles, though there had been plenty and there would be more. Not numbers, not buildings, not learning, not zeal.

By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.

And the test he sets is one an outsider can apply without any theological equipment at all. That is the force of all people. He is handing the world a criterion and inviting it to use it.

Which has been, historically, both the church's great vindication and its great humiliation, and honesty requires saying both. Tertullian could report pagans saying see how these Christians love one another, and the early church's care for its poor and its plague victims was noticed across the empire and is one reason it grew. And the same church has produced schisms, wars, and congregations where the coldness is obvious to any visitor within ten minutes.

He knew what he was risking. The sentence hands unbelievers a fair objection whenever the love is not there, and he said it anyway.

Then Peter, who has not been listening to any of it. Jesus has just given the new commandment, and Peter's question is Lord, where are you going? He is still back at verse 33.

And the answer is gentler than his interruption deserves: you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward. Not a refusal — a postponement, and a promise. What Peter cannot do tonight he will do later, and John will collect on it in the last chapter, where Jesus tells him by what death he would glorify God (21:18-19).

parallels.desc: the death by which Peter would glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." Jesus answered, "Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will lay down my life for you: the same language Jesus used for the good shepherd (10:11, 15). Peter means it; he is not insincere. But he does not yet know himself. Jesus' prediction — the rooster, the three denials, before morning — is spoken not to shame Peter but to prepare him. When the denial comes, Peter will remember these words (Luke 22:61) and weep bitterly — the beginning of the restoration that will be completed in chapter 21. The prediction of failure is an act of mercy: it ensures that when the failure happens, Peter interprets it through what Jesus said, not through despair.

Peter's promise uses the exact words Jesus has used of himself. I will lay down my life for you — tithemi, the verb from the good shepherd (10:11, 15), the verb from laying aside the garments at the start of this evening.

He has been listening to the shepherd language and has taken it on himself. And he means it. That has to be said clearly, because Peter is usually treated as a braggart here and he is not: within a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed cohort in the dark, which is not the act of a coward. He was willing to die. What he was not able to do was survive a servant girl's question by a fire.

Which is a real thing about human courage and worth naming. Most people who fail do not fail at the point they had braced for. Peter had prepared himself for a fight and was undone by a conversation.

Jesus' reply repeats his words back to him as a question — will you lay down your life for me? — and then gives the detail: before the cock crows, three times.

And the specificity is the mercy. A general warning (you will fail) would have been forgotten or argued with. What he gives Peter is a marker so precise that when it happens there can be no doubt it was foreseen — and Luke records the moment it lands, when the cock crows and Jesus turns and looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps (Lk. 22:61-62).

Those tears are the beginning of the restoration, and they were made possible by this verse. Judas also failed that night, and the warnings he had been given did not bring him back; he went out and hanged himself (Matt. 27:5). The difference between the two men is not the size of the sin. It is that one of them had been told in advance and therefore knew, at the worst moment of his life, that he had not surprised the Lord who had washed his feet.

Which is the last thing said in the chapter.

And it is worth holding on to. He knows exactly what every one of them is about to do — Judas going out into the night, Peter by the fire, the rest scattering — and knowing it, he had already knelt down and washed all twenty-four feet.
