He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.<sup>5</sup>Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.<sup>6</sup>He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”<sup>7</sup>Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.”<sup>8</sup>Peter said to him, “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”<sup>9</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you.”<sup>11</sup>For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, “Not all of you are clean.”<sup>12</sup>When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done to you?<sup>13</sup>You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am.<sup>14</sup>If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.<sup>15</sup>For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you.<sup>16</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.<sup>17</sup>If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.<sup>18</sup>I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ’He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’<sup>19</sup>I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he.<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”<sup>21</sup>After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”<sup>22</sup>The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.<sup>23</sup>One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side,<sup>24</sup>so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.<sup>25</sup>So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.<sup>27</sup>Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.”<sup>28</sup>Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.<sup>29</sup>Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.<sup>30</sup>So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.<sup>31</sup>When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him.<sup>32</sup>If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once.<sup>33</sup>Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ’Where I am going you cannot come.’<sup>34</sup>A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.<sup>35</sup>By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”<sup>36</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”<sup>37</sup>Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”<sup>38</sup>Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.

14.title: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Way to the Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus comforts the disciples with the promise of prepared dwelling places in the Father's house, declares himself the way, the truth, and the life, and responds to Philip's request to see the Father with the most concentrated statement of his unity with the Father in the farewell discourse. Prayer in his name is grounded in this unity.

Let not your hearts be troubled (v. 1). The verb is tarasso, and John has used it three times already — every time of Jesus himself. He troubled himself at the tomb (11:33); now is my soul troubled in the temple (12:27); troubled in his spirit at this table an hour ago (13:21). So this is not a man telling frightened people to compose themselves. It is the only person in the room who has been visibly churned up three times in three chapters, and he knows exactly what he is asking. And the remedy is not an explanation but a claim: whatever trust they place in God, place the same in him.

Many rooms (v. 2). The King James mansions is a word that drifted — the Latin mansiones meant stopping-places. What is promised is not grandeur but room to stay permanently, and the emphasis is on many: there is no shortage.

I will come again (v. 3). The language is domestic — I will take you to myself, collecting somebody — not the vocabulary of a summons. And the purpose clause is the whole point: not that you may be in a good place but that where I am you may be also. Heaven is defined here entirely by a location relative to a person.

The way (vv. 5-6). Thomas is the only man honest enough to say he is lost, and his question produces the most quoted sentence in the Gospel. The three definite articles matter, and the last two explain the first: he is the way because he is the truth and the life. The exclusivity is not removable by softening the grammar — if it is not true it is monstrous, and there is no third position. But it says nothing about the merit of those crossing, and it does not address the question of those who never heard, which Scripture leaves joined at the seams (Acts 4:12; Gen. 18:25). Note where the sentence stands: it is not a boundary marker against outsiders but an answer to a frightened disciple asking how to get home.

Show us the Father (vv. 8-9). Philip is borrowing Moses' words — please show me your glory (Exod. 33:18) — the great unanswered petition of the Old Testament, refused at Sinai. And it is enough for us is right: it would be. The answer is that the request has been granted for three years and he has not noticed, which is why have I been with you so long? is disappointment rather than anger. Whoever has seen me has seen the Father forbids the very old suspicion that behind the kindness of Jesus stands a sterner God — a suspicion that survives in people orthodox on paper, who trust Christ and are afraid of God.

Greater works (v. 12). It is claimed too much and believed too little. It cannot mean more spectacular miracles; nobody since has fed five thousand or emptied a four-day tomb. Jesus gives the reason himself — because I am going to the Father — so it is a promise about what the ascension unlocks. The greatness is scope and effect: one man in one province becomes a message in Rome within thirty years, and Peter's single sermon at Pentecost converted three thousand, which nothing in Jesus' ministry did. The reason is that Peter could preach a finished atonement and a risen Lord, and Jesus could only preach a coming one.

Whatever you ask (vv. 13-14). Read as a blank cheque this is falsified by the life of every Christian who ever lived, including the eleven at that table — Paul asked three times and was refused, and Jesus asked for the cup to pass. The qualification is not in the small print: a name in that world was authority and character, so to ask in his name is to ask as his representative, which is why the purpose clause follows immediately. And something must be said to the person whose plainly good prayer was refused: Scripture never explains this, and any commentary offering a formula is selling something.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me is both comfort and exclusivity. Comfort: there is a way to the Father, it is real, it is accessible, it is Jesus. Exclusivity: this is the only way, and all other paths are paths that do not lead to the Father. The exclusivity is not arrogance; it is the necessary consequence of the incarnation. If God has come in one place, in one person, for one purpose, then there is one way home. The scandal of particularity cannot be removed without removing the gospel itself.
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do (v. 13). Prayer in Jesus' name is not a formula attached to the end of requests; it is prayer aligned with his character, his purposes, and his glory. To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as he would ask, for what he would ask for, in the way that honors the Father through the Son. This is why prayer in Jesus' name is effective: it brings human desire into alignment with divine will, and divine will always accomplishes its purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not your hearts be troubled: the command does not deny the trouble but addresses it with a double call to faith — believe in God, believe also in me. The foundation of untroubled hearts is not the absence of difficulty but the presence of the one who has said these words. In my Father's house are many rooms: the rooms, dwellings, suggest permanent, settled habitation — not temporary lodging but the permanent dwelling of the Father's household. The many rooms accommodate the diversity of those who will come; there is room for all the Father has given the Son. I go to prepare a place: the cross is the preparation, the resurrection is the completion.

The verb in the first sentence is one this Gospel has been using carefully, and it changes the weight of the command entirely.

Let not your hearts be troubled. John has used the word three times already, and every time the subject was Jesus. He was greatly troubled at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33). Now is my soul troubled, in the temple, when the Greeks came (12:27). And troubled in his spirit, at this table, an hour ago, when he named his betrayer (13:21).

So this is not a man telling frightened people to pull themselves together. It is the only person in the room who has been visibly churned up three times in three chapters, telling them not to be — and he knows precisely what he is asking, because he has just done it himself and will do it again in a garden before dawn.

The command does not forbid the feeling. It forbids letting it settle in and take charge.

And the remedy he gives is not an explanation. It is two imperatives with an astonishing claim buried in the second: believe in God; believe also in me.

The Greek can be read four ways, since both verbs could be statements or commands, and translations differ. But whichever way it is taken, the structure is the same: whatever trust they place in God, place the identical trust in the man sitting opposite them. Nobody in Israel could have said that sentence and remained a good Jew, unless it was true.

Then my Father's house, and one word in it deserves the reader's attention. The rooms are monai — and the noun comes straight from meno, the abiding word, the one that will run through the whole of chapter 15. A mone is a staying-place, somewhere one remains.

The old mansions of the King James is not a mistranslation so much as a word that has drifted; it came from the Latin mansiones, which meant stopping-places on a road. What the text says is not that there are grand apartments but that there is room to stay, permanently, in the Father's house — and the emphasis falls on many. There is no shortage.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: “if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you.” Family houses were often extended with rooms as the family grew.

parallels.desc: I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will come again: the parousia, the return of Christ, promised in the farewell discourse. The purpose of the return is personal — not merely to judge the world but to take his people to himself: that where I am you may be also. Union with Christ is the substance of eternal life; wherever Christ is, that is where the Christian belongs. You know the way: the disciples do not yet know they know it, as Thomas's question immediately reveals. The way is Jesus himself — they have been walking it for three years without naming it. The familiar is often the last thing to be recognized.

The promise in verse 3 has been read four ways and it is worth knowing which is likely, because a good deal of comfort depends on it.

I will come again and will take you to myself. Some have taken it of the resurrection, which is three days off; some of Pentecost; some of the coming to each believer at death; and most, rightly, of the return at the end.

The reason the last is best is the second half of the sentence: that where I am you may be also. The resurrection appearances did not accomplish that — he left again. Pentecost did not, in the sense meant here. What is being described is a fetching, and a permanent one.

And the verb for it is domestic rather than judicial: paralambano, to take somebody along with you, to receive them to yourself. It is the word for collecting a person, not summoning them.

Which is worth setting against the way the second coming is usually pictured. Most of the imagery that has attached itself to it — the trumpet, the sky splitting, the judgement seat — is genuinely biblical and is not what Jesus reaches for at a supper table with frightened men. What he says is: I am going to get a room ready, and then I am coming back for you personally.

Note the purpose clause, because it is the whole point and it is easy to slide past. Not that you may be in a good place. Not that you may be comfortable at last. That where I am you may be also.

Heaven is defined here entirely by a location relative to a person. Whatever else is true of it — and Scripture says a great deal elsewhere about a body, a city, a new earth — the reason given for the whole operation is that he wants them where he is.

Then the sentence that provokes Thomas: and you know the way to where I am going. He says they know it. Thomas is about to say flatly that they do not. Both are true, which is the point of the exchange — they had been walking the way for three years without ever having heard it named.

verseByVerse.quote: Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the way, the truth, and the life: the sixth great I AM saying of the gospel, and the most comprehensive. Way: the path, the road, the direction — Jesus is not merely the guide to the destination but the path itself. Truth: not merely accurate information but the reality that corresponds to ultimate existence — God as he is. Life: not biological existence but the life of God shared with humanity, the eternal life that begins now and continues forever. No one comes to the Father except through me: the most exclusive claim in human history, spoken by the one whose resurrection vindicates it.

Give Thomas his due first. He is the only man in the room honest enough to say he is lost, and his question produces the most-quoted sentence in the Gospel. Bewildered people who admit it out loud have done the church more good than confident people who do not.

And note the three definite articles, which English keeps but rushes past: I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Not a way, not one truth among others.

The three are not a list of separate titles. The second two explain the first: he is the way because he is the truth and the life. A road that does not correspond to reality leads nowhere, and a road that cannot carry you alive is no use either.

Now the hard half, and it should be met directly rather than managed, because it is the sentence that makes Christianity intolerable to a great many decent people. No one comes to the Father except through me.

Three things need saying, and the first is that the offence is not removable. Every attempt to soften this into Jesus is the way for Christians founders on the grammar. He is not describing a preference. If it is not true it is monstrous, and if it is true it is the best news there has ever been, and there is no third position.

The second is that the exclusivity is not a boast about the people who hold it. It is worth being clear-eyed here, because Christians have used this verse to feel superior and that is a straightforward abuse of it. What the sentence says is that there is one bridge. It says nothing whatever about the merit of the people crossing it, and the whole of this Gospel has been at pains to establish that they have none.

The third is the question everybody actually wants answered: what about those who never heard? And the honest reply is that this verse does not answer it by itself, though Scripture does. Scripture is emphatic that there is no other name (Acts 4:12), and equally emphatic that the Judge of all the earth will do right (Gen. 18:25), and it does not systematically join those two for us. What can be said is that nobody will be lost through a clerical error, that God is not less merciful than we are, and that the people worrying about this question are almost never the ones in danger from it.

What, then, does Scripture say? No one is saved except through Christ, and no one comes to the Father but through him. Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light of creation and conscience they did have (Rom 1:18–20; 2:12–16). Some Christians hope that God may save people who respond to that light without knowing Christ; but Scripture never promises it, and Paul’s argument is that faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Rom 10:14–17). Infants and those unable to understand are a different case, and there we may rest in the mercy of the Judge who will do right.

And notice what the sentence is doing where it stands. It is not a boundary marker put up against outsiders. It is an answer to a frightened disciple asking how to get home — and the answer is that the way is not a map or a technique or a standard, but the man who is talking to him.
verseByVerse.note: This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: no other name
the Way

verseByVerse.quote: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him." Philip said to him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on you do know him and have seen him: the disciples have been in the presence of the Father's self-disclosure for three years without fully grasping it. From now on — from this moment of declaration — they can understand that every encounter with Jesus has been an encounter with the Father. Philip's request — show us the Father — is the deepest human longing expressed in the most direct possible way. It is also the request that has already been answered. Like the disciples in the boat asking if Jesus is a ghost (Matt. 14:26), they are asking for what has been present all along.

Philip's request is the oldest and best request in the Bible, and he does not know whose words he is borrowing.

Moses had asked it: please show me your glory (Exod. 33:18). And he was refused — told he could not see God's face and live, and hidden in a cleft of rock while the glory passed, and permitted to see only the back. It is the great unanswered petition of the Old Testament.

Now a man from Bethsaida asks the same thing, and adds: and it is enough for us. He is right about that. It would be. If a man could see God, nothing else would be needed, ever again.

And the answer he gets is not a refusal. It is that the request has been granted for three years and he has not noticed.

Which is the point of the sadness in the next verse. There is no rebuke in it of the sharp kind — have I been with you so long? is the sentence of somebody who is disappointed rather than angry, and it is one of the very few places where we are allowed to hear what it cost him to be misunderstood by his friends for three years.

Note also what Philip's request assumes: that the Father is somewhere else, and that Jesus might be able to arrange an introduction. That is the natural religious instinct — the visible teacher is a means of access to the invisible God behind him. Everything in this Gospel has been dismantling it, and here it is again, in the mouth of a man who has been present for all of it.

And there is a promise in verse 7 that is easy to miss under Philip's interruption: from now on you do know him and have seen him.

From now on. Something changes tonight — not in what is available to be seen, which has been standing in front of them since Cana, but in their capacity to see it. The Spirit is promised nine verses later, and the whole of chapter 16 will say that the disciples cannot bear things now which they will handle easily afterwards.

Which is worth having for anyone who has read the Gospels a long time and found them flat. The problem is not usually the light.

parallels.desc: please show me your glory

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father: the most direct identification of Jesus with the Father in the entire gospel. The mutual indwelling — I am in the Father and the Father is in me — is the metaphysical ground of the moral claim: what Jesus says is what the Father says, what Jesus does is what the Father does. The Father who dwells in me does his works: the miracles are not Jesus' independent demonstrations but the Father's acts performed through the Son's incarnate presence. The unity of the Trinity is expressed in the unity of words and works.

Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.

There is no larger sentence in the Bible about the knowledge of God, and it is worth stating exactly what it does and does not claim.

It does not say Jesus is the Father — John has been careful about that since the first verse of the book, where the Word was with God and was God, and you cannot be with yourself. It does not say Jesus resembles the Father, or represents him well, or teaches accurately about him. It says that looking at the one is seeing the other.

Which settles something that would otherwise remain permanently open. There is a suspicion, very old and still current, that behind the kindness of Jesus stands a different sort of God — sterner, more remote, harder to please. It survives in people who are perfectly orthodox on paper: they trust Christ and are afraid of God, and they would not put it that way but it governs how they pray.

This verse forbids it. There is no God behind Jesus who is unlike him. The face that wept at a grave, and knelt with a towel, and did not break a bruised reed, is the face.

Then the ground of it: I am in the Father and the Father is in me. The mutual indwelling — later given the name perichoresis — is not offered as a speculation but as the reason his words and works are what they are. And note the odd division of labour in verse 10: the words he speaks are not on his own authority, and the works are the Father's, done through him. He claims almost nothing for himself in a sentence that claims everything.

Here is the test, and it is worth running slowly. Picture God. Not the doctrine — the picture that comes up unbidden when you pray badly, or when you have failed. If what appears is a face that is disappointed, or cold, or busy elsewhere, then something other than this verse is furnishing the image, and it needs correcting from a Gospel rather than from experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater works than these will he do: not greater in miraculous power (no one heals the blind and raises the dead more dramatically than Jesus) but greater in scope — the apostolic mission will encompass the world, bearing the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord through the Spirit's power. The greater works are the harvest of Pentecost: three thousand in a day, the Gentile mission, the planting of churches across the Mediterranean world. Because I am going to the Father: the ascension releases the Spirit, who empowers the greater works. The departure of the Son is the precondition of the greater ministry of the Spirit.

This promise needs working through carefully, because it is claimed far too much and believed far too little, and both errors do damage.

Start with what it cannot mean. It cannot mean more impressive miracles. Nobody in Acts or since has fed five thousand from a boy's lunch, walked on a lake, or called a four-days-dead man out of a cave. If greater means more spectacular, the promise failed immediately and has been failing ever since.

And Jesus supplies the reason himself, in the clause attached: because I am going to the Father. Whatever the greatness consists of, it is unlocked by his departure. So it is not a promise about the disciples' capacities at all. It is a promise about what becomes possible once the ascension has happened and the Spirit has come.

The greatness is therefore in scope and in effect.

In scope: Jesus in his earthly ministry was one man, in one province, speaking one language, restricted to whatever village his feet reached. Within thirty years of that supper the message was in Rome. Within three centuries it was across the empire. He is describing a work that would go where he could not, through people who could be in a hundred places at once because there were a hundred of them.

In effect: on the day of Pentecost, Peter preached one sermon and three thousand people were converted. Nothing like that happened in the ministry of Jesus. His greatest single day ended with a crowd trying to make him king and, by the following evening, almost everyone walking away.

Why? Because the cross had not happened yet. Peter could preach a finished atonement and a risen Lord; Jesus could only preach a coming one. The disciples' sermons were greater in the only sense that finally matters — they could tell people the thing had been done.

Now both guards, because this verse gets abused from two directions.

Against the overreach: it does not license a Christian to expect that he will personally do more remarkable things than Jesus did, and preachers who have promised congregations that have left a trail of disappointed and ashamed people behind them. The works in this Gospel are consistently the works the Father gives — they are not on demand.

Does this mean that miracles and healings continue, and that any believer may expect to do them? Continuationists read it so. But the greater works are the spread of the gospel after Pentecost, when more were saved in a day than in all of Jesus’ ministry. The signs that confirmed the apostles’ message belonged to the founding of the church (2 Cor 12:12; Heb 2:3–4), and have ceased. What continues is the greater work: people born again through the word.

And against the deflation: it is a promise, not a metaphor, and it was fulfilled in things that actually happened in public. Whoever believes — not the apostles, not the specially gifted. The ordinary Christian who says something true about Christ to somebody who then believes it has done a work that Jesus, in the days of his flesh, could not do, because the ground of it was not yet laid.
verseByVerse.note: “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after the Spirit came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever you ask in my name: the promise is anchored in the purpose — that the Father may be glorified in the Son. Prayer in Jesus' name is not a formula but an alignment: asking as Jesus would ask, for what Jesus would ask for, in the confidence that the Son's relationship with the Father guarantees the answer. This is not a blank check for self-interested prayer but an invitation into the Son's own posture before the Father — always seeking the Father's glory, always aligned with the Father's will. The promise is real precisely because it is bounded by the name that carries the character of the one who always did what pleased the Father.

This is the most quoted and most quietly resented promise in the New Testament, and it needs to be met head-on, because there is a person reading it who prayed for something enormous and did not get it.

Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do.

Read as a blank cheque, that sentence is falsified by the life of every Christian who has ever lived, including the men it was spoken to. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be taken away and was refused (2 Cor. 12:8-9). Jesus himself asked for the cup to pass and drank it. Every one of the eleven at that table prayed for things they did not receive, and most of them died violently.

So either the promise is false, or it means something other than the flat reading. And the qualification is not hidden in the small print — it is in the middle of the sentence, and in the clause that follows.

In my name. A name in that world was not a label but a person's authority and character; to act in someone's name was to act as his representative, within his commission. An ambassador can commit his government to anything the government would want and nothing it would not. So to pray in Jesus' name is not to add a few words at the end. It is to ask for what he would ask for, as his representative — which is why the sentence about the purpose comes immediately: that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

That is the boundary, and it is stated openly rather than concealed. The promise is unlimited within it and does not exist outside it.

But something must also be said to the person for whom that is cold comfort, because the honest difficulty is not the greedy prayer. It is the prayer that was plainly good — healing for a child, a marriage saved, a friend brought to faith — and that was refused, and the sufferer knows perfectly well it was the kind of thing the Father is glorified by.

Two things are true and both should be said. The first is that Scripture never explains this. There is no verse that accounts for why one good prayer is answered and another is not, and any commentary that produces a formula is selling something. The second is that the New Testament everywhere assumes the refusals are not indifference: the same Gospel has a man deliberately waiting two days while his friend died, and the family got more than they asked for and nothing like what they wanted at the time.

Note also the textual oddity in verse 14, which a modern Bible may footnote: some manuscripts read if you ask me anything, and some omit the word. If it stands, it is remarkable — prayer directed to Jesus, said by Jesus, at a table with Jews who prayed only to God.
verseByVerse.note: Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus promises another Helper — the Spirit of truth — who will abide with the disciples forever, teaching them all things and bringing to remembrance all that Jesus has said. He gives his peace and prepares them for his departure, explaining that his going to the Father is for their benefit and that his obedience to the Father's command is itself the world's instruction.

Another Helper (v. 16). The ESV margin gives Advocate or Counselor — a legal word, the friend of standing who stood at your side in court. Comforter is Wycliffe's word and has weakened badly; it meant strengthener. And John calls Jesus himself our advocate in his letter (1 Jn. 2:1), so the promise is not a substitute of a lesser order: you are losing me and getting one like me. And forever — they had him three years; this has no term on it.

With you, and in you (v. 17). Two prepositions mark the change of an age. The Spirit had always come upon particular people for particular tasks and gone again. What is promised is permanent residence in ordinary believers.

Orphans (v. 18). Bereaved children — the very picture of disciples whose teacher had died. He names exactly what they are about to look like and denies it. And the promise is not I will send help but I will come to you, which is the plainest statement that the coming of the Spirit is the coming of Christ himself.

Because I live (v. 19). The ground is stated as fact, not condition, and the disciples' living is parasitic on his. Which is where assurance finally rests: the question is not whether my grip will hold but whether he is alive.

Judas, not Iscariot (v. 22). One of the small human touches in this Gospel. There was another Judas among the twelve, and sixty years later John still cannot let the name stand without the note — a mercy toward a man who did nothing wrong and had his name ruined by somebody else. His question is not obtuse: if the Messiah discloses himself, surely that is public.

The word that turns the chapter round (v. 23). We will come to him and make our home with him — and home is mone, the same noun as the rooms of verse 2. He goes away to prepare a dwelling for us in his Father's house; the Father and the Son come and make a dwelling with us. The going and the coming are the same word, and this is the answer to Judas's question: the manifestation is not a display the nations could photograph, it is God moving in. Note the plural — we — and that the Spirit is promised residence in the same chapter. All three, taking up residence in ordinary people, which is the dwelling of 1:14 moving again.

Bring to your remembrance (v. 26). A promise about memory, made to men who had misunderstood almost everything and whose recollection was about to be the only record there would ever be. No notes had been taken. And the boundary is important: the Spirit brings no new material — both verbs are tethered to all that I have said to you — which stands against every claim of fresh revelation that adds to or contradicts these books.

Peace (v. 27). Shalom is simply how a Jew said goodbye, and he takes the pleasantry apart in the next clause. Note the verb: peace I leave with you — what a man does in a will. He is dying tomorrow and disposing of his estate. And shalom is not the absence of trouble but wholeness, which is why it survives the fact that most of the men receiving it would be killed.

He has no claim on me (v. 30). It is the metaphor of a search — the enemy arrives and finds no handhold, no debt, no old arrangement to call in. That is sinlessness in its most practical form, and it is what makes the next three days work (Heb. 2:14; 1 Cor. 15:56).

Rise, let us go (v. 31). And then three more chapters follow before anyone leaves — an honest puzzle, treated below. What should not be said is that a writer capable of removing a few words left a seam nobody noticed. And the words are not a victim's: nobody comes to get him. He ends the meal, opens the door, and sets off toward the garden where Judas knew to find him (18:2).
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (Parakletos — Advocate, Comforter, Counselor) is described with four characteristics in the farewell discourse: he is the Spirit of truth (14:17), the Holy Spirit who teaches and reminds (14:26), the Spirit who testifies about Jesus (15:26), and the one who convicts the world (16:8). Each characteristic is an aspect of the single mission: to continue and apply what Jesus accomplished. The Spirit does not bring new revelation beyond Jesus but illuminates everything Jesus said and did, making it present and personal to each generation of believers.
verseByVerse.examples: My peace I give to you: not as the world gives. The world's peace is the absence of conflict, the management of anxiety, the temporary resolution of problems. Jesus' peace is an interior stability that coexists with external trouble — the shalom of the covenant, the wholeness that comes from being right with God and secure in his love. Not as the world gives: the two kinds of peace are not on the same spectrum; one is the presence of order, the other is the presence of God. The disciples will need this peace before the night is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love me, you will keep my commandments: not 'keep my commandments and I will believe you love me' but the natural outflow of love producing obedience. Obedience is not the condition of Jesus' love but the evidence of the disciples'. Love and obedience are inseparable in the new covenant: the Spirit who is given writes the law on the heart, creating the desire to obey that the law alone could not create. Another Helper — another Paraclete, because Jesus himself has been the first (1 John 2:1). The Spirit continues the ministry of the one who is departing.

The word for what he promises has no good English equivalent, which is why translations disagree: Helper, Comforter, Advocate, Counsellor, and some simply transliterate it — Paraclete.

Parakletos means, literally, one called alongside. In ordinary Greek it was a legal term: the friend you brought to court with you, not a hired advocate so much as somebody of standing who stood at your side and spoke for you. Comforter is Wycliffe's word and it has weakened badly — it meant strengthener, from the Latin fortis, not somebody who soothes.

So the promise is not a substitute of a lesser order. It is: you are losing me, and you are getting one exactly like me. John will call Jesus himself a parakletos in his first letter, using the same word (1 Jn. 2:1), which confirms the reading — the Spirit is the second one because Jesus was the first.

Then the phrase that quietly outdoes everything they have had so far: to be with you forever.

They had him for three years and are losing him tonight. What is coming has no term on it at all.

And verse 15 sets the relation between love and obedience in an order that is worth getting right, because reversed it becomes a machine for producing anxiety. He does not say keep my commandments and that will prove you love me, which is how it is often heard. It is a plain future: if you love me, you will keep my commandments. It is a statement about what love does, not a test love must pass.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” “Another” implies one like Jesus himself.

parallels.desc: an advocate with the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world cannot receive the Spirit of truth: the natural mind is incapable of recognizing the Spirit because the Spirit's presence requires the new birth that creates spiritual perception. The disciples know him because he has been at work in them through Jesus' ministry; after Pentecost, the Spirit will be in them — a distinction between the external work of the Spirit (with you) and the indwelling gift of the Spirit (in you) that marks the new covenant age. I will not leave you as orphans: the fatherly concern behind the entire farewell discourse — Jesus is preparing, not abandoning, his disciples.

Two prepositions do all the work in verse 17, and the shift between them marks the change of an age. The Spirit dwells with you and will be in you.

Alongside, and then inside. The Spirit had always been at work — he came upon judges and prophets and kings, and rested on Jesus without measure — but he came and went, and he came on particular people for particular tasks. What is promised here is permanent residence in ordinary believers, which is precisely what Ezekiel and Joel had said would mark the last days.

Then the word in verse 18, which is more specific than most readers realise. I will not leave you as orphans — bereaved children, the very picture of disciples whose teacher had died.

So he is naming exactly what they are about to be, and denying it. By tomorrow evening they will look, to anybody watching, precisely like a school whose master has been executed: leaderless, frightened, with nothing to do but go home. He tells them in advance that the appearance will be false.

And the promise is not I will send help. It is I will come to you — which is either a change of subject or the plainest possible statement that the coming of the Spirit is the coming of Christ himself to his people. Everything in the chapter points to the second.

Here is the word for whoever needs it. There is a particular loneliness that belongs to people who have lost the person who explained things — a parent, a mentor, a pastor, whoever it was who made the world make sense. This verse was spoken to eleven men about to be exactly that, by the man they were about to lose, and what he promised was not a replacement but his own return by another route.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because I live, you also will live: the resurrection of Jesus is the ground of the disciples' life — both spiritually (they are alive in him) and eschatologically (they will be raised as he was raised). In that day — the day of resurrection, the day of Pentecost, the day of the Spirit's illumination — they will know the mutual indwelling: Jesus in the Father, they in Jesus, Jesus in them. The union of the Trinity becomes the template for the union of Christ and his people: the perichoresis of Father, Son, and Spirit has its analogical echo in the indwelling of Christ and the believer through the Spirit.

Seven words carry the whole Christian hope and they are worth taking on their own: because I live, you also will live.

Note the grammar. It is not if — the ground is stated as a fact, and the consequence follows from it and not from anything about the disciples. Their living is parasitic on his. Paul says the same thing in a sentence that is unanswerable if this one is true: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile (1 Cor. 15:17).

And that is where a Christian's assurance finally rests, which is worth saying plainly because most of us look in the wrong place for it. The question is not whether my faith is strong enough to survive, or whether my grip will hold. It is whether he is alive. If the answer to that is yes, the rest follows by the logic of this verse, and the strength of my grip has nothing to do with it.

Then the three-fold indwelling of verse 20, and the order repays attention: I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.

The chain runs from the life of God outward. First the relation that has always existed, between Father and Son. Then the believer placed inside the Son. Then the Son placed inside the believer. It is not a comparison — your union with me will be a bit like mine with the Father — but a series of nested indwellings, and the outermost is God's own.

And it will be known only in that day. Not tonight, and not by argument. They will find it out afterwards, when the Spirit comes and the whole evening becomes legible.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has my commandments and keeps them — loves me: the second iteration of the love-obedience correlation (vv. 15, 21). The repeated emphasis signals its importance: love for Christ is not sentiment but allegiance expressed in the pattern of life. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father: the chain of love — Father loving the Son, the Son loving the disciple who loves the Son, the Father loving the disciple — is the inner logic of the new covenant. Judas (not Iscariot)'s question is genuinely perplexed: how can Jesus manifest himself to some and not to all? The answer will be the Spirit's distinctive work in the community of faith.

The verb at the end of verse 21 is the one to catch: I will love him and manifest myself to him — make myself visible, show plainly, disclose.

It is a promise of something experienced rather than merely believed, and it is the reason Judas asks his question. He is not being obtuse. If the Messiah is going to make himself plainly visible, surely that is a public event — the whole point of the messianic hope was a disclosure the nations could not miss.

And John's parenthesis — not Iscariot — is one of the small human touches in this Gospel. There was another Judas among the twelve, called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark and Judas son of James in Luke, and by the time John is writing the name has become unusable. Sixty years on he still cannot let it stand without the note.

Which is a small mercy toward a man who did nothing wrong and had his name ruined by somebody else.

Now the chain of love in verse 21, and it is worth setting out because it does not run the way religion expects. He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him.

Read carelessly that is a transaction: love him, and God will love you back. It cannot be, because the same Gospel has already said the Father loved the world first (3:16), and John's letter will make it explicit — we love because he first loved us (1 Jn. 4:19).

What is described is not the beginning of the Father's love but its answering movement. Somebody who has come to love Christ finds himself inside the traffic of a love that was there before he arrived, and now flows toward him in a particular and personal way. Not a reward for loving. A response within a relationship that God started.
verseByVerse.note: This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We will come to him and make our home with him: the Trinitarian indwelling in the believer — both Father and Son making their dwelling in the one who loves and obeys. This is the fulfillment of the temple promise: God dwelling with his people, not in a building of stone but in the human spirit renewed by the Holy Spirit. The word heard is the Father's — ultimate authority, divine origin. Those who reject Jesus' words reject not merely a teacher's instruction but the Father's own word to the world. The stakes of hearing the gospel are as high as the source of the gospel is high.

One word in this verse turns the whole chapter round, and it is invisible in English.

We will come to him and make our home with him — and home is mone. The same noun, in the singular, that stood in verse 2: in my Father's house are many rooms.

So the chapter has two dwelling-places in it, and they point in opposite directions.

In verse 2 he goes away to prepare a mone for us in his Father's house. In verse 23 he and the Father come and make a mone with us. The going and the coming are the same word.

Which is a far better answer to Judas's question than a discussion of visibility would have been. How will he manifest himself to us and not to the world? By moving in. The disclosure is not a display the nations could photograph; it is the Father and the Son taking up residence in a person, which is a thing only that person and God can verify.

And the plural should not be lost: we will come. Father and Son together. In the same discourse the Spirit is given to be with them forever (v. 16) and to be in them (v. 17). All three, in the same chapter, described as taking up residence in ordinary people.

Which is the fulfilment of the promise that ran through the whole Old Testament and was never quite delivered. God dwelt in a tent, and then in a temple, and the glory departed from it in Ezekiel's vision and did not return. John said at the start of this Gospel that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (1:14). Now the dwelling moves again, into people.

Note also the condition, repeated for the third time in this chapter: if anyone loves me, he will keep my word. He will not stop saying it. Whatever else this indwelling is, it is not available to admiration.

parallels.desc: my dwelling place shall be with them

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said: the promise that grounds the authority of the apostolic witness. The disciples could not understand everything Jesus said during his ministry; the Spirit's post-resurrection illumination brought those words to life with new comprehension. This is the inspiration of the New Testament: not dictation of new information but the Spirit's illumination of what Jesus said and did, producing the apostolic witness that became Scripture. The Spirit who reminds is the Spirit who guarantees the reliability of the gospel record.

This is the first time in the Gospel that the full title the Holy Spirit appears in Jesus' own teaching, and the two verbs attached to it are worth separating, because they do different jobs.

He will teach you all things — and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.

The second is the more remarkable and the more consequential. It is a promise about memory, made to men who had spent three years misunderstanding almost everything they were told, and whose recollection was about to be the only record there would ever be.

Think about the position they were in. No notes were taken. Nothing had been written down. The teaching of Jesus existed, at that moment, entirely inside the heads of eleven frightened men, several of whom had already demonstrated that they could not follow a metaphor. Within a few decades they would need to hand on that teaching accurately to churches all round the Mediterranean, and eventually into books.

This verse is the guarantee attached to that. And John, writing sixty years later, is the standing exhibit: he reproduces long discourses, exact phrases, the smell of the ointment, the number of the water jars, what the seating was at a supper. Either he had a remarkable memory, or this promise was kept, and there is no reason it cannot be both.

Note the boundary, because it is important and it is often ignored. The Spirit does not bring new material. Everything in the two verbs is tethered to what Jesus said: teaching all things, and reminding of all that I have said to you. Every claim to fresh revelation that adds to or contradicts what is in these books has this verse standing against it.

Which cuts against a particular kind of enthusiasm and also against a particular kind of dryness. The Spirit is not a source of information beyond Christ. He is also not an idea; his work is to make what Christ said land in a person who has read it many times without it moving anything.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My peace I give to you: the covenant shalom, the wholeness of right relationship with God, given as a bequest from the one who purchased it at the cross. Not as the world gives: the world's peace is temporary, conditional, and dependent on circumstances; Christ's peace is rooted in what he has accomplished and cannot be taken by any external event. The Father is greater than I: within the economy of the incarnation, the Son who has taken the form of a servant operates in dependence on the Father. This is not a statement that the Son is a lesser being than the Father; it describes the place the Son has taken for the work of our rescue.

That sentence has done more service in the denial of Christ's deity than any other in the Gospel. It was the anchor text of Arius in the fourth century, whose teaching the Council of Nicaea was called to answer, and it is the verse a Jehovah's Witness is most likely to open at your door. The reasoning looks unanswerable at first glance: if the Father is greater, then the Son is less, and a lesser God is no God at all. Four things answer it.

First, look at what the sentence is for. It is not a concession wrung out of him in debate; it is a reason he gives his friends to be glad. If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father. He is comforting men who are grieving that he is leaving, and the comfort is that he is going home. Nobody offers a confession of inferiority as consolation.

Second, the word is greater, not better. Greater is the language of position: a king is greater than his son without being more human than he is, and a father is greater than the child who shares his nature entirely.

Third, and this is decisive, consider who wrote it down. The same man in the same book tells us the Word was God (1:1), that Jesus said I and the Father are one (10:30) and before Abraham was, I am (8:58), and closes his account with Thomas saying to him, my Lord and my God, uncorrected (20:28). Whatever John understood this verse to mean, he cannot have understood it to mean that Jesus was a creature, or he would have contradicted himself on every second page. A sentence must be read inside the book it belongs to.

Fourth, remember where he is standing as he says it. He is hours from the cross, in the days of his humbling, having taken the form of a servant — the one whom Paul describes in the same breath as being in the form of God and not counting equality with God a thing to be grasped (Phil. 2:6-7). A man on his way to be crucified saying the Father is greater is telling you where he has placed himself, not what he is. The old answer remains the best one: greater in office, equal in nature. And notice the tenderness of it. He is not lecturing them about the Trinity. He is telling frightened men that where he is going is better, and that if they loved him they would be happy for him.

One more thing about the peace, since it opens the verse and is easily read as a pleasantry.

Peace was simply how a Jew said goodbye. Shalom — it is what you said at a door, and it still is. So the sentence begins as the most ordinary farewell in the language, and he then takes it apart in the next clause: not as the world gives do I give to you.

The world's shalom at a doorway is a wish. It commits the speaker to nothing, costs nothing, and secures nothing — which is exactly what our own take care and all the best amount to. He is distinguishing a bequest from a pleasantry.

And the word he uses twice is worth noticing: peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Leave is what a man does in a will. He is dying tomorrow and disposing of his estate, and this is what is in it.

Then the shape of the promise, which is not what most people want. Shalom in Hebrew is not the absence of trouble; it is wholeness, everything in its right relation, and it is perfectly compatible with a storm outside. What he is bequeathing is not a quiet life. Within a few hours the men receiving it will scatter into the dark, and by the end of their lives most of them will have been killed.

So it cannot mean circumstances. It means that the thing which makes a person whole — being right with God — has been settled elsewhere and cannot be reached by the circumstances.

And then he repeats his opening command, with an addition: let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. The first half is verse 1 word for word; the second is new. He has been talking for a whole chapter and the fear is still in the room, so he says it again, and adds the word for what they are actually feeling.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. “The Father is greater” speaks of the Son in his humble human state, not a lesser divine nature.

parallels.desc: the LORD give you peace

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have told you before it takes place: the same purpose as 13:19 — predictive announcement in service of post-event faith. The disciples will endure the passion with greater faith because they remember these words. The ruler of this world is coming: the devil approaches through Judas, the soldiers, the arrest — and yet he has no claim on Jesus. He has no claim on me: the sinless Son is not subject to the devil's leverage. Sin gives the enemy his foothold; where there is no sin, there is no purchase. Jesus goes to the cross not because the enemy captures him but because the Father's love calls him.

The end of verse 30 is blunt: the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me.

It is a metaphor from a search. The enemy is arriving — through Judas, through the temple police, through the cohort with lanterns — and he will go over this man and find nothing belonging to him. No handhold, no debt, no compromise, no old arrangement he can call in.

That is the claim of sinlessness stated in its most practical form, and it is what makes the next three days work. Everyone else who has ever died had something in them that death could legitimately claim. Hebrews puts it as the devil holding the power of death (Heb. 2:14), and Paul puts the mechanism plainly: the sting of death is sin (1 Cor. 15:56). Take the sin away and the sting has nothing to inject.

So when they come for him in the garden, they are arresting a man over whom they have no rights whatever — and he goes anyway, which is the point of the next verse.

And note what he says he is doing it for: not because I must, and not because you need it, though both are true. So that the world may know that I love the Father.

That is a startling reason to give for a crucifixion, and it is the one he gives. The cross is many things at once — a ransom, a substitution, a victory — and here, at the door of the room, he names it as a demonstration of his love for his Father, put on where the world can see it.

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do as the Father has commanded me: the voluntary obedience of the Son is the world's instruction in what love for the Father looks like. The cross is not merely substitutionary atonement (though it is certainly that); it is also the supreme display of filial love — the Son doing what the Father commands because he loves the Father, giving the world a visible image of the inner-Trinitarian love that is the foundation of all reality. Rise, let us go from here: the departure from the upper room into Gethsemane, into the night where the ruler of the world waits. The Son goes forward in love, not in coercion. Let us go.

There is a real puzzle at the end of this verse and it is better faced than ignored, since any attentive reader trips over it.

Rise, let us go from here — and then three more chapters of discourse follow before anybody actually leaves. Chapter 18 opens with when Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron.

Several explanations have been offered. Some think chapters 15 to 17 were spoken on the way, in the streets and on the slope down to the valley — which is entirely possible, and the vine of chapter 15 has often been connected to the great golden vine on the temple gate they would have passed, or simply to vineyards on the road. Some think the material was assembled here by John from teaching given that night, without concern for the choreography. And some think they stood up at these words and lingered, which is exactly what happens when people are about to part.

What should not be said is that this is a seam left by clumsy editing that nobody noticed. The man who wrote this Gospel was capable of removing a few words if he had wanted to. He left them, and they are the last thing said in the room.

And the words themselves are worth having, because they are not the words of a victim.

Rise — the ordinary word for getting up. Let us go. Not they are coming for me, not it is time to hide. He is the one who ends the meal, opens the door, and sets off toward the garden where he knows Judas will bring the soldiers, because he told him to go and do it quickly.

Nobody comes to get him. He goes.
verseByVerse.note: Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way; others that they rose but stayed.
