15.title: The True Vine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus declares himself the true vine and the Father the vinedresser, then calls his disciples to abide in him as branches abide in the vine — the condition of fruitfulness. Pruning, abiding, and bearing fruit are the central images. The section closes with the commandment to love one another as Jesus has loved, grounded in the friendship that replaces servant-status.

Why "true" (v. 1). Every substantial vine passage in the Old Testament is a passage about failure — Isaiah's vineyard yielding wild grapes (Isa. 5:2), Jeremiah's degenerate choice vine (Jer. 2:21), Ezekiel's whole chapter on vine wood being useless for anything but burning (Ezek. 15), Hosea's vine that yields fruit for itself. When a Jew heard vine he heard a story that had gone wrong. And true does not mean truthful; it means real as against derivative — the genuine article of which the others were copies. So the claim is to be Israel. (Josephus describes a great golden vine over the temple entrance, which they may have passed on the road to Kidron; it cannot be proved and does not need to be.)

Two knives (vv. 2-3). The second knife falls on the healthy branch — both feel a blade, and the difference is what it is for. And the pruning sits beside a cleansing: he prunes it … already you are clean. The pruning is not primarily about yield; it is cleansing — and the instrument is named: because of the word that I have spoken to you.

What abiding actually is (v. 4). Abide occurs ten times in seven verses (vv. 4-10); nothing else is repeated at that rate. And it must be made concrete, because abide in Christ gets preached warmly and leaves people with nothing to do on Monday. The word is ordinary: it means to go on being where you already are, which is a relief: the command is not get in but do not go anywhere. And the chapter supplies the content rather than leaving it vague — verse 7 makes it verbal (his words resident, not visited), verse 9 relational (staying inside a love rather than earning it), verse 10 practical (doing what he said).

Prayer, again (vv. 7-8). The third prayer promise in two chapters, and the conditions accumulate rather than repeat. The mechanism is not a trick: a person saturated in what Christ said begins over time to want different things, so the prayers change before the answers do.

Abide in my love (vv. 9-10). The measure in verse 9 is the largest in the chapter and reads as a pleasantry: as the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. That is the love within the Godhead, from before the world existed (17:24), offered as the quantity. And verse 10 needs its guard: obedience does not purchase the love, as the following clause settles — nobody supposes the Son earns the Father's love by good behaviour.

My joy (v. 11). Extraordinary for when it was said. My joy — a joy belonging to him, being transferred — by a man who will be dead by tomorrow afternoon and knows it. So it cannot be a mood produced by circumstances. And the pastoral half matters: Christians who are flat are often told they ought to be joyful and conclude something is defective in them. Notice that the joy is his, is in them, and arrives by abiding. It is not summoned up, and it has nothing to do with being naturally cheerful.

Greater love (v. 13). It is carved on war memorials and belongs there. But he defines the ceiling of human love and then goes beyond it the next afternoon — Paul makes the point explicitly, that Christ died for us while we were still sinners, and while we were enemies (Rom. 5:7-10). His friends at that moment were not behaving like friends: one had sold him, one would deny him before dawn, and the rest would run.

No longer servants (v. 15). Weigh what has happened. In the whole Old Testament two men are called the friend of God — Abraham (2 Chr. 20:7; Isa. 41:8; Jas. 2:23) and Moses, spoken to face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exod. 33:11). Everyone else is a servant, and that was the title of honour. He takes it off them. And the reason is precise: the servant does not know what his master is doing. The promotion is a promotion in disclosure.

You did not choose me (v. 16). This inverts the practice of their world, where a young man chose his rabbi and hoped to be accepted; several of them had done exactly that with the Baptist first. And the purpose is a job, not a privilege — election runs straight out into mission, and the last word about the fruit is the chapter's keyword: fruit that abides.

What all of it was for (v. 17). These things reaches back over the whole chapter — vine, pruning, abiding, joy, friendship, choosing — and names a single outcome, and it is horizontal. Given a discourse on union with Christ, most of us would land on the vertical. He says the point is that they should love each other — said to men who had spent the meal arguing about which of them was greatest (Lk. 22:24).
verseByVerse.theology: I am the true vine: Israel was the vine God planted (Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7; Jer. 2:21; Ezek. 15; Hos. 10:1). Israel repeatedly failed as the vine. Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be — the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who bears fruit that lasts. The disciples are branches in this vine: their fruitfulness is entirely dependent on their connection to Jesus. Apart from me you can do nothing is the Reformed doctrine of total human dependence stated for the community of disciples. The branch does not produce fruit; it bears fruit — the distinction between human effort and Spirit-mediated connection.
verseByVerse.examples: You did not choose me, but I chose you (v. 16): the elective basis of discipleship. The disciples' following of Jesus is traced back to his choosing, not their decision. This does not make the disciples passive; they are appointed to go and bear fruit. But the initiative, the foundation, and the guarantee of fruitfulness reside in the one who chose, not in those who were chosen. Whatever fruit the Christian life produces is the fruit of the Vine, borne through the branches who abide.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the true vine: the seventh and final great I AM saying of the gospel. Israel was God's vine (Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7), repeatedly failing, repeatedly cut back. Jesus is the true vine — the faithful Israel, the son who does what the national son could not do. The Father as vinedresser: the pruning is not punishment but cultivation — the same care applied to the fruitful branch as to the unfruitful, though differently. The fruitful branch is pruned so that it might bear more fruit. Sanctification understood as divine pruning: God cuts away what is good to produce what is better, removes what is comfortable to make room for what is fruitful.

The force of true only lands once you know what the vine had always meant, and the record is uniformly grim.

Every substantial vine passage in the Old Testament is a passage about failure. Isaiah's song describes a vineyard dug, cleared, planted with choice vines, given a tower and a winepress — and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes (Isa. 5:2), and the vineyard is levelled. Jeremiah: I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate? (Jer. 2:21). Ezekiel devotes a whole chapter to pointing out that vine wood is useless for anything but burning (Ezek. 15). Hosea: Israel is a luxuriant vine that yields its fruit — for itself (Hos. 10:1). Psalm 80 is the one prayer among them, and even it is a lament over a vine whose walls are broken down.

So when a Jew heard vine, he heard a story that had gone wrong. It was the standing image for a people planted with every advantage who produced nothing worth picking.

And alethinos does not mean truthful. It means real as against derivative — the genuine article of which the others were copies, the same word John used of the true light (1:9) and the true bread (6:32). So the claim is: everything that vine was meant to be and never was, I am. The seventh and last of the great declarations, and it is a claim to be Israel.

There is also the possibility that they could see one. Josephus describes a vine of gold above the entrance to the temple sanctuary, with clusters as tall as a man, to which the wealthy added grapes of gold as offerings. If chapter 14 ended with them leaving the room, the road to Kidron ran past the temple. It cannot be proved, and it does not need to be; but a man saying I am the true vine under a golden one worth a fortune would not have needed to explain himself.

Then the two knives in verse 2, and a word about the first. Takes away is airo, which can also mean to lift up — and some have suggested a piece of viticulture here, since a fruitless branch trailing in the mud is lifted onto the trellis rather than cut. It is an attractive reading and it is probably wrong: verse 6 describes the same branch being thrown out, withering, gathered and burned, which is not what happens to a branch that has been tied up.

Can a believer be cut off? The branch taken away is one that bears no fruit at all, and v. 6 shows what becomes of it. It was attached to the vine outwardly, but never drew life from it; it is a professing, not a living, branch (cf. 1 John 2:19).

And the second knife is the important one, because it falls on the healthy branch. Both branches feel a blade. The difference is what it is for.
verseByVerse.note: The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine. This is the seventh of his “I am” sayings in John. Vinedressers cut away dead wood and pruned living branches hard.

parallels.desc: a vine brought out of Egypt
the vineyard that yielded wild grapes
discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you are clean: the cleansing of the disciples has already taken place through the word — the teaching that has been received and has done its purifying work. The foot-washing (13:10) and the word have accomplished the initial cleansing; now the ongoing condition is abiding. Abide in me, and I in you: the mutual indwelling is the condition of fruitfulness. The branch that is cut off — whatever its appearance or past — cannot bear fruit apart from the vine. This is the dependence that pride always resists and grace always establishes: apart from me you can do nothing, which means with me, everything.

There is a piece of wordplay between verses 2 and 3 that no English version can carry, and it changes the tone of the pruning.

He prunes it — kathairei. Already you are clean — katharoi. Same root. The verb for what the vinedresser does to a branch is the verb for making something clean, and John puts the two words in consecutive sentences.

Which means the pruning is not primarily about productivity, as a modern reader assumes — trimming to increase yield. It is cleansing. The blade takes off what is diseased or dead or simply in the way, and what is left is clean.

And the instrument of it is named: because of the word that I have spoken to you. The knife is what he says. That is worth pausing on, because it locates the pruning somewhere unexpected — not primarily in circumstances, though God certainly uses those, but in the word landing on a person and taking something off them.

Now the command, and it is the keyword of the chapter: abide. It occurs ten times in seven verses (vv. 4-10). Nothing else in the discourse is repeated at that rate.

And it has to be made concrete, because abide in Christ is one of those phrases that gets preached warmly and leaves people with nothing to do on Monday.

Start with what the word means. It is not a mystical exercise. Meno is the ordinary word for staying — the disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed with him (1:38-39); he stayed two days in Samaria (4:40); he remained beyond the Jordan (10:40). It means to go on being where you already are.

Which is the first thing to say, and it is a relief. The command is not get in. The branches are already in the vine; he says so in the same breath. The command is: do not go anywhere.

Then the content, and this chapter supplies it rather than leaving it vague. Verse 7 makes it verbal — if my words abide in you, which is Scripture staying resident rather than visited. Verse 9 makes it relational — abide in my love. Verse 10 makes it practical — if you keep my commandments you will abide in my love. So abiding turns out to consist of three ordinary things done continuously: keeping his words in the mind, staying inside his love rather than trying to earn it, and doing what he said.

Nothing there requires a temperament or a technique. It is the difference between a branch attached to a vine and a branch lying on the ground, and the branch does not achieve it. It simply does not detach.

parallels.desc: the washing of water with the word

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apart from me you can do nothing: the most absolute statement of dependence in the gospel. Not a little, not very much — nothing. The branch that is separated from the vine does not produce diminished fruit; it produces no fruit at all. This is the radical impossibility of autonomous Christian living: spiritual fruitfulness requires constant connection, not occasional contact. The warning is equally stark: the non-abiding branch is thrown away and burned. This is not casual; it is the description of apostasy — the branch that seemed to be in the vine but had no living connection is finally revealed and removed.

That answer should not be given quickly, because the words are severe and a reader may be frightened by them, and the difficulty is real. Verse 2 says every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away. In me. How can a branch be in Christ and be cut off and burned, when the same Lord said five chapters earlier that no one is able to snatch them out of his Father's hand (10:29)?

The picture itself supplies the answer. The vine is an image lifted straight out of the Old Testament, where the vine is Israel — a nation full of people who belonged to the covenant community outwardly, carried its sign in their bodies, kept its feasts, and were not the true people of God at all. That is precisely Isaiah's complaint: he looked for grapes and it yielded wild grapes (Isa. 5:2). To be a branch on that vine never guaranteed life in it. And notice who Jesus is speaking to. He is in a room with the Twelve, and one of them has just gone out into the night to sell him (13:30). Judas was a branch in every visible sense — called, trusted with the common purse — and he bore nothing, because there was nothing in him to bear with. John gives us the category plainly in his letter: they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19).

So the two sayings stand together without strain. The fruitless branch is not a sheep prised out of the Shepherd's hand; it is a branch tied on to the vine that never drew a drop of sap from it. Union with Christ that is real produces fruit, always, however slowly and however little — that is what the passage means by fruit, not a level of achievement but evidence of life.

Arminian Christians read this verse as a warning that a true believer can fail to abide and be cut off and lost (cf. Heb 6:4–6; Gal 5:4). The warning is real and must be heeded. But Jesus has already said of his sheep that they will never perish (10:28), and a branch that bears no fruit at all shows that it never drew life from the vine. The more likely reading is that the burned branches are those who seemed to belong to Christ but never did, like Judas, and that the warning is one of the means by which Christ keeps the true branches abiding.

And to the person genuinely alarmed by this verse, one thing more. Ask yourself why you are alarmed. A dead branch does not lie awake fearing that it is fruitless; it feels nothing at all, which is the whole trouble with it. The very desire to abide is sap moving. Christ did not tell his friends this to leave them measuring themselves for the fire; the command in the passage is not examine yourself but abide in me, and abiding is not an achievement to be pulled off. It is a staying put. Stay where you are — in him — and the fruit is his business, not yours.
verseByVerse.note: Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned.

parallels.desc: the wood of the vine

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you abide in me and my words abide in you: the two-directional abiding — in the person of Christ and in the word of Christ. The word abiding in the disciple creates the desires that prayer then expresses; prayers formed by the word of Christ are prayers aligned with the will of Christ, which the Father always answers. By this my Father is glorified: the glory of God and the fruitfulness of the disciples are inseparably connected. The church's mission to bear much fruit is not self-aggrandizement but Father-glorification. The Vine's purpose is the vinedresser's glory; the branches exist to honor the one who plants and tends.

This is the third prayer promise in two chapters, and the conditions are worth laying side by side because they accumulate rather than repeat.

At 14:13 it was whatever you ask in my name. At 14:14, the same. Here: if you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. And at verse 16 it will be tied to being chosen and sent.

So the promise is never bare. Each statement of it carries a boundary, and the boundary here is the most searching of them — not a formula appended to a request but a condition about where the person praying is living.

And notice the mechanism, because it explains why the promise is not reckless. If my words abide in you — a person saturated in what Christ said begins, over time, to want different things. The prayers change before the answers do. That is why ask whatever you wish can be said without qualification after that clause: the wishing itself has been under instruction.

Which is also the answer to the suspicion that this is a trick — that God grants only what he was going to do anyway, so the promise is empty. It is not empty; it is a description of what happens to desire when somebody lives close to Christ for a long time. The wishes are genuinely the person's own. They have simply stopped being arbitrary.

Then verse 8, and the last verb repays attention: so prove to be my disciples is, more literally, and become my disciples. Discipleship is treated as something one grows into rather than a status secured at the start. The fruit does not earn the title. It is how the title becomes visible.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you: the love of the disciples is patterned on and derived from the inner-Trinitarian love of Father and Son. The disciples are loved with the same quality of love that flows eternally between the Father and Son. Abide in my love: love is not merely a feeling to be received but a sphere to live within. Keeping my commandments is not the condition of earning love but the way of remaining in the love already given — as Jesus' own obedience to the Father's commandments is the expression of his abiding in the Father's love. Obedience is love's response, not love's price.

The comparison at the head of verse 9 is the largest in the chapter and it is easy to read past as a pleasantry.

As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you.

The measure is not a great deal, or more than you know. The measure is the love within the Godhead — the love the Father has had for the Son from before the world existed, which chapter 17 will say in so many words (17:24). That is the quantity being reported.

Then abide in my love, which is the phrase that needs unpacking because it can be heard as a threat — stay in it or you will fall out of it.

Read it against the picture. A branch does not generate the sap; it lives in a supply that is already flowing. Abiding in his love is not maintaining his affection at a level, which is impossible and was never asked; it is remaining inside something that is there whether one feels it or not.

And verse 10 gives the way that is done: if you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love.

Now the guard, because this sentence has produced a great deal of misery. It does not say obedience purchases the love. The clause that follows settles it: just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love. Nobody supposes the Son earns the Father's love by good behaviour. His obedience is the mode of a love that was never in question, and the disciples' obedience is being described in the same way.

Here is the test. Ask what happens inside you after a bad week — whether you approach God expecting the temperature to have dropped. If the answer is yes, then something is being treated as a wage that this verse treats as a home.

parallels.desc: keep yourselves in the love of God

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That my joy may be in you: the purpose of the entire farewell discourse is not merely to prepare the disciples for suffering but to fill them with the joy that belongs to Jesus himself — the joy that exists in the inner-Trinitarian fellowship of perfect love and perfect obedience. Full joy is the overflow of abiding in the vine. And then the commandment: love one another as I have loved you. The vine and the branches metaphor now becomes the basis for community ethics: branches in the same vine are branches in relationship with each other. The love of Christ for the disciples becomes the measure of their love for one another.

Stop at the word and at when it was said, because both are extraordinary.

That my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.

My joy. Not joy in general, and not the disciples' cheerfulness — a joy that belongs to him and is being transferred. And the man saying it will be arrested within a few hours and dead by tomorrow afternoon. He knows it; he has been telling them so all evening.

Which means the joy he proposes to hand over is not a mood produced by favourable circumstances, because his circumstances at that moment were the worst that have ever been arranged for anybody. Hebrews describes the same thing from the far side: who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame (Heb. 12:2).

And full is a container word — filled up, brought to the brim. It is what John says of himself elsewhere: we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete (1 Jn. 1:4).

Now the pastoral half, because there is a reader for whom this verse is an accusation. Christians are frequently told they ought to be joyful, and the ones who are not conclude that something is defective in them — which is often untrue and always unhelpful, particularly for people whose flatness is a matter of temperament, exhaustion or illness rather than of the soul.

Notice therefore where the joy is located. It is his, and it is in them, and it arrives by the route the whole chapter has been describing: abiding. It is not summoned up. It is a by-product of staying attached to a vine, and it has nothing to do with being naturally cheerful — several of the most joyful Christians who ever lived were also, by any modern measure, depressed men.

And the location of the sentence tells against the sunny reading. This is not said at a wedding. It is said in a room somebody has just walked out of to fetch soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater love has no one than this: the cross stated as the universal criterion of love's greatness. Not romantic love, not familial love, but the love that gives itself for the beloved at the cost of life itself — this is the greatest love. The disciples are not merely servants now but friends — those admitted to the confidence of the one who chose them (v. 15). The friendship is conditional not because it must be earned but because it is accepted by those who respond to what Jesus commands. Command and friendship coexist: the one who commands is the friend who has laid down his life for those he commands.

This sentence is carved on war memorials all over the world, and it belongs there. A man who dies to bring his friends out is doing something Christ himself calls the greatest love there is, and no Christian should be grudging about it.

But the verse says something the memorials cannot, and the difference is worth stating.

He is defining the ceiling of human love — greater love has no one than this — and then going beyond it the following afternoon. Paul makes the point explicitly: one might conceivably die for a good man, but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:7-8), and a few lines later, while we were enemies.

So the soldier's love is the highest thing available on the human scale and Christ exceeds it, because his friends at that moment were not behaving like friends. One had sold him, one would deny him three times before dawn, and the rest would run. He calls them friends anyway, and the word is not sentimental — philoi, from the affectionate verb, the same root as the word the sisters used of Lazarus (11:3).

Then the condition in verse 14, which reads awkwardly: you are my friends if you do what I command you.

It sounds like a friendship on probation, and the next verse forbids that reading. He does not say you will become my friends if. He has already called them friends and is about to say so again (v. 15). What the conditional does is describe the shape of the friendship rather than set its price — friends of this particular friend are people who do what he says, because of who he is.

And it is worth noticing that a command has been given by somebody who is about to demonstrate compliance with a harder one. He is not asking them to do anything he is unwilling to do first.

parallels.desc: he laid down his life for us

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You did not choose me, but I chose you: the elective foundation of discipleship. The disciples' following of Jesus traces not to their initiative but to his choosing. This is not the language of passive automatons but of those whose freedom has been liberated and directed by grace. Appointed to go and bear fruit that abides: the election is unto mission, fruitfulness, and the prayer-connection that sustains both. The same prayer promise (ask in my name) that appears in 14:13-14 reappears here, anchored now in election — those whom God chose are the ones whose prayers in Jesus' name the Father answers.

Weigh what has just happened, because it is one of the most startling sentences in the Bible and familiarity has worn it smooth.

No longer do I call you servants… but I have called you friends.

In the whole Old Testament two men are called the friend of God. Abraham — Abraham your friend (2 Chr. 20:7; and Isa. 41:8; taken up in Jas. 2:23). And Moses, of whom it is said that the LORD spoke to him face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exod. 33:11). Two, in two thousand years.

Every other great figure is a servant. It is the title of honour: Moses my servant, David my servant, Israel my servant, and the prophets my servants. To be called the servant of the LORD was the highest thing a Jew could aspire to.

And he takes it off them. No longer do I call you servants.

Now the reason, and it is precise rather than sentimental: for the servant does not know what his master is doing. That is the whole difference. A slave is told what to do and not why; the plan is not his business. What defines the friend is being let in on it — all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.

So the promotion is a promotion in disclosure. They have not been given easier commands; they have been given the reasons. And that has been happening all evening: he has told them about the Father's house, the Spirit, the world's hatred, his own death and return, none of which they needed to know in order to obey.

Then verse 16, and it inverts the ordinary practice of the world they lived in. A young man in first-century Judea chose his rabbi. He picked the teacher whose yoke he wanted to take, applied himself, and hoped to be accepted. Everybody at that table would have expected discipleship to work that way, and several of them had done exactly that with John the Baptist first.

You did not choose me, but I chose you.

Is I chose you about salvation, or about the apostles’ office? In the first place it is the choosing of the Eleven for their mission, that you should go and bear fruit; Judas, too, was chosen as an apostle (6:70). But it rests on the same truth that runs through John, that those who come to Christ come because the Father gave them and drew them (6:37, 44). So it is rightly applied to every believer: our faith began with his choice.

And Jesus says he has made known all that I have heard from my Father (v. 15), yet soon says I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now (16:12). He has told them all they need as his friends; the rest the Spirit will bring out after his glory, through the apostles (16:13).

And the purpose is not privilege. It is a job: appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide. Election in this verse runs straight out into mission, and the last word about the fruit is the chapter's keyword — abide. Fruit that stays.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God.

parallels.desc: Abraham, my friend
as a man speaks to his friend

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The entire farewell discourse, the vine-and-branches discourse, the election and appointment — all of it is commanded so that you will love one another. The theological richness of chapters 13-17 is not an end in itself; it is the foundation for community love. Reformed theology at its best is always this: the doctrine of election produces humility; the doctrine of grace produces gratitude; both produce the servant-hearted love of the community of the chosen. The commandment to love is not imposed on top of the theology but is the practical expression of everything the theology has established.

One sentence, and it is doing a specific job: it closes the first half of the chapter by naming what all of it was for.

These things I command you, so that you will love one another.

These things reaches back over everything since verse 1 — the vine, the pruning, the abiding, the joy, the friendship, the choosing. All of it is now said to have been aimed at a single outcome, and the outcome is horizontal.

Which is worth stopping on, because it is not where any of us would have put the emphasis. Given a discourse on union with Christ, most preachers land on the vertical: know him better, depend on him more, pray with confidence. Those are all in the passage. And he says the point of the whole thing is that they should love each other.

Note also the grammar: so that you will love. Not so that you should try to. It is put as an expected result of the teaching taking hold, which fits the vine — fruit is not extracted from a branch by exhortation.

And there is a reason this needed saying to these particular men. They had spent the meal arguing about which of them was the greatest (Lk. 22:24), and within hours they would all abandon him and then spend the weekend locked in a room together, with Peter's failure in the middle of it. The community he is commanding to love one another was, on the available evidence, not good at it.

He gives the command anyway, to them, that night.

And it is worth noticing that this is the third time he has issued it in three chapters — a new commandment at 13:34, this is my commandment at 15:12, and now again at 15:17.

Three times in one evening, to eleven men, about the same thing. Whatever else he wanted them to carry out of that room, this is what he thought needed saying repeatedly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus prepares the disciples for the world's hatred: as the world hated him, it will hate them. The hatred is not arbitrary but the inevitable response of darkness to light. Jesus traces the hatred to his own relationship with the Father and promises the Spirit of truth who will bear witness about him — alongside the disciples' own witness.

The abrupt turn (vv. 18-19). Seventeen verses about a vine, love, joy and friendship — and then, without a pause, hatred. He puts them together on purpose: the community just commanded to love one another is going to need to. And the word is not dislike; hate appears seven times in eight verses. The logic is oddly comforting once seen — if you were of the world, the world would love you as its own — so the hostility is not evidence that something has gone wrong but that they no longer belong to the system doing the hating. Two guards are needed. Against manufacturing it: much of what Christians suffer in comfortable countries is the ordinary consequence of being rude or politically obnoxious, and Peter drew the line himself (1 Pet. 4:15). And against the opposite error: this is not a metaphor for social awkwardness, and a church that reads it that way has quietly excluded most of its own family, since there are more Christians under real pressure now than at most points in the past.

The proverb turned over (v. 20). Remember the word that I said to you points back to the basin: a servant is not greater than his master (13:16). There it argued for washing feet; here the other edge is out. John is the only evangelist who records both uses. And do not miss the clause that follows — if they kept my word, they will also keep yours. The parallel runs both ways, and his own reception included Nicodemus, Nathanael, a Samaritan village and a beggar who worshipped in the street.

No cloak (vv. 22-23). Read flatly, they would not have been guilty of sin says something Scripture denies everywhere else. What is meant is the specific sin of rejecting God with the evidence present — a man cannot refuse a person he has never met. The principle underneath is that responsibility tracks light (Lk. 12:47-48), which makes the position of the well-informed more dangerous, not safer. And no excuse: his coming did not create the guilt but removed the covering that made it deniable.

Without a cause (vv. 24-25). Two unearned things meet at the same cross: he received hatred he had not earned, and those who hated him receive a righteousness they have not earned (Rom. 3:24). Note also their Law, the same distancing as 8:17 and 10:34 — the tone of a man citing the rules of a court he stands outside.

The double witness (vv. 26-27). The filioque is worth knowing about: the creed said the Spirit proceeds from the Father, the West later added and the Son, and by 1054 it was among the causes of a split never healed. This one verse contains both halves — proceeds from the Father, and whom I will send. And the qualification given for the human witness is purely factual: because you have been with me from the beginning. Not eloquence, not courage — neither of which they were about to demonstrate. Because they were there. The Spirit's witness is the one that convinces; nobody in this verse is asked to produce faith in anybody.
verseByVerse.theology: The world's hatred of the church is not an accident to be explained away but a structural feature of the relationship between the kingdom of God and the kingdom of this world. Jesus does not promise that clever strategy or cultural accommodation will eliminate the hatred; he promises that the Spirit will sustain the witnesses through it. The Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (v. 26) — a phrase that has generated centuries of debate about the procession of the Spirit — testifies about Jesus, and the disciples testify because they have been with Jesus from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). The disciple is not above the master. This is simultaneously warning and honor: to be persecuted for Christ is to share in Christ's experience, to enter the fellowship of his sufferings. The church that is never persecuted has either been culturally absorbed to the point of invisibility or is living in an extraordinarily tolerant society — possibly both. The cross-bearing disciple should expect the world's hostility as confirmation, not contradiction, of authentic discipleship.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know that it has hated me before it hated you: the disciples' persecution is not unique but participatory — they share in Jesus' experience because they share his identity. If you were of the world: the world loves its own, a statement of the social logic of the fallen order. The disciples have been chosen out of the world — extracted from the world's value system, called to different loyalties, marked by a different love. This chosenness is the source of both their dignity and their danger. Election unto discipleship is election unto suffering; there is no way to be chosen by God and remain comfortable in the world that rejected God's Son.

The first thing to notice is the change of subject, and it is abrupt. Seventeen verses about a vine, love, joy and friendship — and then, without a pause, hatred.

He puts them together on purpose. The community that has just been commanded to love one another is going to need to, because nobody outside it will.

And the word is not dislike. Miseo is hatred, and it appears seven times in eight verses. He is not warning them about awkwardness at parties.

Then the logic, which is oddly comforting once it is seen. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own. The hostility is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the disciples; it is evidence that they no longer belong to the system that is doing the hating. Belonging elsewhere is the whole cause.

Now two guards, because this passage is misused in both directions and the damage is real.

The first is against manufacturing it. There is a habit of treating any friction as persecution and wearing it as proof of faithfulness — and a great deal of what Christians suffer in comfortable countries is not persecution but the ordinary consequence of being rude, ill-informed, or politically obnoxious. Peter drew the line himself: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler (1 Pet. 4:15). Being disliked for being disagreeable is not sharing in the sufferings of Christ.

The second is against the opposite error, which is commoner in the West. This passage is not hypothetical, and it is not history. There are more Christians under real pressure today than at most points in the past — imprisoned, dispossessed, killed — and a church that reads verse 18 as a metaphor for social awkwardness has quietly excluded most of its own family from the conversation.

The honest position for a comfortable believer is neither to invent a persecution nor to conclude the verse is spent. It is to notice that Jesus said if, and to ask what it means that the answer, in one's own case, is mostly no.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you: the logic of identification runs in both directions. The world's treatment of the disciples mirrors its treatment of Jesus because it sees in the disciples the presence of Jesus. On account of my name: persecution of the church is ultimately directed at Christ. The world that does not know the Father does not recognize the Father's messengers; the ignorance is not innocent but culpable — they have had the opportunity to know and refused. This is why persecution is not random but patterned: it concentrates around those who most clearly bear the name and character of Christ.

Remember the word that I said to you — and the word he tells them to remember is one he said two chapters ago, at the basin: a servant is not greater than his master (13:16).

There it was an argument for washing feet. If the master takes the towel, no servant is above it. Here the identical sentence is turned over, and the other edge is out: if the master is hunted, no servant should expect to be exempt.

The same proverb produces humility in one direction and realism in the other, and John is the only evangelist who records both uses.

Then a clause that is easy to skip and should not be: if they kept my word, they will also keep yours.

The parallel runs both ways. Some will listen. The verse is not a prediction of universal hostility; it is a prediction that the disciples' reception will mirror his, and his was mixed. Crowds followed him for three years. A Samaritan village believed. Some of the authorities believed and would not say so. Whatever happens to the eleven will be the same shape.

Which is worth having, because the passage is often read as though the church should expect nothing but rejection, and that is not what it says. It says the reception will be his reception, and his reception included Nicodemus and Nathanael and a beggar who worshipped in the street.

And then the root of it all, stated flatly: because they do not know him who sent me. The hostility is not fundamentally about the disciples, or their manner, or their politics. It is about the Father, whom the world does not know — which means the disciples are not really the target, and are being hit by something aimed past them.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now they have no excuse: the coming of Jesus and his teaching has removed the plausible excuse of ignorance. Moral and spiritual responsibility is proportional to light received. The Jews who heard Jesus, saw his signs, and rejected him bear a heavier responsibility than those who never had the opportunity. Whoever hates me hates my Father also: the inseparability of Father and Son means that rejection of the Son is rejection of the Father. Those who claim to honor God while opposing Jesus are in self-contradiction; the God they honor has sent the Son they reject.

The sentence needs care, because read flatly it says something Scripture denies everywhere else: if I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin.

He cannot mean they would have been innocent. Paul spends three chapters establishing that the whole world is guilty before God without any reference to the incarnation, and John himself has already had Jesus say that men loved darkness rather than light (3:19).

What is meant is the specific sin the chapter is about: the rejection of God with the evidence in front of them. That sin was not available before he arrived. A man cannot refuse a person he has never met.

And the principle underneath it runs right through the Bible: responsibility tracks light. Jesus states it elsewhere in so many words — the servant who knew his master's will and did not do it receives the heavier beating (Lk. 12:47-48) — and it means that the position of the well-informed is more dangerous, not safer.

Which is worth applying where it actually bites. A person who has grown up hearing the gospel, who owns several Bibles and can predict the sermon, is in this verse's territory. The excuse of not knowing is gone. That is not a comfortable thing to say to a religious reader and it is the plain sense of the passage.

Then no excuse, which is literally they have no cloak for their sin — prophasis, a pretext, the plausible cover story. The image is of something pulled away. What his coming did was not to create the guilt but to remove the covering that had made it deniable.

Then verse 23, which is the sentence underneath the whole passage: whoever hates me hates my Father also.

It is the same claim as 14:9 turned round. If seeing him is seeing the Father, then hating him is hating the Father — the identification does not work in one direction only.

And it closes off a very common position, held sincerely by a great many people: that one may honour God and set Jesus to one side as a good man about whom the church has exaggerated. This verse says the arrangement does not exist. There is no God available behind Christ to be respected while Christ is declined.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Works that no one else did: the signs are themselves witness, and rejection of the signs is culpable because the evidence is overwhelming. Psalm 35:19 and 69:4 — they hated me without cause — are applied to the rejection of Jesus. The hatred is causeless in the sense that Jesus gave no legitimate occasion for it: no sin, no deception, no injustice. The hatred is the pure expression of the world's alienation from God, unmasked by the presence of perfect goodness. When perfect love is rejected by the world, the world's enmity against God becomes fully visible. The cross reveals both sides: God's love and the world's hatred of it.

There is a word in the quotation that does more work than it looks, and it turns up in an unexpected place elsewhere.

They hated me without a cause — the psalm is 35:19 or 69:4 — and the Greek is dorean. It means gratuitously, as a free gift, for nothing.

The same word appears in Romans 3:24: we are justified by his grace as a gift — dorean, freely, for nothing.

So the two great gratuitous acts in the story are described with the identical word. The world's hatred of Christ was unearned, and the sinner's acquittal is unearned, and they meet at the same cross. He received hatred he had done nothing to deserve; the people who hated him receive a righteousness they have done nothing to deserve.

Note also the phrase their Law. He has done this before (8:17; 10:34), and it is not a repudiation of Scripture — he is quoting it as authoritative, which is the point. It is the tone of a man citing the rules of a court he is standing outside of, to men who administer it.

And the psalm he quotes is worth looking up. Psalm 69 is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament, and it supplies the zeal for the house that consumed him (2:17), the vinegar offered on the cross (19:29), and this line. David wrote it out of an experience of being hated for no reason he could identify, and it turned out to be a description of somebody else.

Then verse 24, and the escalation matters: the works that no one else did. Not works in general. He is claiming a category of evidence nobody else had ever produced — which the previous chapters have set out at length, and which the council itself conceded in closed session (11:47).
verseByVerse.note: “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms.

parallels.desc: those who hate me without cause

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father: the double mission of the Spirit — from the Father, sent by the Son — is the basis of the great filioque controversy that divided Eastern and Western Christianity. Whatever the precise formulation, the Spirit's testimony is the primary witness about Jesus in the world after the ascension. And the disciples will bear witness because they have been with Jesus from the beginning: the apostolic witness is grounded in eyewitness experience, and the Spirit will illuminate and sustain that witness across generations. The Spirit and the church together continue the testimony to Christ that will not be silenced.

A word about the phrase that divided the church, since the verse raises it and a reader may want to know what actually happened.

The Nicene Creed, as agreed in the fourth century, said the Spirit proceeds from the Father — which is this verse. Western churches later added and the Son, in Latin filioque, and by 1054 it was among the causes of the split between East and West that has never been healed.

What is worth knowing is that this single verse contains both halves of the argument. The Spirit proceeds from the Father, and in the same sentence Jesus says whom I will send to you. The East protects the Father as the single source within the Godhead; the West protects the Son's full involvement. Both are defending something the verse says.

It is not a small matter and it should not be waved away, but a reader can hold the sentence as it stands: from the Father, sent by the Son, and the two clauses were written by the same hand in the same breath.

Which side is right? The Western churches, Reformed and Lutheran among them, hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The reasons are that he is called the Spirit of Christ (Rom 8:9) and the Spirit of his Son (Gal 4:6), that the Son sends him here, and that the Son breathes him on the disciples (20:22). The Eastern concern to keep the Father as the one source is real, but the more likely reading is that the Spirit comes from both.

Then the double testimony, which is the point of the passage. He will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness.

Two witnesses — which is the requirement of the law that has run through this whole Gospel (8:17). And the qualification given for the human half is purely factual: because you have been with me from the beginning. Not because they are eloquent or brave, neither of which they were about to prove. Because they were there.

Which is the shape of Christian testimony still, and it takes the pressure off in a useful way. The Spirit's witness is the one that convinces; the disciples' job is to say what they saw. Nobody in this verse is asked to produce faith in anybody.

And the last phrase is worth holding against what is about to happen. You have been with me from the beginning — said to eleven men who would, before the night was over, all be somewhere else.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.”

parallels.desc: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit

As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.<sup>5</sup>I am the vine; you are the branches.
