Abide in my love.<sup>10</sup>If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.<sup>11</sup>These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.<sup>12</sup>“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.<sup>13</sup>Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.<sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you.<sup>15</sup>No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.<sup>16</sup>You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.<sup>17</sup>These things I command you, so that you will love one another.<sup>18</sup>“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.<sup>19</sup>If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.<sup>20</sup>Remember the word that I said to you: ’A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.<sup>21</sup>But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.<sup>22</sup>If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin.<sup>23</sup>Whoever hates me hates my Father also.<sup>24</sup>If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father.<sup>25</sup>But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ’They hated me without a cause.’<sup>26</sup>“But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.<sup>27</sup>And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus continues warning the disciples about persecution, explaining that telling them in advance is itself an act of pastoral care. He promises the Spirit who will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, and will guide the disciples into all truth — not independently but in full dependence on what he receives from the Son and Father.

Killing as worship (vv. 1-3). The purpose of the warning is to put the obstacle where it can be seen. And verse 2 is chilling: offering service to God. What is predicted is not violence later justified but killing performed as an act of worship. Paul is the case study — I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus (Acts 26:9) — and he is also the hope buried in it, since the first man to fulfil this prophecy on a large scale ended up writing a quarter of the New Testament. Verse 3 gives the diagnosis, and it cuts against the modern account: religious violence is caused not by too much God but by not knowing him.

Sorrow that stops the questions (vv. 5-6). None of you asks me where I am going — but Peter did (13:36) and Thomas nearly did (14:5). None of them is asking now. Verse 6 says why. Sorrow does not make people curious; it closes the questions down, and the verb is exact — sorrow has filled the heart, like a vessel with nothing left over. Jesus does not tell them to stop, or explain that the grief is misplaced. He names it and takes responsibility for having caused it.

To your advantage (v. 7). Caiaphas made a calculation in the council chamber: it is better for you that one man should die for the people (11:50). Here is the same shape of reckoning, once as cold arithmetic and once as the tenderest thing said to frightened friends. As to why the Spirit could not come earlier, the Gospel answers directly: the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified (7:39). The gift is downstream of the cross.

Convict (v. 8). Elencho is a courtroom word — to cross-examine, expose, prove a case. It does not mean to make somebody feel bad, and the confusion between the two does real damage. Conviction from the Spirit is specific, names a thing, and has a door out of it; the other kind is vague, cumulative, about the whole self, and suggests nothing to do. And the middle count is the hard one: concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father — the ascension is the appeal court overturning the world's verdict on a man it executed as a blasphemer, and the Spirit's job is to convince the world of a vindication nobody watched.

What he did not say (v. 12). One of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. Bear is to carry a weight — not that they would fail to understand but that they could not hold it. He has more to say, it is true, it would eventually be good for them, and he stops. Most Christians suspect at some point that God expects more of them than they can manage; here he is doing the arithmetic in the other direction.

The test of every spiritual claim (vv. 13-15). Guide is to lead along a road — a guide does not invent the terrain — and Jesus states the limit himself: he will not speak on his own authority. Then the sentence to keep ready to hand: he will glorify me. That is the Spirit's job description, given by the Son, and it is the one test of a spiritual movement that cannot be faked — does it end with people thinking more of Jesus Christ? The Spirit is the person of the Trinity who habitually stands slightly out of the light and points. And all that the Father has is mine (v. 15) is not all that the Father has given me: there is no smaller supply reserved for people at this end of the chain.
verseByVerse.theology: The conviction work of the Spirit operates on three fronts: sin (the world's refusal to believe in Jesus), righteousness (the vindication of Jesus in his ascension to the Father), and judgment (the condemnation of the ruler of this world at the cross). This Trinitarian work of conviction is not coercive but illuminating — the Spirit opens eyes to what is actually true about the world's condition, about Jesus' identity, and about the decisive verdict already rendered at Calvary. Evangelism that presents the gospel as optional enhancement rather than rescue from genuine condemnation has not yet let the Spirit do his convicting work.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all truth (v. 13): the Spirit's hermeneutical function is ongoing, not merely the initial inspiration of the apostolic witness. The community that has the Spirit has access to the interpretive presence of the one who knows the mind of God (1 Cor. 2:10-11). This does not mean every Christian's interpretation is equally valid; it means that the Spirit-guided community reading the Spirit-inspired text under the guidance of the Spirit through his word can arrive at the truth Jesus promised. The church's theology is a work of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To keep you from falling away: the purpose of the persecution warning is not to terrify but to fortify. Forewarned disciples are not surprised disciples; they can interpret their suffering through the framework Jesus has given. Whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God: the most dangerous form of persecution is the kind motivated by religious conviction. The Zealot who kills a Christian for apostasy, the inquisitor who burns the heretic for God's honor, the jihadist who executes the infidel — all believe they serve God. This religious violence is not a contradiction of religion but the expression of religion that has become severed from knowledge of the Father (v. 3).

Two words in this deserve the reader's attention, and the second is genuinely chilling.

The first is falling away, which is skandalizo — to be tripped, to stumble over something in the road. It is not the word for apostasy or for renouncing the faith. The picture is of a man walking who catches his foot on an obstacle he did not see, and the obstacle Jesus has in mind is persecution arriving without warning.

Which explains the purpose of the whole passage, and it is worth stating because it looks at first like a discouraging thing to say to frightened men. He is not trying to prepare them for the worst in the modern sense. He is removing a stumbling-block by putting it in the road ahead of them where they can see it. Suffering that has been predicted by the one you are following is a different experience from suffering that seems to prove he was not in control.

The second word is in verse 2, and the English softens it. Whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God — the word is latreia, which is not general service but priestly worship, the technical term for what went on in the temple. Paul uses it of presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice, your spiritual worship (Rom. 12:1).

So what is predicted is not that religious people will do something violent and afterwards justify it. It is that the killing will be performed as an act of worship — offered up, like a sacrifice, by men who go home afterwards believing they have pleased God.

And the case study was sitting in the audience of the early church, writing letters. Paul says of himself: I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth (Acts 26:9); he had been extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Gal. 1:14), and he hunted Christians to death sincerely.

Which is the hope buried inside the warning, and it should not be missed. The very first man to fulfil this prophecy on a large scale ended up writing a quarter of the New Testament. Nothing in verse 2 puts a person beyond reach.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God.

parallels.desc: Paul’s zeal as a persecutor

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have not known the Father, nor me: the theological root of religious violence. Those who truly know the Father — who has sent the Son, who loves the world, whose nature is self-giving grace — cannot persist in violence against those who bear the Son's name. Religious persecution is always a form of theological ignorance dressed in piety. I told them to you: the remembered word of Jesus is the anchor for the disciple under pressure. When the persecution comes, the memory of these words produces not despair but confirmatory faith: this is what he said would happen, and it is happening, therefore he is true.

The diagnosis in verse 3 is the most important sentence in the passage and it should be stated flatly: religious violence is not caused by too much God but by not knowing him.

They will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me.

That cuts against the standard modern account, which holds that strong religious conviction is itself the danger and that the cure is holding beliefs more loosely. Jesus says the opposite. The men who will kill his followers as an act of worship are not people who know God too well. They do not know him at all, and their zeal is the evidence rather than the exception.

And it gives a Christian a usable test, which is more than most explanations of religious violence provide. Any conviction that makes a person willing to destroy someone in God's name has, by that fact, revealed itself as ignorance of the God who sent his Son to be destroyed rather than to destroy.

Then the last clause of verse 4, which is a small window into how he had handled them for three years: I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.

He had known all of this from the start and had not told them. Not because it was untrue, and not to protect them from reality — he tells them now — but because there had been no need while he was there to absorb it. The warnings come out on the last night, when they are about to be needed.

Which is worth knowing about God's dealings generally. There is information he holds back, and the holding back is not deception. It is timing.

parallels.desc: I had acted ignorantly in unbelief

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of you asks me where I am going: Peter did ask (13:36), and Thomas did ask about the way (14:5), but now in the face of the full disclosure of what lies ahead, the disciples are overwhelmed by sorrow and have stopped asking the theological question. Sorrow has filled your heart: the disciples are in grief, processing the news of Jesus' departure and the coming persecution. Their grief is real and Jesus acknowledges it — he does not minimize it. But what they cannot yet see is that his departure is the precondition of a greater presence, not its termination.

The apparent contradiction should be dealt with directly, because a careful reader trips on it. Jesus says none of you asks me, Where are you going? — and Peter had asked precisely that three chapters earlier: Lord, where are you going? (13:36). Thomas had asked something very close (14:5).

The resolution is in what is happening in the room: none of you asks me — now, at this moment. Peter asked earlier and did not want the answer; he immediately turned the conversation to his own loyalty. Nobody is asking now, and verse 6 says why: sorrow has filled your heart.

That is a real observation about grief and it is worth pausing on. Sorrow does not usually make people curious. It closes the questions down. These men have stopped enquiring about where he is going because they have absorbed only the one fact — that he is going — and it has filled up all the available room.

The verb is exact: sorrow has filled the heart. Not touched, not troubled. Filled, like a vessel with nothing left over.

And notice what Jesus does not do with it. He does not tell them to stop being sad, or explain that their sorrow is misplaced, or hurry past it. He names it — because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart — and he takes responsibility for having caused it. Then he begins, slowly, to give them the one thing that will eventually turn it round, which is not an argument but a fact about the Spirit.

Here is the test, and it is a gentle one. In a season of grief, notice which questions have gone quiet. Not the loud ones — the ordinary ones, the curiosity about what God is doing, the interest in anything beyond the loss. Their absence is not sin and does not need repenting of. But it is worth knowing that it happens, because the disciples in this room were not rebuked for it, and because the answer to it came from outside them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is to your advantage that I go away: the most counterintuitive statement of the farewell discourse. How can the physical absence of Jesus be better than his physical presence? Because the Spirit, given through the glorification of the Son, creates a presence that is not limited by geography. Jesus in the flesh could only be in one place at a time; the Spirit indwells every believer simultaneously in every location. The church's global expansion required the local limitation of the incarnation to give way to the universal presence of the Spirit. The going away is itself an act of love for the entire world, not only for the disciples in that room.

One verbal detail here is remarkable and easy to miss. It is to your advantage that I go away — the verb is sympherei, it is expedient, it is better for you.

It is the same word Caiaphas used: it is better for you that one man should die for the people (11:50). John made a point of telling us that the high priest prophesied without knowing it.

So the word runs twice through this Gospel, once in a council chamber as cold political arithmetic and once in an upper room as the tenderest thing anybody has ever said to frightened friends. Caiaphas meant: better for us that he dies. Jesus means: better for you that I go. The same calculation, and the difference is everything.

Now the question the verse raises and does not fully answer: why could the Spirit not come while Jesus was here?

The passage gives one reason directly and implies another. Directly: the Spirit is sent by the glorified Son — if I go, I will send him to you — and John has already told us that the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified (7:39). The gift is downstream of the cross. There was nothing to apply until the work was done.

Implied, and this is the part that touches the disciples' grief: a body is in one place. For three years, being near Jesus meant being in the same room as Jesus, and it could not be otherwise. Everything about the arrangement was local. What is coming is not a replacement for his presence but a distribution of it — with them, and in them, and everywhere at once.

Did Old Testament believers not have the Spirit? They did: David prayed take not your Holy Spirit from me (Ps 51:11), and they too were born of God (3:10). What came at Pentecost was the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, dwelling in them permanently, on the ground of Christ’s finished work. That is what Jesus means: the Spirit as the promised gift of the new covenant could not come until he had gone.

Which is why the sentence is not a consolation prize dressed up. He is not saying you will manage. He is saying the arrangement they are grieving the loss of was the inferior one.

parallels.desc: they were cut to the heart

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me: the Spirit's conviction of sin does not begin with a catalogue of moral failures but with the root sin — the rejection of the Son. Every other sin is a fruit of this tree. The Spirit's work of evangelism is to expose the fundamental wrong that underlies all wrong: alienation from God expressed as refusal of the one God sent. Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father: Jesus' ascension is the Father's vindication — he who was condemned by the world as a blasphemer and criminal is welcomed into the Father's glory, demonstrating that he was righteous all along. The Spirit announces that righteousness.

Start with the verb, because the English has drifted and the drift causes real damage.

He will convict the world — elencho. It is a courtroom word. It means to cross-examine, to expose, to bring to light, to prove a case. It does not mean to make somebody feel bad.

That distinction is worth having very clearly, because a great many Christians confuse the Spirit's work with something else entirely, and the confusion is destructive. What the Spirit does is show a person what is true. What the accuser does is press a person about what they are. The one produces clarity and moves toward a remedy; the other produces a fog of general unworthiness and moves nowhere at all.

Here is the test, and it is practical. Conviction from the Spirit is specific — it names a thing, and it can be dealt with, and there is a door out of it marked with the name of Christ. The other kind is vague, cumulative, and always about the whole self rather than an act, and it never once suggests anything to do. If what you are hearing has no exit, it is not this verse.

Then the three counts, and the middle one is the strange one.

Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me. Not concerning sins, plural, catalogued. The root, singular. The Spirit's first move is not to make the world ashamed of its behaviour but to expose what is underneath it.

Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father. This is the difficult clause and it repays the work. A man was tried, convicted, and executed as a blasphemer and a criminal. On the world's verdict he was guilty. The ascension is the appeal court: the Father receives him, which is a public overturning of the sentence. So the Spirit's second work is to convince the world that its judgement of Jesus was wrong — and by implication, that the standard of righteousness it applied was itself the thing on trial.

And the phrase you will see me no longer belongs to that argument. The vindication is invisible. Nobody watched the Father receive him. The Spirit's job is to convince the world of a verdict that was handed down out of sight.

parallels.desc: raised for our justification

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged: the cross was the decisive judgment of the devil. The Spirit convicts the world that the verdict of Calvary is permanent and binding — the enemy has been condemned, death has been overcome, the power of accusation has been broken. You cannot bear them now: the pastoral restraint of a teacher who knows what his students can receive. Not all revelation is given at once; the Spirit will guide into truth progressively as the disciples are able to receive it. This is the principle of theological development — not new revelation but the deepening reception of what was always there.

The third count completes the courtroom scene, and the tense is what matters: the ruler of this world is judged — already. Said before the cross, about the cross.

Which means the Spirit is not prosecuting an open case. He is publishing a verdict already entered. That is worth knowing when the world looks as though the enemy is winning, which it frequently does: the question of who governs was settled on a Friday afternoon and nothing since has reopened it.

Then verse 12, and it is one of the kindest sentences in the Gospel: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.

The word is bear, to carry a weight. It is not that they would fail to understand; it is that they could not hold it. He has more to say, it is true, it would be good for them eventually, and he stops — because there is a limit to what people can carry on a given night, and he can see where theirs is.

Consider what that means about the God who deals with us. He is not indifferent to capacity. There is truth he has and withholds, and the withholding is not evasion but mercy, timed to what a person can lift.

Here is the comfort in it, and it runs the opposite way to how this is usually felt. Most Christians at some point suspect that God is expecting more of them than they can manage. This verse has him doing the arithmetic in the other direction — measuring what he says against what they can carry, and stopping short.

And note that he does not say they will never hear it. The Spirit will bring it, later, when the weight can be borne. Nothing is being permanently withheld; it is being postponed to a point where it will help rather than crush.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will guide you into all the truth: not all truth about everything (chemistry, politics, astronomy) but the truth about God, salvation, and the meaning of Jesus. The Spirit's guidance is not autonomous new revelation but the illumination of what Christ has already accomplished and revealed. He will not speak on his own authority: the Spirit's dependence on the Son is the same as the Son's dependence on the Father — perfect, voluntary, non-diminishing. He will glorify me: the Spirit's entire ministry is Christ-centered, Christ-glorifying, Christ-revealing. Any spiritual movement that shifts the center from Christ to the Spirit's own activity has lost the Spirit's own stated purpose.

The verb in verse 13 is worth having: he will guide you — hodegeo, from the word for a road. It means to lead somebody along a way, and it is what a guide does for a traveller who does not know the country.

Which sets a boundary that this verse badly needs, because he will guide you into all the truth has been claimed by every movement that ever wanted to add something to Scripture. A guide does not invent the terrain. He takes people over ground that is already there.

And Jesus states the limit himself in the next clause: he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak. The Spirit is not a second source. He reports.

Then the sentence that is the single best test of any spiritual claim ever made, and it should be kept ready to hand: he will glorify me.

That is the Spirit's stated job description, given by the Son, on the last night. So the question to ask of any teaching, experience, movement or manifestation that claims the Spirit is not whether it is impressive, or emotional, or accompanied by power. It is simpler and much harder to fake: does it end up with people thinking more of Jesus Christ?

A great deal that has gone under the Spirit's name over the centuries fails that test on its own terms — because the attention settles on the phenomenon, or on the man producing it, or on the Spirit himself as the object of interest. The Spirit does not seek his own glory, which is a striking thing to notice about the third person of the Trinity: he is the one who habitually stands slightly out of the light and points.

Is this a promise to every believer, or to the apostles? In the first place it is to the apostles, who received the Spirit’s guidance into all truth and wrote it down in the New Testament. Believers today share in the promise through their word, as the Spirit opens our eyes to it (1 Cor 2:12–13). It is not a promise of new revelation beyond Scripture.

And the things that are to come should not be inflated. It is not a promise of prediction to individual believers about their own futures. Read alongside the rest of the New Testament it most naturally means the things the apostles would be given to understand and write — the meaning of the cross, the shape of the age, the end.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father has is mine: the comprehensive claim of the Son to the Father's resources — not a grab for divine property but the natural statement of their shared nature. The Spirit mediates the Son's fullness to the church: everything in the divine treasury flows from Father to Son to Spirit to the church. A little while, and you will see me no longer; again a little while, and you will see me: the riddle of absence and return — the cross will hide him, the resurrection will reveal him. The little while has the elasticity of divine time: real anguish, real return, the shape of all Christian experience.

All that the Father has is mine.

Stop on that, because it is one of the largest claims in the Gospel and it is dropped in almost casually as the reason for something else. Not all that the Father has given me, which would be the language of a servant entrusted with an estate. All that the Father has. Without limit and without qualification.

And the logic of the sentence is the point: therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. The Spirit takes from the Son, and everything the Father has belongs to the Son, so what the Spirit brings to the church is drawn from the whole wealth of God. There is no smaller supply reserved for people at this end of the chain.

Then the riddle of verse 16, which is about to occupy the disciples for four verses: a little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me.

And the two little whiles are not the same length. The first is about eighteen hours. The second is three days — and behind it, arguably, the whole age of the church, since the seeing that began on Easter has not ended. That elasticity is not a trick. It is how the New Testament always speaks about the interval: yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay (Heb. 10:37), written two thousand years ago.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The last teaching of the night: the riddle of a little while, the childbirth image, the great prayer promise, the scattering of the eleven, and I have overcome the world.

The riddle (vv. 16-19). A little while occurs seven times in four verses, and the two intervals are not the same length — the first about eighteen hours, the second three days, and behind it arguably the whole age of the church. And the disciples' response is worth reading aloud: they repeat the riddle to each other twice, verbatim, add another of his sayings in case it is a clue, and give up — without asking him, though he is sitting there. On the last night, after three years, the eleven have understood almost nothing. Whatever is required to follow him, comprehension on the night is evidently not it.

Turned into joy (v. 20). Three verbs, and they are not one activity in different moods: weep, then lament — formal wailing, the sound made at a funeral — and the world will rejoice. Two rooms on the same afternoon, and one of them celebrating. That is the hardest thing about the cross for the people who loved him: not only grief, but grief while other people were pleased. Then the preposition that carries the promise: the sorrow will turn into joy, not be followed or replaced by it. Nothing is deleted. The thing they wept over on the Friday is the thing the church has sung about ever since.

Childbirth (vv. 21-22). Two details are deliberate. Her hour has come is his own word, running through this Gospel since Cana and meaning the cross almost throughout — here it is used of ordinary human anguish. The image is chosen carefully because it is not the obvious one: it does not say the pain passes like weather, or that it is a price worth paying, but that the pain is the way the joy arrives. Nobody gets the child by another route. Note also the direction in I will see you again — not you will see me, which is what they were arguing about. And no one will take your joy: a person, not a circumstance, in a chapter that has just said the ruler of this world stands judged.

Asking (vv. 23-24). In that day you will ask nothing of me — the questions they have been putting all evening will be over — and whatever you ask of the Father in my name is promised. The verse-by-verse gives the full treatment of the promise itself, including the honest handling every Christian who has prayed for long will need.

No one to be got round (vv. 25-28). I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf is not a withdrawal of the intercession (Heb. 7:25; 1 Jn. 2:1) but the dismantling of a picture — the warm Son working on a reluctant Father. Verse 27 says why it is wrong, and the stress falls on himself: the Father himself loves them. The verb is phileo, the word Martha and Mary used of Lazarus (11:3), and John uses it of the Father's love for the Son as well (5:20). And verse 28 is the whole Gospel in one line, in four movements: from the Father, into the world, leaving the world, to the Father.

The scattering (vv. 29-32). Their now you are speaking plainly is touching and slightly absurd — nothing has been solved, and what has convinced them is that he answered a question they had not asked out loud. Faith attaches itself to whatever evidence is in front of it, which is mostly harmless until it is tested. Then each to his own home: not a heroic collapse, just people going back where they came from, and it fulfils Zechariah 13:7, which Matthew records him quoting the same night. And yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me must be held together with the cry from the cross rather than traded against it — the abandonment at Golgotha is real, is the sin-bearing, and fell on him so that it would never fall on them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chapter's second half turns on a claim about time. Everything Jesus promises here is stated as though it has already happened: the sorrow will turn into joy, the ruler of this world is judged, and — in the last verse — I have overcome the world, in the perfect tense, before the arrest. The disciples are being taught to live inside an outcome that is settled but not yet visible, which is the permanent situation of the church.

This is why the childbirth image governs the section. It is not a picture of pain compensated afterwards by an unrelated good, which is how providence is usually consoled about. It is a picture of pain that turns out to have been productive — the same event, read from the far end, carrying a meaning it could not disclose at the time. Applied to the cross, this is the interpretive key to the whole Gospel: the worst thing that ever happened is the thing the church sings about, and nothing had to be deleted for that to be true.

And the prayer promise sits in the middle of it for a reason. Prayer in the name of Jesus is not a technique for extracting outcomes; it is the practice of people who believe the outcome is already secured and are asking to be brought into line with it. Its stated end in verse 24 is not acquisition but fullness of joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
In the world you will have tribulation (v. 33) is the sentence to set against every version of Christianity that promises exemption. Not may, not could — will, spoken by the one person entitled to say it, on the last free evening of his life. And it stands beside in me you may have peace without contradiction, because the two prepositions name two locations and a believer is in both at once. That is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon.

The pastoral use of verse 22 is worth naming: no one will take your joy from you is not a promise of cheerfulness. The joy in this passage is grounded in his seeing them, not in their managing to feel anything, which is precisely why it cannot be confiscated — nobody can reach the thing it depends on.

And verse 12 — you cannot bear them now — is the answer to the reader who suspects God is asking more than can be carried. Here is the Son measuring what he says against what eleven exhausted men can hold, and stopping short, on the one night when he had most to say and least time to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' confusion is honest and endearing: they are trying to understand, talking among themselves, genuinely puzzled. The riddle of absence and return — the cross, the death, the resurrection — is not yet intelligible because the event that will make it intelligible has not yet occurred. This is the pre-Pentecost condition of even the most devoted disciples: partial understanding, genuine confusion, sincere seeking. Jesus does not rebuke the confusion; he addresses it with the image of childbirth that will give them a framework when the events unfold.

These two verses are worth reading aloud, because John has recorded something almost comic and entirely human.

They repeat the riddle back to each other twice, verbatim, as though saying it again might help. They add the other thing he said, about going to the Father, in case it is a clue. And then they give up: we do not know what he is talking about.

Notice that they do not ask him. He is sitting there. They discuss it among themselves in what must have been an audible mutter, and the next verse says he knew they wanted to ask — which means nobody did.

Why not? Probably the same reason anybody sits on a question in a room where the mood has turned: it has been a long evening, they have already been told one of them is a traitor and that they will all be scattered, and asking would mean admitting in front of the others that they had not followed.

And it is worth saying to whoever needs it that this is the last night, these are the eleven, and they have understood almost nothing. Not the foot-washing, not the betrayal, not the vine, not the going away. Three years of the best teaching that has ever been given, delivered by the Son of God in person, and on the final evening they are muttering to each other that they cannot make out what he means.

Which puts the ordinary Christian experience of not understanding into a more forgiving light. Whatever is required to follow him, comprehension on the night is evidently not it. What changed these men was not a better explanation. It was Easter, and then the Spirit, and both were entirely outside their control.

There is also a small mercy in the way John has recorded it. He was in that room. He is one of the men muttering, and when he came to write the account sixty years later he could have left this out, or tidied it, or given himself a better line.

Instead he preserves the exchange in full — including the flat admission at the end, in the first person plural, with his own name inside it: we do not know what he is talking about.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew that they wanted to ask: the pastoral omniscience that meets the disciples where they are before they can articulate their need. Their coming grief — weeping and lamenting at the crucifixion while the world celebrates — is named and validated. But your sorrow will turn into joy: not be replaced by joy (as if the sorrow never happened) but transform into joy, as the same event that produced grief (the cross) is understood as the ground of joy (the resurrection, the atonement, the gift of the Spirit). The sorrow and the joy share the same object: the death and resurrection of the Son of God.

Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him. They had said nothing to him. He answers the question they did not put.

And what he gives them is not the explanation they were after. They wanted the timetable decoded — what does a little while mean? He tells them instead what it is going to feel like, which is the thing they will actually need.

The three verbs in verse 20 are worth separating. You will weep — the ordinary word for shedding tears. And lament — formal mourning, the sound made at a funeral, wailing. But the world will rejoice. Those are not the same activity in different moods; they are two rooms on the same afternoon, and one of them is celebrating.

That is the hardest thing about the cross for the people who loved him, and it is worth naming. It was not only grief. It was grief while other people were pleased.

Then the promise, and the preposition is everything: your sorrow will turn into joy. Not will be followed by. Not will be replaced with. The sorrow itself becomes the joy — which is exactly what happened, because the thing they wept over on the Friday is the thing the church has sung about ever since. Nothing was deleted. The same event changed meaning.

Which is a different promise from the one people usually hear, and a better one. It does not say the bad thing will be compensated for later by a good thing. It says the bad thing is going to turn out to have been the good thing, seen from the wrong end.

And notice that he does not tell them the sorrow will be short. He tells them it will be real, that the world will be enjoying itself while they endure it, and that it is going to change into something else.

Which is a more useful thing to know in advance than a timetable would have been. The disciples on the Saturday did not need to be told how many hours were left; they needed to have been told that what they were feeling was not the end of the story, by somebody who had known it would happen.

parallels.desc: weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The childbirth image is perfect: the same event (labor) is anguish before and joy after; the anguish does not negate the joy but is the pathway to it. So also you have sorrow now: the cross will be anguish. But I will see you again: the resurrection appearance, the Pentecost presence, the final parousia — all are the 'seeing again' that produces the joy. No one will take your joy from you: resurrection joy is indestructible because its basis (the risen Christ) is indestructible. Circumstantial joy can be taken; the joy rooted in the resurrection and the Spirit's witness cannot be extinguished by any power in heaven or earth.

One detail in the image is more deliberate than it looks.

The first: because her hour has come. That is his word. It has been running through this Gospel since Cana — my hour has not yet come — and it has meant, almost throughout, the cross. He now puts it in the mouth of a woman in labour, the one place where it is used of ordinary human anguish.

Now the image itself, which is chosen with great care, because it is not the obvious one. He could have said the sorrow passes, as weather passes. He could have said it is worth it, as a price is worth paying. Childbirth says something neither of those says: that the pain is not incidental to the joy but is the way the joy arrives. Nobody gets the child by another route.

And the clause about forgetting deserves honesty, because it can be overstated: she no longer remembers the anguish. No mother forgets that labour hurt. What is meant is that the pain stops being the thing the day is about. It is still in the account and it has ceased to be the headline, displaced by something in the room that was not there before.

Then the reason the joy holds: I will see you again. Notice the direction. Not you will see me, which is what verse 16 promised and what they were arguing about. He will see them. The joy is grounded in his looking at them, not in their managing to catch sight of him.

And the last clause: no one will take your joy from you. Not nothing — no one. It names a person rather than a circumstance, which is fitting in a chapter that has just said the ruler of this world stands judged. There is someone whose business is taking things from Christians, and this is on the list of what he cannot reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that day — the post-resurrection, post-Pentecost era — prayer operates in a new mode: in Jesus' name, directed to the Father, mediated by the Spirit. Until now you have asked nothing in my name: the disciples have prayed, but not with the full understanding of what it means to pray in and through the completed work of the Son. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full: prayer is presented not as duty but as the pathway to the full joy Jesus has been promising throughout this discourse. The invitation is open, the name is given, the Father listens — the disciples need only to ask with the confidence that the name they carry is the guarantee of their hearing.

The promise stands here at full stretch, and it has to be handled honestly, because every Christian who has prayed for long has asked and not received. A parent prays for a dying child. A wife prays for twenty years for a husband who never turns. To leave the sentence unqualified is to hand such people either a false hope or a private verdict on their own faith, and neither is what Jesus is doing on the last night of his life.

Two things keep the promise from becoming a formula. The first was said at 14:13 and is worth holding on to: in my name is not an incantation attached to the end of a request. A name stands for a character and an authority, so to ask in his name is to ask as his representative, for what he himself would ask. John states the qualifier plainly when he comes to write his letter: this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14). The promise is not that God will do our will if we invoke the right name, but that he will not refuse his own.

The second is that Jesus had prayed such a prayer himself, and John recorded it four chapters back. Standing before the cross he said, now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? And then he answered his own question: but for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). He raises the request and declines to press it, because there was something he wanted more. That is what praying in his name looks like from the inside, and it is why the promise is safe. The Father did not save him from that hour, and the whole world was saved through it.

So notice what this verse actually guarantees, because it is easy to misread as a guarantee of acquisition. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full. The stated end is joy, not delivery of goods. Some prayers God grants outright; some he answers with something better than we had the wit to ask for; and some he answers with himself, which is why saints who received almost nothing they asked for have so often been the gladdest people in the room. The prayer that goes unanswered in the form we wanted has not fallen to the ground. It has been taken up by a Father who is committed to the fullness of our joy and not merely to the shortening of our discomfort.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In figures of speech: much of the farewell discourse has used the indirect language of vine, shepherd, bread, water — figures that point beyond themselves. The hour is coming — after the resurrection, through the Spirit — when the meaning will be plain. I do not say that I will ask on your behalf: not that Jesus no longer intercedes (he always lives to intercede, Heb. 7:25) but that the disciples' access to the Father is direct, through the Son's name, not requiring an intermediary to carry their requests. The Son's mediation is not distance but access; the name of Jesus opens the door, not stands between the petitioner and the Father.

There is a small verbal fact in verse 23 that clears up an apparent oddity, and it is invisible in English because we use one word for two things.

In that day you will ask nothing of me — the verb is erotao, which is to ask a question. It is what the disciples have been doing all evening: Peter asking where he is going, Thomas asking about the way, Philip asking to see the Father, the whole group muttering about a little while.

Then, in the same verse: whatever you ask of the Father in my name — and that is aiteo, to make a request, to petition.

So the sentence is not saying that petitioning Jesus will cease, which would sit oddly with the rest of the New Testament. It is saying the questions will stop, because the thing that has confused them all night will have happened and be plain. The interrogation ends; the asking begins.

Which is a good description of what the resurrection did to these men. There is no record after Easter of the disciples asking Jesus what he meant. They ask about the timing of the kingdom once, and are told it is not their business, and then they go and preach.

And verse 25 says the same thing from the other side: the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. The word for figures is paroimia, the same word John used of the shepherd discourse that nobody followed (10:6).

Then the delicate clause in verse 26: I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf.

It sounds at first like a withdrawal of the intercession, and it is not — Hebrews says he lives forever to make intercession (Heb. 7:25), and John's own letter calls him our advocate with the Father (1 Jn. 2:1). What he is dismantling is a picture: the idea of a Son who has to work on a Father, of prayer as something extracted by a sympathetic mediator from a reluctant judge. The next verse says exactly why that picture is wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father himself loves you: the disciples' access to the Father is not reluctantly granted through a reluctant Son interceding with a reluctant Father. The Father himself loves those who love the Son. The chain of love runs from the Father to the Son to the disciples, and the disciples' love for the Son creates the occasion for the Father's direct love. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving: the entire arc of the incarnation in one sentence — origin, arrival, departure. The movement is complete: from eternity into time and back into eternity, having accomplished the Father's redemptive purpose.

The Father himself loves you. The emphatic himself is doing deliberate work. Not the Father will be persuaded to love you. Not the Father loves you because I ask him to. The Father, himself, loves them — independently, directly, without anything having to be arranged.

Which is the correction of the commonest distortion in the Christian imagination, and it is worth naming plainly because it survives in people who would deny holding it. The picture runs: the Father is holy and severe, the Son is warm and merciful, and Christian safety consists of the Son standing between us and him. It is a picture with no basis in this Gospel and it makes prayer into a kind of legal manoeuvre.

Here the Son takes it apart in one sentence. There is nobody to be got round. The Father does not need talking into it.

Then verse 28, which is the whole Gospel in a single line, and John has been building to it since chapter 1. Four movements: I came from the Father — pre-existence. And have come into the world — incarnation. And now I am leaving the world — the cross. And going to the Father — resurrection and ascension.

Does the Father’s love, then, depend on ours? No. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Jesus is speaking of the Father’s fatherly delight and fellowship with those who love his Son (cf. 14:21, 23), not of the love that chose them before they loved. Their love for Jesus is itself the fruit of God’s love, and the Father rejoices in it.

It is a creed before there were creeds, said conversationally at a supper table, and the disciples' response in the next verse is the first sign all evening that something has got through.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you are speaking plainly: the disciples experience a moment of clarity and express the faith that has been building throughout the discourse. Now we know that you know all things: omniscience as the ground of confidence in Jesus' authority. We believe that you came from God: the disciples' confession is genuine, but Jesus will immediately test it with the prediction of their scattering (v. 32). The clarity they experience is real but not yet tested; the faith they express is authentic but not yet refined by the fire of the passion. The distance between expressed faith and proved faith is always the cross.

There is something touching and slightly absurd about this, and John does not spare them.

Ah, now you are speaking plainly! — after a sentence about coming from the Father and going to the Father, which is arguably no plainer than anything else he has said that evening. They have not solved the riddle. Something has simply landed, and the relief in their voices is audible.

And notice what they seize on as the ground of their faith: now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you.

What has impressed them is the incident ten verses back (v. 19), where he answered the question they had not asked out loud. He read the room. That is what has convinced them — not the vine, not the Spirit, not the four-stage summary of his own descent and return, but a display of knowing what they were thinking.

It is a real thing to have noticed and it is a very small basis for what is coming. And they state their conclusion in the largest possible terms: this is why we believe that you came from God.

Which is worth having, because the pattern is universal and mostly harmless until it is tested. Faith attaches itself to the evidence that happens to be in front of it — an answered prayer, a coincidence too neat to dismiss, a sermon that seemed addressed to one person in the room. None of that is false. It is simply lighter than it feels, and the weight it will have to carry is not known in advance.

Jesus does not disparage their confession. He asks one question about it, and then tells them what will happen before dawn.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you now believe? — the question probes the foundation of their confidence. The hour is coming — indeed it has come: the disciples' scattering is imminent, happening even as they speak. Each to his own home: the specificity of the prediction is its own kind of mercy — Jesus is not surprised by their failure; he has accounted for it in advance. Yet I am not alone: the Father's presence in the darkest moment is Jesus' own source of peace. The one who will face the cross abandoned by his disciples is not abandoned by his Father — yet — though the desolation of Golgotha will briefly shadow even that. The Father's presence is the source of the peace Jesus offers.

Do you now believe? The Greek can be read as a question or a flat statement — so now you believe — and either way there is no mockery in it. He does not say they are wrong. He says what their believing is about to do.

And the prediction is drawn from Scripture. You will be scattered is the language of Zechariah: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zech. 13:7), which Matthew records him quoting explicitly that same night (Mt. 26:31). He has spent chapter 10 as the good shepherd. Now the shepherd tells the flock what is about to happen to them when he is struck.

The detail is what makes it hurt: each to his own home. Not a heroic collapse. They will simply go back to where they came from, individually, the way people do when something ends.

Then the sentence that has to be handled with great care, because it stands a few hours from a cry that appears to contradict it: yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.

On the Friday he will say my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mk. 15:34). Both are true and the church has always held them together rather than choosing. What can be said is this. The abandonment at Golgotha is real — it is the sin-bearing, the cup, the thing he asked to be spared — and it is not a rupture in the Trinity, which cannot be ruptured. It is the Son experiencing, in our place, the one thing he had never known.

Which is why the words here are not made false by the words there. He is telling them, on the Thursday, that the Father is with him. What happens on the Friday is the specific, temporary, substitutionary exception — and it fell on him precisely so that it would never fall on them.

There is a comfort in this for anybody who has been left. He knows what it is to have every friend go home. And he knows, in a way nobody else ever will, what it is to have the Father turn away — which means that the sentence I will never leave you nor forsake you is not a slogan. It cost something to be able to say it.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the world you will have tribulation: not might, not possibly, but will. This is the sober realism of the farewell discourse — no promise of exemption from suffering, persecution, scattering, grief. But take heart; I have overcome the world: the word is already accomplished — the victory is already won, even though the disciples are about to experience it as defeat. The cross is the moment when the world thinks it has conquered and the resurrection is the moment when the conquest is revealed. The disciples face tribulation inside a victory that has already been secured. This is the peace Jesus offers: not absence of trouble but presence of the overcomer.

Take the verse in three parts, because it is built as a hinge and each part turns on the one before.

In me you may have peace. The location is stated first and it is not a place or a circumstance. Peace is available in a person, which is the same preposition the vine chapter has been using — and it means the peace does not depend on the state of the world outside, because it is not stored there.

In the world you will have tribulation. The word is thlipsis, pressure, the same word used of the woman in labour twelve verses ago. And the verb is not conditional. Not may, not could — will. It is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for correcting expectations, and it is spoken by the one person entitled to say it.

Notice the two prepositions side by side. In me — peace. In the world — tribulation. Both are true simultaneously and of the same people, which is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon. It is not a contradiction. It is two locations, and a believer is in both at once.

But take heart; I have overcome the world.

And the tense is the thing. Nenikeka is perfect — a completed action whose result stands. Not I will overcome. Not I am overcoming. He says it is done, and he says it before the arrest, before the trial, before the nails, on the last free evening of his life, to men who are within hours of running away.

The verb is the ordinary word for winning — the root behind Nike, victory. John will use its noun in his letter: this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith (1 Jn. 5:4).

So the arithmetic of the verse is this. The trouble is guaranteed, the peace is available, and the outcome was settled before the fight started. That is the order, and it is not the order anybody would have chosen: he does not remove the tribulation, and he does not promise to. He tells them where the peace is kept and who has already won.

It is worth saying, finally, what this sentence is not. It is not a slogan for getting through a difficult week, though it has carried a great many people through a great many of those. It is the last thing he says to his friends before he goes out to the garden — the closing sentence of four chapters of farewell — and the next words out of his mouth are a prayer.

He had overcome nothing yet, by any measure available that evening. The crowd was gone, the traitor was out arranging the arrest, the eleven were about to scatter to their own homes, and the man himself would be dead in eighteen hours.

And he says it in the perfect tense. Finished, standing, done — with the whole of it still in front of him, because he had never once been in any doubt about how it ends.

parallels.desc: the victory that has overcome the world
