17.title: The High-Priestly Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 17 is the longest recorded prayer of Jesus, spoken before the arrest as both farewell and intercession. He prays for his own glorification (vv. 1-5), for the eleven who remain (vv. 6-19), and for all who will believe through their testimony (vv. 20-26). It is the theological summit of the fourth gospel, containing the most sustained exposition of the Son's relationship with the Father and his prayer for the church's unity.

The posture and the hour (vv. 1-2). He lifted up his eyes to heaven — open, head up, which was the ordinary Jewish attitude in prayer; the bowed head and closed eyes are a later Christian habit. Set it beside the one man in the Gospels who could not do it, the tax collector who would not even lift up his eyes (Lk. 18:13). Both were heard. And the hour has come closes a thread running the length of the book: three times not yet (2:4; 7:30; 8:20), then four times come (12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1). The not-yet had been a protection, and it has now expired by his own announcement.

What eternal life is (v. 3). The nearest thing to a definition anywhere in Scripture, and it is not the one most people carry. Not duration, not a destination — that they know you, the knowledge of a person. Two consequences: it has already begun for anyone who has it, since a relationship starts when it starts; and endless existence without God would not be eternal life at all. The verse is also used against the deity of Christ, and the guard is given in the verse-by-verse — the sentence puts knowing Jesus Christ in the same clause, joined by and, and the man who wrote it also wrote that the Son is the true God and eternal life (1 Jn. 5:20).

Glory before the world (v. 5). One of the boldest sentences in the Bible, and it is a request: glorify me… with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. Moses asked to see God's glory; this is a man asking for his own back. And the preposition is the Prologue's — with you (1:1). Something was set down (Phil. 2:6-7), and this is that fact from the inside.

A generous verdict (v. 6). They have kept your word — said of eleven men who had understood almost nothing all evening, had argued about rank at the meal, and were an hour from running. Not they are trying. It is worth asking why his assessment of them differs so sharply from the one we habitually run on ourselves.

I am not praying for the world (v. 9). The coldest-sounding sentence in the warmest chapter, and three things settle it: it states the scope of one petition, not a disposition; the same prayer turns to the world twice, asking unity so that the world may believe (vv. 21, 23); and before the next morning was out he would be praying aloud for the men driving the nails (Lk. 23:34). Note too that yours are mine (v. 10) is a claim no creature could make.

Holy Father, and the son of destruction (vv. 11-12). Holy Father occurs nowhere else in the Bible, and the attribute fits the petition — keeping unholy-world-dwellers. Then not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction. On Judas and that the Scripture might be fulfilled, the New Testament holds two things without strain and never derives one from the other — he is never treated as a victim (12:6; 13:27; Acts 1:25), and it was written. Anyone claiming to have resolved that has almost certainly dropped one half.

Why it was said out loud (v. 13). These things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. He is praying, they are listening, and he says he is doing it in their hearing for their sake. There is a difference between being told you are valued and overhearing it said to a third party, and this prayer was engineered to be the second.

In but not of (vv. 15-16). The verse refuses both shortcuts. I do not ask that you take them out of the world rules out withdrawal — the compound, the bubble — and he had every reason to want it for men about to be hunted. They are not of the world rules out assimilation. The last phrase can mean from the evil one or from evil (the ESV margin gives both), exactly as in the Lord's Prayer — which this prayer keeps brushing against: a Father addressed, a name, a keeping from evil, a glory. And what is asked is protection, not exemption. Most of them died for it.

Sanctify (vv. 17-19). Sanctify is not primarily moral; the ESV margin gives set them apart (for holy service to God), which is why the next verse is about being sent. And the grammar of the last clause is a noun, not an adjective: your word is truth, not is true. The instrument God uses to make people fit for himself is named here in four words, and the answer is a book. Verse 18 is this Gospel's Great Commission, hidden inside a prayer and repeated to their faces at 20:21. Verse 19 puts priest and sacrifice in one sentence — in the old ritual those were two parties; here one person does all of it to himself.

The reader is in this prayer (v. 20). I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word. In one sentence the prayer opens from eleven men to the whole church in every century. The chain is specified — through their word — so everything that follows is asked for the ordinary Christian who has never seen a miracle and finds prayer difficult.

Loved as the Son is loved (v. 23), and I desire (v. 24). You loved them even as you loved me — said to the Father in prayer, so it is not a figure of speech aimed at encouraging anybody. Then the verb changes: everything has been asking, and here it is I desire, the only place in a recorded prayer where he speaks like that — and he spends it on getting the people he is leaving to where he is.

The last words (vv. 25-26). Righteous Father, again unique, used at the moment a right verdict is about to be withheld by every court he will stand in before morning. And the prayer ends without a petition — no request, no summary, just a destination that is not a place: and I in them.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is called the High-Priestly Prayer because it parallels the High Priest's prayer on the Day of Atonement — the one moment in the year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to intercede for the people. Jesus is simultaneously the priest and the sacrifice; he intercedes for his people while preparing himself for the offering that will accomplish what he prays for. His prayer for their sanctification (v. 17), protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), and unity (v. 21-23) is the charter of the church's life.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on and derived from the inner-Trinitarian unity of Father and Son. This is not organizational uniformity or ecclesiastical merger but the living unity of love, shared purpose, and mutual indwelling. The church's unity is the Father's means of witnessing to the world (v. 21, 23): the divided church contradicts its own evangelistic witness. The prayer for unity is also the prayer for effective mission — they are inseparable in Jesus' own intercession.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Father, the hour has come: the moment that the entire gospel has been building toward is now named in prayer. Glorify your Son: not a self-aggrandizing request but a Trinitarian one — the Son's glorification through the cross and resurrection will glorify the Father, because the Father's redeeming love will be fully displayed. Authority over all flesh: the universal scope of the Son's redemptive mission, given by the Father. To give eternal life to all whom you have given him: election and the gift of eternal life are correlated — the Father has given specific persons to the Son, and the Son gives them eternal life. None of those given will fail to receive it.

Begin with the posture, because John records it and it is not what most readers picture.

He lifted up his eyes to heaven. Eyes open, head up, looking. That was the ordinary Jewish attitude in prayer — standing, face raised, hands often spread — and the bowed head and closed eyes we default to are a later Christian habit, not a biblical instruction. He did the same at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41).

It is worth having because it changes the scene. This is not a man with his face in his hands. It is a man looking his Father in the face on the last evening of his life.

And it is worth setting beside the one man in the Gospels who could not do it — the tax collector in Luke's parable, who would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast (Lk. 18:13). Both were heard. There is no single correct posture; there is a Son who looks up, and a sinner who cannot, and the Father receives them both.

Then the address, and it will repeat: Father. Six times in this prayer, and twice with an adjective — Holy Father at verse 11 and righteous Father at verse 25, neither of which occurs anywhere else in the Bible. He is not reaching for formality. He is using the family word, and qualifying it only where the petition needs it.

And the hour has come closes a thread that has run the whole length of the book. Seven times John has used it. Three times it was not yet: at Cana to his mother (2:4), and twice when men tried to seize him and could not (7:30; 8:20). Then, from the arrival of the Greeks onward, four times it has come (12:23; 12:27; 13:1; here).

The verse has two scopes. Christ has authority over all flesh, every human being; but he gives eternal life to all whom you have given him. Some read given as those the Father foresaw would believe. But Jesus says, I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me (v. 9), which suggests that the giving is the Father’s choice, not his foresight.

Which means this prayer sits on a hinge that has been visible since the first miracle. For three years the answer was not yet, and the not-yet was a protection. It has now expired, by his own announcement, and the first thing he does with the news is pray.
verseByVerse.note: John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays for himself, his disciples and all future believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is eternal life, that they know you: the most important definition of eternal life in the New Testament. Eternal life is not primarily duration but relationship — knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. The knowing is relational: the knowing of intimate, personal, covenantal relationship, not merely intellectual acquaintance with facts about God. I have accomplished the work: spoken from the threshold of the cross as if it is already done. The prayer treats the crucifixion as accomplished — the eternal Son, who operates in eternal time, speaks the cross as past even as he walks toward Gethsemane.

Verse 3 is the nearest thing to a definition of eternal life anywhere in Scripture, and it is not the definition most people carry.

This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Not: eternal life is living forever. Not: eternal life is going to heaven when you die. Both of those are true and neither is what he says. Eternal life is knowing — and the verb is ginosko, which in this Gospel and in the Old Testament behind it means the knowledge of a person rather than of a subject.

Which has two consequences and both matter.

The first is that eternal life has already started for anyone who has it. If it were duration, it would begin at death. Because it is a relationship, it begins when the relationship does, and dying does not interrupt it — which is precisely what he told Martha at the tomb (11:25-26).

The second is more searching. It means that endless existence without God would not be eternal life at all. Take the test seriously: suppose a person were granted unlimited time, health restored, every faculty intact, and God were simply absent. That is not the offer being described here, and on this verse's terms it would not be life. What makes eternal life eternal is not the length of it but who is in it.

Now the guard, because this verse is used against the deity of Christ — the only true God is read as excluding Jesus, and the argument is a serious one that deserves an answer rather than a dismissal.

Notice what the sentence actually does. It makes knowing Jesus Christ part of the definition of eternal life, standing in the same clause and joined by and to knowing the only true God. No monotheist would put a creature there. And John, who wrote this sentence, wrote in his letter that the Son is the true God and eternal life (1 Jn. 5:20), using the same two words. The verse distinguishes the Father from the Son, which orthodoxy has always done. It does not divide them.

One curiosity worth flagging honestly: this is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus uses the full name Jesus Christ of himself. Some think John has glossed his Lord's words for readers a generation later, which would be entirely in keeping with how he writes. Nothing turns on it.
verseByVerse.note: “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information.

parallels.desc: that he understands and knows me
“It is finished”

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory that I had with you before the world existed: the pre-incarnate glory of the eternal Son, temporarily veiled in the humility of the incarnation, now to be fully restored in the resurrection and ascension. I have manifested your name: the entire ministry of Jesus — teaching, signs, foot-washing, and the cross — is the disclosure of the Father's name, his character, his love. Yours they were, and you gave them to me: the disciples belonged to the Father before they were given to the Son. Election is the Father's prior claim on the people the Son will redeem. They are not first the Son's and then the Father's; they are first the Father's and then, through gift, the Son's.

Weigh what is being asked in verse 5, because it is one of the boldest sentences in the Bible and it is said as a request.

Glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.

No prophet ever prayed anything remotely like it. Moses asked to see God's glory; this is a man asking for his own back. And the claim inside the request is the whole of the Prologue in a single clause: he had glory, with the Father, before there was a world to have it in.

Note the preposition — with you. It is the same construction as 1:1, the Word was with God. Not glory God gave him at some point, but glory possessed alongside the Father when nothing else existed.

Which locates the incarnation exactly. Something was set down. Paul's language is that he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped but emptied himself (Phil. 2:6-7), and this prayer is the same fact from the inside — a man asking to be given back what he had before, having spent some thirty years without it.

Then verse 6, and one phrase in it is startlingly generous: they have kept your word.

Look at who he is talking about. Eleven men who have understood almost nothing all evening, who spent the meal arguing about rank, who are within an hour of running into the dark, and one of whom will deny knowing him three times before the birds are up.

And this is his report to his Father about them. Not they are trying. Not they will improve. They have kept your word.

Here is the test, and it is worth doing slowly. Think of what an honest assessment of your discipleship would sound like — the version you would give if pressed, with the failures included. Now notice that Jesus, praying to the Father about men whose failures were about to become proverbial, did not give that assessment. He is not blind, and he is not flattering. He is describing them as what they had become by receiving his word, which is a different measurement from the one we habitually run on ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have received the words and come to know that I came from you: the progression of the disciples' understanding — receiving the words, coming to know the divine origin, believing in the sending. This is the apostolic faith that will ground the New Testament: not a speculative philosophy but the reception of words given by the Father through the Son, producing the saving knowledge that Jesus is the sent one. They have believed that you sent me: this is the core of saving faith — that Jesus is the Father's envoy, carrying the Father's redemptive word and accomplishing the Father's saving purpose.

There are four verbs in these two verses and they are laid out as a sequence: I have given them the words, they have received them, they have come to know, they have believed.

Given, received, known, believed. That is the entire mechanism of Christian faith set out in one sentence, and it is worth noticing that only the first is God's action in the grammar — though the whole prayer has been saying that the rest are his doing too.

And the order is instructive. Knowing comes before believing here, which is not how we usually put it; we tend to speak of believing first and understanding later. But look at what is known and what is believed. They came to know that I came from you — his origin. They believed that you sent me — his commission. The recognition of who he is precedes the trust in what he was sent to do, and both rest on words that were handed over rather than worked out.

Which is a quiet correction of two errors at once. Faith is not a leap made in the absence of content — there are words here, given and received. And it is not a conclusion reached by unaided reasoning either, since the words came from outside.

Note also the phrase in verse 7: now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. Everything. The teaching, the signs, the authority, the men themselves. Nothing in the ministry of Jesus originated with Jesus considered apart from the Father, and the disciples have finally grasped it — on the last night, about an hour before it stops mattering to them temporarily.

And there is a quiet dignity in how he reports it to the Father. He does not say they have begun to understand, or they are nearly there. He says they know, they have received, they have come to know, they have believed — four completed actions, credited in full.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am not praying for the world: a clarification of the specific scope of this part of the prayer, not a statement of indifference to the world (v. 21, 23 will pray for the believing world). This prayer is the intercessory intercession of the High Priest for his people — specific, named, elect. All mine are yours, and yours are mine: the perfect mutual ownership of Father and Son extends to encompass the disciples. They belong simultaneously to the Father (given to the Son) and to the Son (who gives them eternal life). I am glorified in them: the disciples' existence is the Son's ongoing glory — the exhibition of what grace produces in those who receive it.

I am not praying for the world. It is the coldest-sounding sentence in the warmest chapter in the Bible, and it should not be hurried past, because people are genuinely troubled by it.

Three things settle it, and the first is simply what the sentence is.

It is a statement about the scope of this petition, not about the disposition of the one praying. He is at that moment asking for something specific — that these eleven men be kept, in a world that is about to try to kill them — and the world cannot be the subject of that request. One does not pray for the fire and the house in the same sentence.

The second is that the same prayer turns to the world twice, a few verses on. So that the world may believe that you have sent me (v. 21); so that the world may know (v. 23). The unity he asks for is asked for the world's sake. A man indifferent to the world does not make its persuasion the goal of his petition for the church.

The third is the plainest. Within hours the man who said I am not praying for the world would be praying, out loud, from a cross, for the men driving the nails: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Lk. 23:34). That is not a prayer for the church.

So what the verse does say — and it does say it — is that there is a particular intercession which has a particular object, and the object is the people the Father gave him. This is the High Priest with the names on his breastplate. He is not praying generically. He is praying for named individuals, and the naming is the comfort rather than the offence.

Then the clause that sounds like accounting and is not: all mine are yours, and yours are mine.

Any of us could say the first half. Everything I have is God's — that is ordinary piety, and it is true. Nobody can say the second half. Yours are mine is a claim to hold the Father's property as one's own, and Luther is said to have observed that no creature could utter it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep them in your name: the prayer for the disciples' preservation after Jesus' departure. Their security in the world does not rest on their own spiritual strength but on the Father's keeping power. That they may be one, even as we are one: the Trinitarian unity as the pattern and source of ecclesial unity — not organizational but relational, not uniformity but the unity of shared love and purpose. Not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction: the eleven's preservation is contrasted with Judas' defection, which is not a failure of the keeping power but the fulfillment of the Scripture — divine sovereignty encompassing even apostasy.

Holy Father — and it occurs nowhere else in the Bible.

He has been saying Father all evening and will say it three more times. Here, and only here, he adds holy, and the reason is in the petition attached: he is asking that these men be kept in a world that is unholy, and that they be made one. Holiness is exactly the attribute being drawn on.

Then a wordplay in verse 12 that no English version can show, and it is the sharpest thing in the passage. Not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction — apoleto and apoleias, the same root twice in one clause. Not one was lost except the son of lostness. The man is named by the very thing that did not happen to anybody else.

The phrase itself turns up once more in the New Testament, for the man of lawlessness (2 Thess. 2:3), and it is a Hebrew way of saying what somebody belongs to or is destined for.

Now the hard question, and it must not be dodged: that the Scripture might be fulfilled. Was Judas free?

Two things have to be held and the New Testament holds them both without visible strain. Judas is never once described as a victim. He is called a thief who helped himself to the bag (12:6), the devil enters him after he takes the bread (13:27), and Peter says he turned aside to go to his own place (Acts 1:25) — his own, chosen, fitting. Nothing in any account treats him as a man who wanted otherwise.

And equally, Scripture had said it would happen, and the prayer says so here, and Peter preaching at Pentecost says the whole event went forward according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God — in the same breath as you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23).

What Scripture never does is derive one from the other. It does not say Judas betrayed him because it was written; it says it was written, and he did it, and both are true. Anyone who claims to have resolved that has almost certainly done so by quietly dropping one half.

The Scripture Jesus means is probably Psalm 41:9, which he quoted of Judas the night before: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (13:18). Peter later applies Psalm 109:8 to him: Let another take his office (Acts 1:20).

What is worth adding is the pastoral note. This verse is not given to help us classify anybody. It is given to explain why the keeping did not fail — I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost — and the exception is the man who was never inside the guarding in the first place.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction — Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves: the joy Jesus has in the Father's presence and in the accomplishment of the Father's will — this is what he prays will fill the disciples. Joy is not incidental to Christian life but its intended condition. I have given them your word: the word that has separated them from the world is the same word that sustains them through the world's hatred. The world hates because the disciples are not of the world — the election that brings them out of the world's system makes them targets of its hostility. The cross of the disciples is the natural consequence of the election that saved them.

Notice the reason he gives for having said any of it out loud: these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.

He is praying. They are listening. And he says he is praying audibly, in their hearing, for their sake — so that they will have his joy.

That is a strange and rather moving thing to realise about this chapter. It is a genuine prayer, addressed to the Father throughout, and it is also being said where eleven frightened men can hear every word. He wanted them to overhear it. Everything in it about their being given to him, kept, guarded, loved, sent — they heard him say to his Father, which is a different thing from being told it directly.

Here is the test. Consider the difference between somebody telling you they value you, and accidentally overhearing them say it to a third party when they did not know you were listening. The second is the one that lands. This prayer was engineered to be the second, and the disciples were meant to spend the rest of their lives remembering what he said about them when he was talking to his Father.

And my joy fulfilled in themselves is the third time joy has come up in about an hour (15:11; 16:24; here). He keeps returning to it on the worst night of his life, which tells you something about what he thought his friends were going to need.

Then the sober half: the world has hated them because they are not of the world. He does not pray it away. He states it as the present condition — has hated, already, before the arrest — and moves straight on to what he will ask instead.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not take them out of the world: the Christian life is not withdrawal from culture but engaged presence within it under divine protection. The prayer is for preservation in the world, not extraction from it. Keep them from the evil one: the specific threat named — not suffering or persecution but the evil one whose strategy is to snatch them from the Father's hand (10:28-29). The prayer for protection is precisely the Father's answer to the enemy's strategy. They are not of the world: the ontological status — belonging to the new creation, to the kingdom of God, to the Father — remains even while they inhabit the old world. Citizens of heaven on embassy in the world.

This is the verse that settles what a Christian is supposed to do with the world, and it does it by refusing both of the available shortcuts.

I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.

The first shortcut is withdrawal — the monastery, the compound, the Christian bubble, the instinct to arrange a life in which one need never deal with anybody who does not already agree. It is an ancient instinct and it is not wicked; it is usually motivated by a genuine desire not to be contaminated. He declines to ask for it, and he had the strongest possible reason to want it for men he loved who were about to be hunted.

The second is assimilation, which the next verse blocks: they are not of the world. Staying in it is not the same as belonging to it.

So the position he prays for is the uncomfortable middle, and it is the only one on offer. Fully in, not of. And the practical shape of it is not withdrawal from the neighbours but a difference in what one is loyal to, which is much harder to arrange and impossible to fake.

A note on the last phrase, which is genuinely ambiguous in the Greek. Keep them from the evil one could equally be rendered from evil — the form is the same, and translators differ. It is the identical ambiguity in the last line of the Lord's Prayer, and for the same reason.

Which is itself worth noticing. This prayer keeps brushing against that one: a Father addressed, a name hallowed, a will done, a keeping from evil, a glory at the end. He taught them to pray it, and here he is doing something very like it himself, on the last night, with the petitions turned toward them instead of toward himself.

And what he asks for is protection rather than exemption. Not that nothing will happen to them — a great deal did, and most of them died for it — but that the one who wants them will not get them.

parallels.desc: deliver us from evil

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sanctify them in the truth: sanctify means to set apart for holy purpose (so the ESV margin) — the same word applied to Jesus' own consecration (v. 19). The disciples are to be made holy by the truth — the word of God that is the means of ongoing sanctification. Your word is truth: the Scriptures as the instrument of the Spirit's sanctifying work. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them: the mission of the disciples is patterned on and derived from the mission of the Son. The Father sent the Son; the Son sends the disciples. The same commission, the same authority, the same purpose — world-mission in the Father's name.

Two things in verse 17 are sharper than the English suggests.

The first is that sanctify is not primarily a moral word. Hagiazo means to set apart for a purpose — it is what was done to vessels, to a day, to a priest. The moral content follows from the setting apart rather than the other way round: a thing devoted to God must then be fit for him. So the petition is not first make them better but make them yours, for this job — which is exactly why the next verse is about being sent.

The second is the grammar of the last clause. Not your word is true, which would be a claim about accuracy. Your word is truth — a noun, not an adjective. It does not merely correspond to reality; it is the thing reality is measured by.

And the instrument named for the sanctifying is that word. Not an experience, not a discipline, not a decision. If a person wants to know what God actually uses to set people apart and make them fit for him, this verse answers in four words, and the answer is a book.

Which is worth stating plainly for the reader who feels stuck. The most common Christian instinct when growth has stalled is to look for a new technique or a stronger resolution. This verse points somewhere duller and more effective, and it is the same place the pruning came from in chapter 15 — you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (15:3).

Then verse 18, which is this Gospel's version of the Great Commission and is usually overlooked because it is inside a prayer: as you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. He will say it again to their faces on Easter evening (20:21). And the comparison is not modest. The pattern for how the church is sent is how the Son was sent — which meant coming all the way in, living among people at their level, and being at their disposal.
verseByVerse.note: To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy.

parallels.desc: your law is true

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I consecrate myself: the language of priestly sacrifice — Jesus sets himself apart as the holy offering that will accomplish the sanctification he prays for the disciples. His death is not incidental but the means of their holiness. Those who will believe through their word: the prayer expands beyond the eleven to encompass every believer throughout history, including those reading this prayer in every generation. The High-Priestly Prayer is an intercession that reaches forward in time, encompassing the entire church that the apostolic word will gather. Every Christian stands within the scope of this prayer.

Verse 19 has the priest and the sacrifice in one sentence, and the verb is the one from two verses earlier. For their sake I consecrate myself — hagiazo again, the same word he has just used of them.

In the Old Testament ritual those were two different operations performed by two different parties. The priest was consecrated; the animal was consecrated; the priest consecrated the animal. Here one person does all of it to himself, for other people, the night before it takes effect.

And the logic is stated: that they also may be sanctified in truth. Their being set apart depends on his. He goes first, and what he does to himself is the reason the thing can be done to them at all.

Then verse 20, and the reader should stop here.

I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.

The prayer has been about eleven men in a room. In one sentence it opens out and takes in everybody who would ever come to faith through what those men would go on to say — which is the entire church, in every century, including whoever is reading this page.

That is not a devotional flourish; it is what the sentence means. The chain is specified: through their word. The eleven spoke, and people believed, and those people spoke, and it has not stopped. Anybody who believes in Christ today believes because that word arrived, by however long a route, and this verse says such a person was in view on the Thursday night.

So everything that follows — the unity, the glory given, being loved as the Son is loved, being with him where he is — is not asked for the apostles alone. It is asked for the ordinary Christian who has never seen a miracle and finds prayer difficult.

He knew, in that room, that there would be people two thousand years later who would come to him because eleven frightened men eventually told somebody. And he did not merely foresee them. He prayed for them by name in the only way a person can be named who does not yet exist — those who will believe in me — and then he went out and made it possible.

Nobody has ever been prayed for like that. Not because the requests are large, though they are, but because of when it was said: with the arrest an hour off, in the last quiet he would have, spending it on strangers who had not been born.

parallels.desc: sanctified through the offering of his body

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they may all be one: the great prayer for ecclesial unity, patterned explicitly on Trinitarian unity. The church's unity is not achieved by human effort but given by participation in the Trinitarian life — they may be in us. The purpose is missional: so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The divided church is the church whose witness is compromised; the united church is the church whose common life is itself an argument for the gospel. The glory given to the disciples — the shared life of the Son — is the source of the unity that becomes the world's witness.

This is the verse on which the whole question of a divided church turns. Three answers are given to it. Rome reads the prayer as asking for one visible institution under one visible head, and takes the existence of separated churches as the standing wound this prayer was meant to prevent. The ecumenical movement of the last century read it as a mandate to merge structures, and set about doing so. And a good many Protestants have read it as a prayer for an invisible unity only, on the comfortable assumption that since all true believers are already one in Christ, our visible divisions cost nothing.

The prayer itself rules out each of them. Against the single-institution and merger readings, look at the pattern Jesus gives: as you, Father, are in me, and I in you. The unity he asks for is modelled on the life of the Trinity, where the persons are genuinely distinct and the unity is one of love, life and will rather than of administration. Nothing in that picture requires a single earthly organisation, and the apostolic churches of the New Testament were plainly not one. But against the invisible-only reading, look at the purpose clause: so that the world may believe. A unity the world cannot see cannot persuade the world of anything. Whatever this unity is, it must show.

Which leaves the harder and better answer. It is not a summons to dissolve our confessions into one institution, and it is not permission to be comfortable about our divisions. It asks for a love between Christians that outsiders can actually observe and cannot account for — believers who honour one another across the lines, refuse to caricature, and are visibly glad of grace wherever it appears.

And one thing more must be said, because it is in the same prayer. Four verses earlier Jesus asked, sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth (v. 17). Unity and truth are petitions of one prayer and cannot be traded against each other. A unity bought by agreeing to say less than the gospel says is not the answer to this prayer but a counterfeit of it, and the Reformers, who did not leave lightly, understood that. What is asked here is not that we stop caring what is true. It is that those who hold the truth should stop treating each other as enemies.

One further thing about verse 22, which is easy to pass over: the glory that you have given me I have given to them.

Given. Past tense, before the cross, to eleven men who were about to run. Whatever this glory is, it was already in their possession while they were behaving at their worst — which rules out reading it as a reward for anything.

What is it? The prayer answers in the same breath: that they may be one even as we are one. The glory given is the shared life that produces the unity. Not radiance, not status, not visible splendour — a participation in what the Father and the Son have between them.

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You loved them even as you loved me: the astonishing statement that the Father's love for the disciples is of the same kind as the Father's love for the Son. The beloved Son shares his belovedness with those the Father has given him. I desire that they may be with me where I am: the final petition of the prayer is for the presence of the disciples with Jesus in the Father's glory. The prayer is eschatological: the cross that is hours away, the resurrection three days beyond, and the consummation when the Father's loved ones behold the Son's eternal glory — all are held in this single desire.

Two clauses in these verses are among the most difficult things in the Bible to believe about oneself, and they should be stated as plainly as possible.

The first: you… loved them even as you loved me.

Not loved them. Not loved them very much. Even as you loved me — the same comparison he used at 15:9, now made to the Father in prayer, which means it is not a figure of speech aimed at encouraging anybody. He is telling the Father what is the case.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable. Most Christians will affirm that God loves them, and most, if pressed, would describe that love as something a good deal cooler than the love of the Father for the Son — a settled goodwill, perhaps a determination to put up with them. This verse forbids it. The measure is not a lot; the measure is the love that has existed between the Father and the Son from before the world was made, and the sentence has no qualifier in it anywhere.

The second is verse 24, and the verb changes. Everything up to now has been asking. Here: Father, I desire. It is the only place in any recorded prayer of his where he speaks like that. It is the language of a son who knows exactly where he stands, exercising a right.

And what he uses it for is not deliverance, or vindication, or a shorter road. He uses it to ask that the people he is leaving should end up where he is.

That they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory.

Which is the second time in this prayer he has looked back before the world existed — first to ask for his glory back (v. 5), now to say why the Father gave it: because you loved me before the foundation of the world. The love came first. Before light, before time, before there was anything to be glorified in front of, there was a Father loving a Son — and this prayer asks that a crowd of latecomers be brought in to watch.

verseByVerse.quote: "O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will continue to make it known: the present ministry of the risen, ascended Son — through the Spirit, through the word, through the preaching of the apostles and their successors — continues the making-known of the Father's name. That the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them: the final note of the prayer is love and indwelling — the Trinitarian love flowing into and dwelling within the disciples, the Son himself making his home in those he has chosen and redeemed. The prayer ends not with requests but with presence: I in them. This is the goal of all of redemption — God with his people, in his people, as the consummation of the covenant love that preceded the foundation of the world.

O righteous Father — the second and last of the qualified addresses, and again unique in Scripture.

He reaches for righteous at the point where he is contrasting the world's ignorance with his own knowledge and the disciples' recognition. It is the word for a judge who gets the verdict right, and it is used at the moment when a right verdict is about to be spectacularly withheld by every human court he will stand in before morning.

Then I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known.

Two tenses, and the future is the striking one. He is an hour from arrest and speaks of a work of disclosure that will go on. Not I have finished making it known — he said at verse 4 that he had accomplished the work he was given, and here he says the making-known continues. Both are true: the accomplishing is the cross, and the disclosing does not stop at the cross. It goes on through the Spirit and through the church, and it is going on now.

And then the last words of the prayer, which are also the last words he speaks before the garden.

That the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.

Not that they may know about the love. That the love itself — the actual love of the Father for the Son, the specific one — should be located inside them. And then four words with nothing after them: and I in them.

The prayer ends without a petition. He does not close with a request or a summary; he ends by naming a destination, and the destination is not a place. Four chapters of farewell, a discourse about a vine, a promise of the Spirit, an intercession for the whole church across every century — and the final word is a preposition and a pronoun. In them.

That is where all of it was going. Not to a system, not to an institution, not even to heaven considered as a location, but to the Son of God taking up residence inside ordinary people. He asked for it out loud, where they could hear, and then he stood up and went out to make it possible.
