Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.<sup>7</sup>Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you.<sup>8</sup>For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.<sup>9</sup>I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.<sup>10</sup>All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.<sup>11</sup>And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one.<sup>12</sup>While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.<sup>13</sup>But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.<sup>14</sup>I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>15</sup>I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.<sup>16</sup>They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>17</sup>Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.<sup>18</sup>As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.<sup>19</sup>And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.<sup>20</sup>“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,<sup>21</sup>that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.<sup>22</sup>The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,<sup>23</sup>I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.<sup>24</sup>Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.<sup>25</sup>O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me.<sup>26</sup>I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

18.title: The Arrest, the Denial, and the Trial Before Pilate

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — Gethsemane, the Arrest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus crosses the Kidron valley and enters the garden where Judas knows to find him. When the soldiers arrive with Judas, Jesus steps forward to identify himself — the sovereign initiative of the one who lays down his own life. Peter denies three times as predicted. Jesus is taken to Annas and then Caiaphas.

The Kidron and the garden (vv. 1-2). There is an Old Testament scene underneath this crossing. A thousand years earlier another king went out of Jerusalem by night, betrayed — the king crossed the brook Kidron (2 Sam. 15:23) — and the man who betrayed David was Ahithophel, his own counsellor, who then set his house in order and hanged himself (2 Sam. 17:23). David crossed to save his life; the son of David crosses to lay his down. John also declines to name the place Gethsemane: he calls it a garden, and he alone does, and he will use the word again at 19:41. The story that went wrong in a garden is being put right in one. And the detail that hurts is that Judas knew the place because it was theirs.

The absurd arrest (vv. 3-4). A band of soldiers with its captain (v. 12) suggests a Roman cohort — six hundred men at full strength, a couple of hundred as a detachment, and Romans rather than temple police, which means Pilate had already been approached. They come with lanterns and torches at Passover, which falls at full moon: fire carried on the brightest night of the month to find the Light of the world. And his first words in the passion — whom do you seek? — echo the first words he speaks anywhere in this Gospel (what are you seeking?, 1:38), now put to men with weapons.

Let these men go (vv. 8-9). It is the shepherd chapter acted out. He negotiates at the moment of arrest and uses his only leverage to get his friends released — not a hearing, not fair treatment, not time. Every one of the eleven survived that night, which is not what usually happened to the followers of an executed insurrectionist. And John says it fulfilled the prayer they had overheard an hour earlier (17:12): the prayer and the answer to the prayer are the same person.

The sword and the cup (vv. 10-11). Peter is the only man in the New Testament who ever drew a weapon for Jesus, and he was outnumbered several hundred to one — whatever else it was, it was not cowardice. John alone names both him and Malchus, the same late-witness pattern as with Lazarus. What Peter had got wrong was not his courage but his conclusion: he had heard about the cup and the hour and arrived believing his job was to prevent it. The verse-by-verse treats the cup at length, including why this Gospel has no Gethsemane scene.

Annas (vv. 13-14). He had been high priest until Rome removed him, but five of his sons and his son-in-law held the office after him — for half a century the high priesthood was a family business, which is why Luke can name two men for one office (Lk. 3:2). Taking Jesus there first is not a legal step; it is a private call at the house of the family with the most to lose.

The other disciple (vv. 15-16). Traditionally John, though a Galilean fisherman being known to the high priest is not obvious and the Gospel does not explain it. What is certain is what he does with the access: he brings Peter in — and inside is exactly where Peter fails. The kindness was real. If Peter had been left in the street, the worst night of his life would not have happened.

I am not (v. 17). The girl's question expects the answer no; she is not accusing him. No threat has been made and nobody has drawn anything. And Peter's I am not is the exact negation of the I am Jesus said in the garden (the ESV note at 18:5). Denial in the New Testament is rarely dramatic — it is usually this: taking the answer somebody has already assumed, because correcting them would be awkward.

The Annas hearing (vv. 19-24). Note first what John omits — the Sanhedrin session with witnesses and the blasphemy charge, which the other three record; he alone gives us Annas, and the “other disciple” who was in the courtyard was very probably John himself. The high priest asks about two things, his disciples and his teaching, and Jesus answers only the second: not one word about the disciples, an hour after getting them out of the garden. Then the slap — an open-handed strike, the standard gesture for putting an inferior in his place, which is exactly how the officer justifies it. The first violence done to Jesus is not judicial or even angry; it is etiquette enforcement by a member of the temple staff. Isaiah had described it, and the verbs are worth having: I gave my back… I hid not my face (Isa. 50:6). And his reply objects on a point of law without a trace of retaliation, which is worth noticing, since turn the other cheek is often taken to require silence.

The rooster (v. 27). John reports the most catastrophic failure in the New Testament in ten words and moves on. Luke supplies what happened next: the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Lk. 22:61), and Peter remembered the saying. The crow did not condemn him; it reminded him — which is the mercy hidden in the prediction. A failure nobody warned you about is evidence that everything has come apart; a failure your Lord described to your face beforehand is inside the story rather than the end of it. And John leaves the weeping out because he is saving it for a beach and another charcoal fire.
verseByVerse.theology: I am he — ego eimi — spoken in the garden, is the same divine Name Jesus has been claiming throughout the gospel. When he says it, the soldiers fall to the ground: the mere self-identification of the Son of God is enough to flatten an armed cohort. Jesus surrenders not because he is overpowered but because he chooses to. This is the theology of the atonement in action: the Lamb who lays down his own life, the Shepherd who gives himself for the sheep. The arrest is simultaneously Jesus' most vulnerable moment and his most sovereign act.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter's denial happens at the same fire where the servants are warming themselves — the detail is vivid and specific. He denies knowing Jesus to a slave girl, to bystanders, to a relative of the man whose ear he cut off. Three denials as predicted, completed at the crowing of the rooster. Peter's failure is not moral weakness alone but the collapse of self-confident discipleship — the faith that depends on its own resources rather than on grace. His restoration (ch. 21) will be built on a different foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Across the Kidron Valley: in the Passover season, by one tradition, the blood of the thousands of sacrificed lambs ran down into this valley. Jesus crosses the valley of blood to meet his own death. The garden where he often met with his disciples is the place Judas knows — the private place of fellowship becomes the place of betrayal. This is the pattern of all intimate betrayal: the enemy uses knowledge gained in trust. Jesus goes there deliberately, not avoiding the place Judas knows but going to the known place on his own terms, at his own time.

There is an Old Testament scene underneath this crossing, and once it is seen the whole night changes shape.

A thousand years earlier another king went out of Jerusalem in the dark, betrayed. And all the land wept aloud… and the king crossed the brook Kidron (2 Sam. 15:23). David is fleeing Absalom, and he goes up the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare.

And the man who had betrayed him was Ahithophel, his own counsellor, the friend whose advice had been as if one consulted the word of God (2 Sam. 16:23). David prayed that his counsel would be turned to foolishness. And when Ahithophel saw that it had been, he set his house in order and hanged himself (2 Sam. 17:23).

A king crossing the Kidron by night, out of Jerusalem, betrayed by a trusted intimate who then hangs himself. It has all happened before, and the son of David is now walking the same ground with the opposite purpose — David went over it to save his life, and this King goes over it to lay his down.

Two details in John's own wording repay attention. The Kidron is a cheimarros, a winter torrent — a stream bed that is dry most of the year and runs only after rain. And there is a tradition, impossible to verify, that the blood from the temple sacrifices was channelled down into it, which at Passover would have been the blood of thousands of lambs.

And John does not call the place Gethsemane, though he plainly knows it. He calls it a garden — kepos — and he is the only evangelist who does. He will use the word again at 19:41: in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. The story that went wrong in a garden is being put right in one, and John has quietly bracketed the passion between two of them.

Then the detail that hurts: Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples. It was not discovered. It was known, because it was theirs. The place they had gone to be together is the place that made the arrest possible, and the only reason Judas could find him in the dark is that he had been welcome there.
verseByVerse.note: The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; it is usually dry except in the rainy season. Matthew and Mark name the garden Gethsemane.

parallels.desc: David, betrayed, crosses the Kidron weeping

verseByVerse.quote: So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing all that would happen to him, he came forward: the sovereign initiative of Jesus in his own arrest. They came with torches to find the Light of the world in a garden; Jesus steps forward to meet them before they can search. Whom do you seek? — the question reverses the dynamic: the hunter is asked to identify his quarry, as if Jesus is in charge of the proceedings, which he is. This is John's consistent presentation of the passion: Jesus is never the passive victim of forces beyond his control but the sovereign Lord arranging the circumstances of his own self-offering.

Two things about the arresting party are worth measuring, because both are absurd and the absurdity is the point.

The first is the size. John says a band of soldiers — speira, which is the Greek for a Roman cohort. At full strength that is six hundred men; even a detachment would be a couple of hundred, and if they are Romans, as the word suggests, Pilate had already been approached. Add the officers from the chief priests. That force has been assembled to take one teacher and eleven followers, in a garden, at night.

The second is the equipment: lanterns and torches. It is Passover, which falls at full moon. They have come out on the brightest night of the month, carrying fire, to look for the Light of the world — and they will not find him until he steps out and tells them where he is.

Then the question, and it is the first thing he says in the passion narrative: whom do you seek?

It is worth noticing what those words are. They echo the very first words Jesus speaks in this Gospel — what are you seeking? — asked of two men following him in chapter 1. The book opens with him asking what people want, and the arrest opens with the same question put to men with weapons.

And John tells us why he asked it, which removes any suggestion of theatre: Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward. Not was found. Not was seized. He went out to them. Everything that follows in this Gospel's account of the passion is governed by that verb.

And John pauses to tell us what he knew as he did it: knowing all that would happen to him. Not the general shape of it. All of it — the ropes, the courtyard, the slap, the flogging, the nails, the cross.

There is a kind of courage that depends on not knowing quite how bad it will be. This is the other kind, and it is much rarer. He walked out of the trees toward the torches with the entire afternoon of the following day already in view.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion — Roman troops joined with the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am he — ego eimi: the divine Name, spoken without predicate, the same declaration that drove his opponents to reach for stones (8:58-59). Now the soldiers fall to the ground. A soldier with a weapon is undone by three words from the one he came to arrest. This is not a display of power intended to prevent the arrest — Jesus will surrender momentarily — but a disclosure: the one they have come to take is the I AM, the God of the exodus. The falling is involuntary reverence before the presence of the Holy One. Even those who came to destroy him cannot stand before him without his permission.

The Greek here is barer than the English can be. They say they want Jesus of Nazareth, and he answers with two words: ego eimi. There is no he. The pronoun in most translations is supplied because English needs it.

Which means the sentence he says in the dark is grammatically identical to the sentence that made them pick up stones at 8:58, and to what God said out of the bush.

And then the strangest verse in the arrest: they drew back and fell to the ground.

It is worth being careful about what this is and is not. It is not a rescue — nobody is prevented from anything, and within seconds he is being tied up. It is not a threat. He does not follow it up. The soldiers get up and do their job.

What it is, is a demonstration placed at exactly the point where the reader most needs it. From here to the end of the book, everything done to him is done by other people: he is bound, struck, tried, flogged, sentenced, nailed. John puts one moment at the front of that sequence in which an armed cohort goes over backwards at three words, so that nobody afterwards can say he was overpowered.

Note also the placement of a single clause: Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. John will not let it pass. He has already said in verse 2 that Judas knew the place; now, in the middle of the sentence about the divine Name, he records where the man was standing.

He was among the soldiers. And when they went down, he went down with them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verse 8 — the words of the divine name.

parallels.desc: my adversaries stumble and fall

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let these men go: the shepherd securing the safety of the flock even in the moment of his own surrender. He negotiates the disciples' freedom as the condition of his submission to arrest — the good shepherd laying down his life for the sheep is literally arranging that the sheep escape while he remains. John will note (v. 9) that this fulfills Jesus' own prayer — not one of them was lost (17:12). The cross is both the fulfillment of the prayer and the guarantee of the disciples' preservation. What Jesus prayed, he enacted through his own surrender.

If you seek me, let these men go.

It is a condition. He is negotiating, at the moment of his arrest, with a cohort that has just been knocked off its feet — and the only thing he asks for is that his friends be allowed to walk away.

Consider what he does not ask for. Not a hearing. Not fair treatment. Not time. Not that the disciples be permitted to come with him, which is what they had all sworn they wanted a few hours earlier. He uses the one piece of leverage he has to get them out of the garden.

And it worked. Every one of the eleven survived that night, which is not what usually happened to the followers of an executed insurrectionist. The Romans had every reason to take the lot of them.

Then John's note in the next verse, and it is the reason the negotiation is in the account at all: this was to fulfill the word that he had spoken, of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.

He had prayed that an hour before, out loud, where they could hear (17:12). And here he is making it true himself, with soldiers in front of him, by giving himself up on condition that they are released.

Which is worth having as a picture of what he does generally. The prayer and the answer to the prayer are the same person. He asked the Father to keep them, and then kept them, and the keeping cost him the thing he was keeping them from.

Note also that John applies a saying about eternal security to a matter of physical safety on one particular night. That is either a misapplication or a hint. Given who is writing, it is a hint: the man who will not let them be arrested in a garden is the same man who will not let them be lost at the end, and the second promise is made credible by watching him keep the first.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one." Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant's name was Malchus.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's sword-blow is the last act of self-reliant discipleship — the attempt to defend Jesus by force, to prevent the arrest, to fight what Jesus has already embraced. The name Malchus is remembered because eyewitness testimony preserves particulars that were present at the scene. Peter's violence is simultaneously loyal and misguided: loyal to Jesus in intention, misguided about what Jesus requires. The right ear cut off will be restored by Jesus (Luke 22:51) — one last healing before the cross, one last demonstration that his kingdom does not advance by the sword.

Peter is the only man in the New Testament who ever drew a weapon in defence of Jesus, and it is worth being fair to him before drawing the lesson.

He was outnumbered several hundred to one. He had been told an hour earlier that he would deny his master before dawn and had flatly contradicted it. He drew anyway, and swung at a man's head, and if his aim had been better he would have killed him. Whatever else this is, it is not cowardice, and the same man will be denying everything within the hour — which tells you something true and uncomfortable about how little courage in one form predicts courage in another.

And the naming is worth noticing. John alone tells us it was Peter, and John alone gives us Malchus. The other three Gospels say only that one of those who stood by struck the servant of the high priest. It is the same pattern as with Lazarus: John writes last, a generation on, when a man who assaulted the high priest's household — and the household member who could identify him — are both beyond the reach of anybody who might have made trouble.

Then the thing Peter had got wrong, which was not his courage but his reading of the situation. He had heard the prediction and concluded that the arrest must be prevented. He had heard about the cup and the hour and the good shepherd laying down his life, and he arrived at the garden believing his job was to stop it.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable for zealous people. Ask what you are currently defending God from. If the honest answer involves preventing something he has already said he intends to do — a loss, a humbling, a door closing — then the sword is out, and the most likely outcome is somebody else's ear.

Luke, who was a doctor, is the one who tells us Jesus touched it and healed him (Lk. 22:51). The last miracle before the cross was the repair of damage done by a disciple.
verseByVerse.note: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me? The cup is the language of divine wrath and suffering throughout the Old Testament (Ps. 75:8; Isa. 51:17; Jer. 25:15). Jesus does not merely accept suffering; he embraces the specific cup the Father has prepared — the cup of wrath that his people deserved to drink. The binding of Jesus: the Creator bound by his creatures, the Lord of all submitted to the authority he has given to human governments. The arrest is real, the binding is real, and both are within the sovereign purpose of the Father who sent him.

That word cup should prompt a question, because of what John has not told us. All three of the other Gospels place at this spot the most famous prayer ever prayed in a garden: Jesus falling on his face, sweating, asking three times that the cup might pass, and the disciples asleep a stone's throw away. John gives us none of it. He brings Jesus across the Kidron, and the next thing that happens is that Judas arrives with lanterns. A reader who knows the other accounts will notice the silence at once.

He is not concealing the anguish, and the proof is that he assumes it here. Jesus speaks of the cup the Father has given me as of something already settled between them — you cannot resolve a struggle you never had, and the sentence only makes sense if there was one. John has simply written the agony in his own place and his own way. He put it in chapter 12, in daylight, in public, before a crowd: now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? But for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). That is the same prayer, the same request raised and the same refusal to press it, only moved out of the dark and into the open where everyone could hear.

And that is the shape of the whole passion in this Gospel. The others show us a man overtaken by horror and holding on; John shows us a man walking into it with his eyes open — going out to meet the soldiers rather than waiting to be found, asking whom they seek, knocking them off their feet with a word, and then holding out his hands. Both are true and the church has always needed both. Take John without the others and you may forget what it cost him. Take the others without John and you may forget that nobody took his life from him.

One more thing about the binding at verse 12, which is easy to read past.

They arrested Jesus and bound him. There was a man in Israel's memory who had been bound by his father and laid on wood on a mountain, and who was old enough to have resisted and did not (Gen. 22:9). The Jewish tradition called it the Akedah, the Binding, and it was one of the great themes of Passover-season devotion.

Isaac was released and a ram was found. This time the ropes stay on.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had given him to bear.

verseByVerse.quote: First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Annas first: the elder statesman of the priestly establishment, deposed by Rome but still holding enormous influence. The procedural irregularity of a nighttime hearing before the former high priest is part of the expedient that abandons legal principle for political outcome. It was Caiaphas who had advised: John's reminder of 11:49-50 connects the procedural irregularity to the larger political calculation. The high priest who declared it better for one man to die is now presiding over the arrangements for that death. He is accomplishing his own prophecy without understanding it.

A word about who Annas was, because the arrangement is odd and the oddity matters.

He had been high priest himself from about AD 6 to 15, until the Romans removed him. But five of his sons held the office after him, and Caiaphas was his son-in-law — so for roughly half a century the high priesthood of Israel was a family business run out of one house. Luke can write of a year during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas (Lk. 3:2), naming two men for an office that had one holder, because everybody understood who was actually in charge.

Which is why Jesus is taken to him first. It is not a legal step. Annas holds no office. It is a private call at the house of the man whose family had the most to lose, before anything official begins.

And John reminds us of what Caiaphas had already said: it would be expedient that one man should die for the people. He recorded it at 11:49-50 and told us it was prophecy the man did not know he was uttering. Now the prophet is the presiding judge.

There is something worth noting about the whole night's proceedings here. Jewish law as later codified forbade capital trials at night, forbade them on the eve of a festival, required a full day to elapse before a death sentence, and required the court to sit in its own chamber. Every one of those is broken in the next few hours. How much of that law was in force in the AD 30s is genuinely disputed, and the point should not be pressed further than the evidence allows. But the men conducting this are the guardians of the law, and they are working in the middle of the night in a private house.
verseByVerse.note: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and he remained the power behind it. Only John records this first hearing.

parallels.desc: the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beloved disciple has access to the high priest's courtyard — a detail that has generated much discussion about John's social connections. What matters is the proximity: two disciples are present for the trial, one inside and one brought in through the other's connection. This is the geography of the passion: the disciples who scattered are here at the margins of the trial, watching. The one who stands by Jesus at the cross (19:26) begins by standing in the courtyard. Fidelity under pressure begins with the willingness to be present where the pressure is greatest.

The other disciple raises a real question and it deserves an honest answer rather than a confident one.

Traditionally he is John himself, which fits the way this Gospel refers to its author in the third person and never by name. The difficulty is the next clause: he was known to the high priest — and a Galilean fisherman's acquaintance with the household of Annas is not obvious. Some have supposed a family fish business supplying Jerusalem; some that John's mother was related to Mary and therefore, distantly, to a priestly family; some that the disciple is somebody else entirely, unnamed. The Gospel does not say, and neither should a commentary.

What is not in doubt is what he does with the access. He goes back out to the door and gets Peter in.

And that is worth sitting with, because it is one of the small ironies of the passion. The man with the connections uses them to bring his friend inside — and inside is precisely where Peter will fail. Nobody intended it. The kindness was real. If Peter had been left standing in the street he would have gone home, and the worst night of his life would not have happened.

Which is not a reason to be careful about kindness. It is a reason to be honest about how failure actually arrives: not usually through malice, and often through a door somebody opened for us out of love.

Note also the small detail that the door is kept by a servant girl. She is about to ask Peter a question, and the whole weight of the most famous denial in history will come down on an exchange with a young woman doing a menial job at a gate.
verseByVerse.note: The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" He said, "I am not." Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first denial is to a servant girl — the least threatening possible interrogator — and Peter denies without hesitation. I am not: the direct inversion of Jesus' ego eimi. Where Jesus said I am he, Peter says I am not. The charcoal fire is a sensory detail that eyewitness memory preserves; a charcoal fire appears only here and in 21:9, where Peter's restoration happens at another charcoal fire. The smell of the fire will become the smell of remembered failure and, eventually, of grace received.

Look at the form of the question, because it makes what follows worse rather than better.

You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you? The Greek construction expects the answer no. She is not accusing him. She is a girl at a door, making conversation, and the way she frames it hands him the answer she assumes — probably without much interest either way.

No threat has been made. No soldier is looking at him. Nobody has drawn anything. And Peter, who a few hours ago swung a sword at an armed man's head in the dark, says I am not.

It is the exact negation of what Jesus had said in the garden: I am (so the ESV note at 18:5), and now I am not. The Lord identifies himself and a cohort goes over backwards; the disciple un-identifies himself to a girl minding a gate.

Then the fire, and John's eye for it is the eye of a man who was there. A charcoal fire, because it was cold — and Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself. Among the officers who arrested his master, at their fire, getting warm.

Here is the test, and it does not require anybody to have faced a tribunal. Denial in the New Testament is rarely dramatic. It is much more often what Peter does here: taking the answer somebody has already assumed, because correcting them would be awkward and nothing much is at stake. The conversation at work where it would be easier not to say. The assumption left standing. It costs nothing at the time, which is exactly why it is so easy, and Peter's version began the same way.

One further detail in verse 18 is worth having, because John chose an unusual word. The fire is an anthrakian, a charcoal fire — and that noun occurs exactly twice in the New Testament. Here, and at 21:9, where the risen Christ has one burning on a beach with breakfast on it.

John is the only writer who mentions either. He put a charcoal fire in the courtyard where Peter denied him and another on the shore where Peter was restored, and he did not explain the connection. Smell is the sense most closely tied to memory, and every man who has ever cooked outdoors knows what charcoal smells like.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John mentions a charcoal fire again when Peter is restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have spoken openly to the world: Jesus' defense is the public nature of his entire ministry. There has been no secret teaching, no hidden agenda, no clandestine doctrine. He has taught in synagogues and the temple — the most public venues available — in full hearing of all who chose to listen. This is the confidence of a ministry that has nothing to hide because it has been entirely the Father's word faithfully spoken. The authorities are conducting a nocturnal interrogation about public teaching — the irony is complete. The Light has only ever operated in the light.

Before the exchange itself, a word about what John does not give us here, since a reader comparing the Gospels will notice it.

Matthew and Mark record a full session of the Sanhedrin with witnesses, the charge about destroying the temple, the high priest's direct question under oath, and the verdict of blasphemy. John has none of it. He gives us this brief and irregular interview with Annas and then, in a single sentence at verse 24, sends Jesus on to Caiaphas without describing what happened there.

The likeliest reason is the one that explains most of John's omissions: the other accounts were long in circulation and he supplies what they lacked. Nobody else records the Annas hearing at all, and the “other disciple”, very probably John himself, was inside the courtyard that night.

Now the interrogation, and the shape of it is telling. The high priest asks about two things — his disciples and his teaching. He is trying to establish the size of the movement and the content of the doctrine, which is what a security official asks.

Jesus answers only the second, and refuses the first entirely. Not one word about the disciples. He has just got them out of the garden; he is not going to name them in a courtyard.

And his answer is a flat statement of method: I have spoken openly to the world… I have said nothing in secret. The word for openly is the one John uses of speaking with boldness, in public, without concealment — and it is a claim that can be checked, because everything he taught was taught in the two most crowded buildings available.

Which high priest is this? John calls both Annas and Caiaphas high priest. Annas had held the office and still bore the title, and many read v. 19 as his questioning, with Jesus then sent to Caiaphas (v. 24). Others read vv. 19–23 as Caiaphas. The first is the more likely.

And I have said nothing in secret does not deny that Jesus taught the Twelve privately. His private teaching explained the same message he preached openly (Mark 4:34); there was no secret doctrine for insiders.

Which lands where it was aimed. He is standing in a private house, in the middle of the night, before a man who holds no office, being asked about a movement — and he replies that his practice has been to say everything in daylight in front of everyone. The contrast is not stated. It does not need to be.

parallels.desc: I did not speak in secret

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said." When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, "Is that how you answer the high priest?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ask those who have heard me: the legal procedure Jesus invokes — question the witnesses, not the accused in isolation — is correct Roman and Jewish legal practice. The hearing is already procedurally compromised. The officer's slap is the first physical violence of the passion narrative: the Creator struck by a creature, the Lord of glory receiving a blow from one of his own made image-bearers. The passion begins not with the cross but with this slap — the escalating humiliation that will end in crucifixion.

The slap should be allowed its full weight, because familiarity has made it almost decorative.

The word is rhapisma, which can mean a blow with a rod but here almost certainly means an open-handed strike across the face. It is not primarily a way of causing pain. It is the standard gesture for putting an inferior back in his place — which is why the officer explains himself in exactly those terms: is that how you answer the high priest?

So the first violence done to Jesus is not judicial and not even angry. It is an act of etiquette enforcement by a junior official who thought the prisoner's tone was wrong.

And it is worth registering what has just been established. This is the man through whom all things were made, standing bound in a courtyard, being corrected on his manners by a member of the temple staff.

Isaiah had described it, and the wording is worth having beside the scene: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6). Note the verbs. I gave. I hid not. The servant in that passage is not overwhelmed; he presents himself.

Then the question Jesus asks in reply, which is not the answer most of us would give: if what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?

He does not turn the other cheek in the sense of saying nothing — which is worth noticing, because his own instruction in the Sermon on the Mount is often taken to require silence. He objects. He objects on a point of law, calmly, and he does it without a trace of retaliation. Whatever turn the other cheek means, it evidently permits a man to say plainly that what has just been done to him was unjust.

parallels.desc: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I said something wrong, testify about the wrong: Jesus continues his calm appeal to legal procedure — evidence, testimony, due process. Why do you strike me? — the question exposes the illegality of the violence but does not generate retaliation. Jesus is fulfilling what Isaiah 53:7 described: as a sheep before its shearers is silent, he does not open his mouth in self-defense but only in the defense of justice. Sent bound to Caiaphas: the chain of unjust authorities — Annas to Caiaphas — passes the bound Lord along as if justice is a bureaucratic procedure.

The reply is a small masterclass in what to do with an injustice, and it is worth taking apart because most of us have only two settings.

He does not absorb it silently, and he does not retaliate. He states the principle: there are two possibilities, and the blow is wrong under both of them. If what he said was wrong, produce the evidence — that is what a court is for. If it was right, the blow has no justification at all. Either way the officer has skipped the only step that mattered.

Notice that he does not appeal to who he is. He could have. The argument he actually uses is one that would protect any prisoner in any courtyard, and it is the same argument he made to the officers of the temple police and to the men with stones: examine the case.

And then, on the receiving end of it, nothing. No further protest, and no retaliation of any kind.

Peter, who was standing near enough to watch this, wrote about it afterwards, and his summary is the best one there is: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet. 2:23). The last clause is the mechanism. It is possible to say plainly that a thing is unjust and still not fight it, provided one genuinely believes there is a court that will sit later.

Then verse 24, which is one line of narrative and easy to skip: Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas.

Still bound. He has been questioned by a man who holds no office, struck by a member of that man's staff, and is now passed on — with the ropes still on him — to the next stage of a process whose outcome had been decided at 11:53, weeks earlier.

Nothing has been established. Nobody has produced a charge. He is simply being moved.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "You also are not one of his disciples, are you?" He denied it and said, "I am not." One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second and third denials happen in rapid succession, to different questioners. The relative of Malchus is the most dangerous interrogator — he was present in the garden and saw Peter there. The specificity of the accusation matches the specificity of Peter's failure in the garden: the ear cut off is still remembered, the face is still recognized. Peter's violence in the garden has become evidence of his presence, which has become the occasion for his most dangerous denial. Our sins always find us out — even the well-intentioned ones.

Watch the pressure increase, because the sequence is exact and it is the reason this story is in all four Gospels.

The first questioner was a servant girl at a gate, asking idly. The second is a group at the fire — they said to him, plural, several men at once, and the same expected-no construction. The third is a relative of the man Peter had assaulted, and he is not asking whether Peter is a disciple. He is saying he saw him: did I not see you in the garden with him?

That is a different order of danger. This man was there. He has a family grievance and an eyewitness identification, and Peter is standing in the household of the injured party warming his hands.

So the escalation is real, and the honest thing to say is that by the third question Peter had something to be afraid of. The first denial cost him nothing and was therefore inexcusable. The third might have cost him his life.

Which is worth naming for anyone tempted to be superior about Peter. Nothing in the account suggests that a braver man would have done differently — and the others, apart from the unnamed disciple who got him in, are not in the courtyard at all, having taken the option Peter declined. He failed in a place none of them went.

Note also what the questioner's memory contains. The ear. Peter's one act of courage that night has become the evidence against him, and the thing he did to prove his loyalty is what makes him identifiable when he wants to deny it. Bravery in the wrong form does not bank anything for later.

There is one more thing worth saying about the interval, and John's structure makes it visible in a way the other Gospels do not.

He has interleaved the two scenes deliberately. Verses 15-18: Peter denies. Verses 19-24: Jesus is questioned and struck. Verses 25-27: Peter denies twice more. The two men are within a few yards of each other, and both are being asked who they are.

One is asked You also are not one of his disciples, are you? and says no. The other is asked about his disciples and will not name a single one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At once a rooster crowed: the precision of Jesus' prediction — before the rooster crows, you will have denied me three times (13:38) — is fulfilled in a single night. The rooster crow in Luke's account (22:61) is the moment when Jesus looks at Peter, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly. John does not record the weeping but implies it in the three-fold restoration of chapter 21. The crowing is simultaneously judgment and mercy: judgment on the denial, mercy in the remembered word that will become the beginning of restoration. God uses the ordinary sounds of creation to mark the moments of human failure and begin the work of grace.

And at once a rooster crowed.

John says nothing else. No weeping, no look, no comment. The most catastrophic failure in the New Testament is reported in ten words and then the narrative simply moves to Pilate.

Luke is the one who supplies what happened next, and it is unbearable: and the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Lk. 22:61). Perhaps he was being moved from Annas to Caiaphas at that moment. He turned his head.

Then Luke's next clause: and Peter remembered the saying of the Lord. The crow did not condemn him. It reminded him — of something Jesus had said in advance, which meant that the worst moment of his life had been foreseen and spoken about by the man he had just disowned, and had not stopped him being at that supper, or having his feet washed, or being prayed for by name.

Which is the mercy hidden in the prediction, and it is why Jesus made it. A failure nobody warned you about is evidence that everything has come apart. A failure your Lord described to your face beforehand is inside the story rather than the end of it.

Here is the test, for anyone carrying a particular memory. Ask whether Christ knew about it before it happened. He did — that is what omniscience means, and this chapter is the demonstration. Then ask what he did with that knowledge in Peter's case. He announced it, washed the man's feet anyway, prayed for him by name, arranged his escape from the garden, and three days later sent word specifically to him by an angel: go, tell his disciples and Peter (Mk. 16:7).

The Gospels differ in who asked Peter each question, a servant girl, another girl, the bystanders, a relative of Malchus, and in where he stood. They agree on three denials and the rooster. In a crowded courtyard several people may have spoken at each turn, and each writer records the voices he chose. Mark adds that the rooster crowed twice (Mark 14:72).

And John, who leaves the weeping out here, has not forgotten. He is saving it. There will be another charcoal fire, on a beach, and three questions to match the three denials, and a man given his work back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — The Trial Before Pilate: What Is Truth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Jewish leaders bring Jesus to Pilate before dawn, refusing to enter the praetorium to avoid defilement. Pilate interrogates Jesus about his kingship; Jesus declares that his kingdom is not of this world and that he came to bear witness to the truth. Pilate finds no guilt but is caught between the crowd's demands and his own assessment. He offers Barabbas as an alternative.

The threshold (vv. 28-29). A Jew entering a Gentile dwelling contracted a defilement lasting till evening, which would have barred him from that day's festival meals — so they stand in the street and make Pilate come out. The mechanism is not hypocrisy in the crude sense: as far as we can tell they were sincere about the purity rule, which is what makes it frightening. It is entirely possible to keep a real conscience about small things in perfect working order while the large thing goes past. The scruple is functioning; it is pointed at the wrong object. (The chronology question raised by could eat the Passover is treated at 13:1.)

Why Rome had to be involved (vv. 30-32). Their first answer is not an answer — if this man were not doing evil is a request that a Roman court ratify a verdict without hearing the grounds. Then the sentence that forces everything: it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death. Historians note that Stephen was stoned in Acts 7, and the distinction is between lynching, which happened, and formal judicial execution, which in a province belonged to the governor. And John supplies the reason it matters: stoning was the Jewish penalty and crucifixion the Roman one, and everything Jesus had said about being lifted up (3:14; 8:28; 12:32) requires a cross. There is more in it still — the law said a hanged man is cursed by God (Deut. 21:23), and Paul builds the atonement on that verse (Gal. 3:13). The men insisting on correct paperwork were arranging it.

The prisoner interrogates the judge (vv. 34-35). Do you say this of your own accord? is not evasion; it separates two entirely different conversations, and it is an offer — the same offer made to Nicodemus and the woman at the well, extended to the prefect of Judea in the early morning. Pilate refuses it with the most self-revealing thing he says, am I a Jew?, and then immediately asks what have you done? That is his tragedy throughout: he asks good questions and repeatedly declines to stay for the answers.

Not OF this world (v. 36). The ESV's own next clause gives the sense: my kingdom is not from the world. It is a statement about origin, not location. Read as location it becomes a charter for a Christianity that concedes the world to other powers and retreats into private religion, which is the arrangement every tyranny has been happy to grant the church. Read as origin it is far more disturbing to Pilate. And the evidence Jesus offers is checkable: my servants would have been fighting — one sword was drawn in the garden and its owner was told to put it away.

Born for this (v. 37). The only time in this Gospel he speaks of his birth; everywhere else it is I came or I was sent. To a Roman with no framework for descent from heaven, he says it the ordinary way. And the purpose named is not to reign or to conquer or even to die, but to bear witness to the truth — the humblest possible job description, and the one that gets him killed.

What is truth (v. 38). There are two ways to say it and the scene permits both. What settles it is not the tone but the timing: John records that he asked and then went back outside. The distance between Pilate and the answer was about four feet, and he had authority to keep the man as long as he liked. Note too that having acquitted him he does not release him, which is what an acquittal requires — he offers a deal, and from that moment Jesus is not being tried but negotiated over. (No source outside the Gospels attests the Passover amnesty, though governors are known to have released prisoners to please a crowd.)
verseByVerse.theology: Are you the King of the Jews? is the question Pilate must answer, and his ironic placard — THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS — will become the most accurate theological statement of the passion narrative. Jesus' kingdom is not from this world: it does not advance by the sword (as Peter demonstrated), does not require political coercion, does not depend on earthly armies. It advances by truth — by the witness of the one who is the truth, received by those who are of the truth. Pilate's question — What is truth? — is asked by the man standing in front of the answer.
verseByVerse.examples: The Barabbas exchange is the gospel in miniature: the guilty goes free, the innocent is condemned. Barabbas is released while the Son of the Father is crucified. He is a robber and insurrectionist — exactly the kind of person Jesus' opponents had accused Jesus of being. The crowd chooses the wrong son. In choosing Barabbas, they choose the kind of liberation they wanted — political, violent — and reject the liberation they needed — spiritual, sacrificial.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The supreme irony of the passion: the men who are arranging the execution of the Passover Lamb are careful not to be defiled so they can eat the Passover lamb. Their scrupulousness about ritual purity coexists with moral catastrophe. Pilate goes outside to them — a small act of accommodation that grows into capitulation. The governor of a Roman province is already accommodating the crowd before the trial begins. When authority loses the will to be just, it becomes the instrument of injustice however good its formal procedures appear.

The detail about the Passover in verse 28 is the one on which the whole question of the Last Supper's date turns, and it is treated at length at 13:1, where the tension between John and the other three Gospels is set out and resolved. Two things only need saying here.

First, the Passover in ordinary usage covered the whole seven-day festival, so eating it can refer to the meals of the following days rather than to the lamb itself.

Second, the entering itself: a Jew who went into a Gentile dwelling contracted a ritual defilement lasting until evening, which would have barred him from the festival meals of that day. So they stand in the street and make Pilate come out.

And that is the picture to hold. Men who will not step over a threshold because of a ceremonial rule, arranging a judicial murder on the other side of it.

It is worth being careful with this, because it is the easiest thing in the world to read as a lesson about somebody else. The mechanism is not hypocrisy in the crude sense of knowing better and pretending. These men were, as far as we can tell, sincere about the purity rule. That is what makes it frightening: it is entirely possible to keep a real conscience about small things in perfect working order while the large thing goes past unnoticed. The scruple is functioning. It is simply pointed at the wrong object.

And Pilate goes out to them, which is the first move of the trial and sets its direction. A Roman governor was not obliged to conduct business in the street to accommodate the religious sensibilities of a subject people. He does it anyway, and by the end of the morning he will have conceded everything.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean for the festival.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you." Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he were not doing evil: a non-answer designed to transfer authority rather than provide evidence. They do not specify the evil; they simply assert it and demand Pilate's cooperation. Take him and judge him by your own law: Pilate initially resists jurisdictional responsibility. It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death: the authorities need Rome's cooperation for a capital execution. This is not about justice for them but about method: the mob-stoning they attempted in chapters 8 and 10 would have been their own judgment; crucifixion requires Roman authority and ensures maximum shame.

Their first answer is not an answer, and Pilate notices. If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you — which is to say: trust us. They are asking a Roman court to ratify a verdict already reached without hearing the grounds for it.

Pilate's reply is procedurally correct and also an attempt to get rid of the case: take him yourselves and judge him by your own law. Rome generally left internal religious matters to local jurisdiction.

Then the sentence that forces everything: it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.

Historians have debated this, since Stephen is stoned in Acts 7 and the woman in chapter 8 was nearly stoned in the temple. The distinction is between mob action or lynching, which happened and which Rome punished when it noticed, and a formal judicial execution, which in a Roman province was reserved to the governor. What they are saying is not that killing him is impossible but that killing him legally requires Pilate.

And John adds the note that turns the whole exchange: this was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die.

Which is the point of the entire procedural wrangle. Stoning was the Jewish penalty; crucifixion was the Roman one. If the Sanhedrin had been able to act alone, he would have been stoned — and everything he had said about being lifted up (3:14; 8:28; 12:32) requires a cross.

Why does John keep saying the Jews handed Jesus over? He uses the phrase for the Jerusalem leaders and those who followed them, not for the whole people; Jesus, his disciples and the first believers were all Jews. Pilate himself says Your own nation and the chief priests (v. 35). The guilt for the cross belongs to those who planned it, to Pilate who allowed it, and, in the deepest sense, to all of us whose sins put him there. Peter says the Jerusalem crowd and their rulers acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and the gospel was preached to them first. The charge of collective Jewish guilt, used to justify persecution, has no ground in John or anywhere in Scripture.

So the jurisdictional technicality that looks like an accident of Roman administration is the mechanism by which the manner of his death was secured. And there is more in it than the shape of the execution. The law said a hanged man is cursed by God (Deut. 21:23), and Paul builds the doctrine of the atonement on precisely that verse: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:13). He had to die that way, under that sentence, and the men insisting on the correct paperwork were arranging it.
verseByVerse.note: Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea.

parallels.desc: Stephen stoned by a mob

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, "Are you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To show what kind of death he was going to die: crucifixion rather than stoning. The mode of death was prophetically determined — Lifted up (3:14; 12:32-33) required the Roman cross. Pilate's question goes to the center: Are you the King of the Jews? It is the political question, the charge that could justify execution under Roman law. Jesus' answer will redefine the question: yes, he is king, but not in the way that threatens Rome. His kingdom is not a rival political power but a different order altogether.

The Greek of Pilate's question puts the pronoun first and it is doing work: su — you are the King of the Jews?

It is contemptuous, and understandably so. In front of him is a man in his thirties, unarmed, beaten, tied up, handed over by his own nation's leadership, with no supporters visible anywhere in the building. Pilate has spent years managing genuine insurgencies in this province, and he has seen what a claimant to a throne looks like. This does not.

Which is why the question sits at the exact centre of the trial. It is the only charge that could interest a Roman court — treason, a rival king, maiestas — and everything the priests want depends on making it stick. They have not brought a charge of blasphemy to Pilate, because he would have thrown it out.

And they were right that he was a king, and wrong about what kind, and Pilate is about to be right for the wrong reasons and write it on a board.

And John's note in verse 32 has already told us why the case had to come here at all: to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. The jurisdictional wrangle of the previous verse was not an administrative detail. It was the mechanism that produced a cross rather than a heap of stones.

Note also that Pilate has gone back inside to ask this. The accusers would not enter; so the trial proper — the one conversation in which Jesus explains himself — happens in a room they refused to walk into. They arranged the whole thing and were not present for the only part of it that mattered.

It is worth noting how much of this trial happens on a threshold. Pilate goes out (v. 29), comes in (v. 33), goes out again (v. 38), and will keep moving for the rest of the morning.

The physical shuttling is the picture of the man. He never settles anywhere — not with the accusers, not with the prisoner, not with his own verdict — and by noon he will have signed a death warrant for someone he three times declared innocent.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” pointed to Roman crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?" Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus' counter-question forces Pilate to identify his sources: is the kingship question Pilate's own concern or the crowd's charge? Am I a Jew? — Pilate's exasperation reveals his political instrumentality. He has no personal interest in Jewish messianic expectations; he is managing a crowd's complaint. What have you done? — the question of guilt, implying that Pilate is open to an exculpatory answer. This is the one moment in the trial when justice might have been served; Jesus will provide the answer, but Pilate will not have the courage to act on it.

Something remarkable happens in verse 34 and it is easy to miss because it is phrased as a question.

The prisoner starts interrogating the judge.

Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me? That is not evasion. It is the question that separates two entirely different conversations. If Pilate is asking on his own account — if a Roman governor genuinely wants to know whether this man is a king — then there is an answer worth giving. If he is merely processing somebody else's accusation, the word king means rebel and the answer would be no.

So Jesus asks him which he is doing. It is, in effect, an offer: the offer he made to Nicodemus and the woman at the well and the man born blind, extended to the Roman prefect of Judea in the early morning.

And Pilate refuses it, with the most self-revealing sentence he speaks: am I a Jew?

He is declining to be personally involved. Whatever this is about, it is not his world and he does not intend to enter it. The tone is dismissive and the effect is to shut the door on the only conversation in the room that could have done him any good.

Then, immediately after refusing to be interested: what have you done?

He does still want to know. That is the tragedy of Pilate throughout this narrative — he is not a monster and he is not stupid. He asks good questions and repeatedly declines to stay for the answers, and by the end he will hand over a man he has three times pronounced innocent because the alternative is inconvenient.

Note also what his second question concedes. Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me — he has already worked out that this is an internal matter being routed through him, which is the first thing an experienced administrator would notice and the reason he keeps trying to hand it back.

He knows he is being used. He says so out loud. And he goes through with it anyway, which is the difference between seeing a thing clearly and being willing to pay for acting on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world." Then Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My kingdom is not of this world: the political exoneration and the theological claim simultaneously. Jesus does not deny kingship — you say that I am a king — but defines it: born for this purpose, sent to bear witness to the truth. The kingdom of truth advances through testimony, not troops; through the word, not the sword. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice: the same election-and-hearing language as 10:27. To be of the truth is to be capable of hearing the one who is the truth. Pilate, standing before the truth, is about to ask his famous question.

One preposition in this answer carries more weight than anything else in the trial, and English versions have obscured it for centuries.

My kingdom is not of this world — and the Greek is ek, out of, from. It is a statement about origin, not about location. He is not saying his kingdom is somewhere else, in heaven, spiritual, not down here. He says it does not come from here. Its source is elsewhere; its territory is very much this world, which is why he is standing in a Roman courtroom.

That distinction is not academic, and getting it wrong has done real damage. Read as a statement about location, the sentence becomes a charter for a Christianity that concedes the actual world to other powers and retreats into private religion — which is precisely the arrangement every tyranny has ever been happy to grant the church.

Read as a statement about origin, it says something far more disturbing to Pilate: there is a kingdom operating in his province whose authority did not come from Rome, does not depend on Rome, and will outlast Rome.

And Jesus gives the evidence in the form of a fact Pilate can check: if my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting. There had been exactly one sword drawn in the garden and its owner had been told to put it away. The absence of a fight is the proof of the kingdom's origin.

Now the guard, because this verse is pulled in two directions. It does not mean Christians should have no interest in justice, government or public life; the prophets and the whole of Scripture forbid that reading, and Jesus is at that moment giving evidence in a court about a real charge. What it does rule out is advancing the kingdom by coercion. Every time the church has reached for the sword — and it has, repeatedly, and worse than Peter did — it has been contradicting the sentence its Lord gave at his own trial.

Then for this purpose I was born, which is the only time in this Gospel he speaks of his birth. Everything else has been I came, I was sent, I came down. To a Roman, who would have no framework for descending from heaven, he says it the ordinary way: I was born for this.

Does this mean Christians may never fight? Some Christians, pacifists, read it so. But Jesus is speaking of his kingdom: it will never be advanced by force. That does not abolish the state’s God-given sword (Rom 13:4), nor forbid a Christian to serve as a soldier or police officer (Luke 3:14), nor to defend life. The church must never use force to spread the gospel; a Christian citizen may share in the just defence of others.

And the purpose named is not to reign, or to conquer, or even to die. To bear witness to the truth. He describes himself to the Roman governor as a witness — which is the humblest possible job description, and it is the one that gets him killed.

parallels.desc: the good confession before Pontius Pilate

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, "I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is truth? — the most famous unanswered question in the gospel. Pilate asks and then walks away without waiting for the answer, because the question is rhetorical — the cynicism of a man who has governed long enough to believe that truth is always a cover story for power. The answer is standing in front of him; Jesus does not respond because the answer has already been given (14:6: I am the truth). I find no guilt in him: three times Pilate will declare Jesus innocent (18:38; 19:4; 19:6). The Roman judicial verdict is innocence; the execution will be a miscarriage of justice confirmed by the highest legal authority present.

The question deserves better than the contempt it usually gets, because there are two ways to say it and they are not the same.

It can be a sneer — the tired cynicism of a career official who has watched every faction in a difficult province dress up its interests as principle, and who has concluded that truth is a word people use when they want something. That is the usual reading and it fits the man.

It can also be genuine, and something in the scene allows it. He has just been told by a bound prisoner that there is such a thing as truth and that men can be of it. Pilate may be, for one moment, actually asking.

What settles it is not the tone but the timing. John records that he asked the question and then went back outside. Whatever he meant by it, he did not wait.

Which is the most human thing in the chapter and the most damning. The distance between Pilate and the answer was about four feet, and he had the authority to keep the man there as long as he liked. He asked the largest question a person can ask, in the presence of the only being who could have answered it, and left the room.

And then the three acquittals begin: I find no guilt in him — here, and at 19:4, and at 19:6. Three times the Roman judicial system, in the person of its highest local representative, returns a verdict of not guilty, and three times it proceeds anyway.

Note what he does immediately after acquitting him. He does not release him, which is what an acquittal requires. He offers a deal — the Passover custom, a prisoner released to the crowd — which means that from this moment Jesus is no longer being tried. He is being negotiated over. An honest note: no source outside the Gospels attests this amnesty, though provincial governors are known to have released prisoners to please a crowd, and Pilate would hardly be the first official to invent a precedent when he needed one.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out again, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" Now Barabbas was a robber.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not this man, but Barabbas: the crowd's choice is the gospel in reverse — the innocent condemned, the guilty released. Barabbas goes free while the Son of the Father is handed over. He was a robber and an insurrectionist — the charges laid against Jesus (that he was a revolutionary and a thief of people's loyalty) applied accurately to Barabbas. In choosing Barabbas, the crowd chooses the kind of liberation — violent, political — that Rome can suppress. In choosing Jesus, they could have chosen the liberation that no power can overcome. They choose the lesser freedom and lose the greater.

The word John uses for Barabbas is lestes, and it has a history in this Gospel. It is the word for the thieves and robbers who climb into the sheepfold another way (10:1, 8) — the violent kind of intruder, as opposed to the sneak-thief. It is what Josephus calls the insurgents of the period. Mark tells us he was in prison with the rebels who had committed murder in the insurrection (Mk. 15:7).

So the man the crowd asks for is a real one: an armed nationalist with blood on his hands, of exactly the kind Rome crucified in batches, and of exactly the kind Jesus had been accused of being.

And there is the name. Bar-abbas is Aramaic for son of the father. Some early manuscripts of Matthew give his first name as Jesus — Jesus Barabbas — which, if it stood, would mean Pilate asked the crowd to choose between Jesus son of the father and Jesus who is called Christ. The evidence is genuinely divided and it should not be leaned on. The surname alone is enough.

Because what happens next is the doctrine of substitution acted out in a courtyard, once, in front of witnesses, before anybody had a word for it. Two men. One guilty of insurrection and murder, one three times declared innocent by the judge. The crowd chooses, and the guilty man walks out of a Roman prison free while the innocent one is taken away to the cross that had been prepared.

Barabbas is the only human being who can say, in the most literal sense available, that Jesus of Nazareth died in his place. That morning he was a condemned man, and somebody else was nailed up in his place, and he went home.

Nothing is recorded of what became of him. He walks out of the story and out of history — no conversion, no repentance, nothing asked of him and nothing given. He did not choose it, did not deserve it, and as far as we know never thanked anybody.

Which is the exchange, and there has never been a clearer picture of it. Not a bargain, not a reward, not a transaction anybody entered into. A guilty man's sentence served by an innocent one, arranged by people who were trying to do something else entirely, on the morning of the Passover.
verseByVerse.note: Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection; “robber” was often used for violent rebels.

Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,<sup>16</sup>but Peter stood outside at the door.
