19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Pilate has Jesus flogged, the soldiers mock him as king, and Pilate presents him to the crowd as 'the man' and then 'your king.' The crowd demands crucifixion; Pilate, fearing both the crowd and Caesar, hands Jesus over. The inscription on the cross — JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS — is placed in three languages.

Why the flogging comes here (v. 1). It looks like a procedural muddle and is not. The severe scourging, verberatio, immediately preceded crucifixion; this one is in the middle of the trial, before any sentence, and Luke gives Pilate's reasoning in his own words — I will therefore punish and release him (Lk. 23:16). It is an attempted compromise: a beaten man offered to the crowd instead of a dead one. Which makes it worse than a straightforward miscarriage, since Pilate has now savagely punished a man he has three times declared innocent, as a bargaining position.

The coronation nobody intended (vv. 3-4). Hail, King of the Jews is a straight parody of Ave Caesar, and these are Roman auxiliaries who know what they are imitating. Robe, crown, acclamation, homage: every element of an accession, all inverted.

Behold the man (v. 5). Pilate's strategy assumes something decent about the crowd: that if they see the man they will stop wanting him dead. He has miscalculated, and the miscalculation is instructive — the sight of suffering does not reliably produce pity. There may also be a note from Zechariah audible here: behold, the man whose name is the Branch (Zech. 6:12), in a context about a man who will be crowned and be a priest on his throne.

The real charge, and Pilate's fear (vv. 7-8). After an hour on the charge of kingship, the actual conviction comes out: he has made himself the Son of God — and their law did prescribe death for it (Lev. 24:16), and he had claimed it. Then even more afraid: which means he was already afraid, and John has not said so until now. A Roman would not hear son of God as nonsense — Augustus was officially divi filius — and Matthew supplies the detail that fixes the mood, his wife's message about a dream (Mt. 27:19).

The silence (vv. 9-10). Also absent above, and it is the pastoral centre of the chapter. Where are you from? is the question this Gospel has been asking since chapter 1, asked at last by the right man for the right reason — and he gets nothing. Not sullenness (Isa. 53:7), and not the silence of a man with nothing to say. Pilate had already asked what is truth? and walked out before the answer. What the verse establishes for a reader who has met God's silence is narrow and worth having: a silent Christ and an absent Christ are not the same thing, and in the one case Scripture describes in detail, the man was at that moment in the process of dying for the person he would not answer.

Authority from above (v. 11). From above — the same word that baffled Nicodemus in chapter 3 (see the ESV note at 3:3). The authority by which a prefect is about to execute the Son of God was issued to him, from above, for the purpose. It does not make the act right: the next clause grades the guilt, and the greater sin is singular, most probably Caiaphas, who had the Scriptures and the office. Scripture consistently grades culpability by light received — uncomfortable for the well-taught, merciful toward the ignorant.

Not Caesar's friend (v. 12). The lever that actually decided the case, and it worked because they knew his file. Amicus Caesaris was close to a formal designation, and Pilate had already been forced to remove military standards from Jerusalem after riots, and been overruled by Tiberius personally over the votive shields. Within a few years he would be recalled to answer for a massacre in Samaria. Everything — the three acquittals, the fear, the attempts to release him — collapses the moment his career is named.

We have no king but Caesar (v. 15). The most catastrophic sentence in the passion. Said by the chief priests, at Passover, in Jerusalem, about the emperor of the occupying army, in order to secure the execution of their Messiah — by the office that existed to represent a nation founded on the proposition that it had no king but God (1 Sam. 8:7; Judg. 8:23). Forty years later Caesar's soldiers burned the temple down. The guard matters: this is a sentence by named officials on one morning, not a verdict on a people (Rom. 11:1), and it lands nearest to those who most resemble the men who said it. There is always a Caesar available — the authority one cannot risk displeasing when the true King is inconvenient.

Simon of Cyrene (v. 17). John says he bore his own cross; the other three have Simon carrying it. Both are true of different stretches of the same walk — Luke says the cross was laid on Simon to carry it behind Jesus (Lk. 23:26), which fits a man who has collapsed part of the way. John, whose passion insists that nothing was taken and everything given, records that he went out carrying it himself. And note the restraint of there they crucified him: four words, no description, in an age that has produced a great deal of art determined to supply what the evangelists withheld.
verseByVerse.theology: Behold the man (v. 5) and Behold your King (v. 14) are Pilate's two presentations of Jesus to the crowd — each one a deeper truth than Pilate knows. Ecce Homo is the great statement of the incarnation: here is humanity in its representative, here is the man who is also the king. Pilate intends mockery and irony; the Spirit intends revelation. The crown of thorns (the curse of Gen. 3:18 placed on the head of the one who came to bear the curse), the purple robe (borrowed royalty that will soon be stripped), and the reed scepter — all are parodies of kingship that are simultaneously truths about the king who reigns from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: They crucified him, and with him two others — one on either side (v. 18): the king flanked by his 'court,' the condemned alongside the condemned, the innocent among the guilty. The inscription in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek — the languages of religion, law, and culture — makes the proclamation universal: in every language, beside a road just outside the city, in the full light of Passover day, the truth is declared. The chief priests want it changed to 'he said he was king'; Pilate refuses: What I have written, I have written.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flogged: Roman flogging (flagellum) with leather thongs embedded with bone and metal was severe enough to kill; it was standard preparation for crucifixion. The crown of thorns: the thorns of the curse (Gen. 3:18 — thorns and thistles it shall bring forth) pressed onto the head of the one who came to absorb the curse. The purple robe: the color of royalty borrowed as mockery. The soldiers are doing theology without knowing it: they are robing the King, crowning him, dressing him for his throne. The mockery of the soldiers is the preparation of the sacrifice; they are adorning what they intend to destroy.

The placement of this flogging is worth understanding, because it looks at first like a procedural muddle.

Roman law knew several grades of beating. The severe one, verberatio, was the standard prelude to crucifixion and was done immediately before it. This one is not there. It comes in the middle of the trial, before any sentence, and Luke supplies the reasoning in Pilate's own words: I will therefore punish and release him (Lk. 23:16).

So the flogging is an attempted compromise. Pilate has three times found no guilt, and he is trying to give the crowd something short of a death — a beaten man, visibly punished, whom they might then let go. It is the classic manoeuvre of an official who knows what justice requires and is looking for a cheaper alternative.

It did not work, and it is worth saying why the attempt is worse than a straightforward miscarriage would have been. Pilate has now inflicted a savage punishment on a man he has publicly declared innocent, not as a sentence but as a bargaining position. Nobody has yet said he is guilty of anything.

Then the crown, and the Greek word is not the one for a royal crown. A diadema is what a king wears. What they twist together is a stephanos — the victor's wreath, the circlet given to the winner of the games or to a general on his return.

They meant it as part of the joke. It is the wrong joke. In three days the man wearing it will have won, and the word they chose is the one the New Testament uses for the crown he will give away: the crown of life, of righteousness, of glory that does not fade.

And the thorns. Genesis is explicit that the ground was cursed and thorns and thistles were its sign (Gen. 3:18) — the first visible consequence of the fall, the thing every farmer since has fought. A handful of it is pressed onto his head by men who are laughing.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hail, King of the Jews: the soldier's taunt is the correct title. They slap him as they address him as king — and in doing so, enact the paradox of the incarnation: the King who receives blows rather than inflicts them, who absorbs rather than exercises power. Pilate's second declaration of innocence in John — I find no guilt — is addressed to the crowd before presenting Jesus after the flogging. Pilate is trying to satisfy the crowd's desire for punishment while stopping short of execution. The flogged and crowned figure is Pilate's offer: see, I have punished him. It will not be enough.

Hail, King of the Jews! — a straight parody of the imperial salute, Ave Caesar. These are Roman auxiliaries; they know exactly what they are imitating.

What the mockery does, without anybody intending it, is stage a coronation. There is a robe, a crown, an acclamation, and a court paying homage. Every element of an accession is present and every one is inverted — and John, who tells us the mockery in detail, is the evangelist most interested in the kingship. He wants the reader to see the crowning.

Then they struck him with their hands, and it is worth remembering that this is happening between the flogging and the crucifixion, to a man who has been awake all night.

And out of the middle of it Pilate comes back to the crowd and says, for the second of three times, I find no guilt in him.

Set the two things side by side and the horror is administrative rather than dramatic. The verdict is innocent. The prisoner has just been flogged and is being beaten by soldiers. Both facts are being reported by the same man in the same breath, and he can see no contradiction because the punishment is not a sentence — it is an offer.

And there is a detail worth registering in how he puts it: I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him. He wants credit for the verdict. He is asking the crowd to notice his fairness, in the same sentence in which he produces a man he has had beaten half to death for no offence.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold the man: ecce homo — the word that has generated more art and theological reflection than almost any other in the gospels. Pilate presents the beaten, crowned, robed figure as an object of pity that might satisfy the crowd. But the Spirit's meaning is deeper: here is THE man, the representative human, the new Adam who bears the curse of the old, the one who is simultaneously king and condemned. The crowd's response — Crucify him — is as theologically precise as Pilate's presentation: this is what the world does with its king when he comes in truth rather than in power.

Three words, and no scene in the Gospels has been painted more often. Behold the man.

What Pilate means by it is fairly clear and entirely cynical. Look at him. Look at the state of him. This is your dangerous insurgent — a beaten man in a borrowed robe who can barely stand. He is inviting the crowd to be embarrassed by their own charge.

And it is worth noticing that the strategy assumes something decent about them. Pilate is betting that if they see the man they will stop wanting him dead. He has miscalculated, and the miscalculation is instructive: the sight of suffering does not reliably produce pity. It can produce the opposite, and here it produces a howl.

Then the deeper thing, which Pilate cannot have intended.

There is a line in Zechariah that might be heard behind those words: behold, the man whose name is the Branch (Zech. 6:12) — and the context there is a man who will be crowned, and who will build the temple, and who will be a priest on his throne. Whether anyone in that courtyard caught it cannot be known. John has recorded the phrase that makes it audible.

And what is being pointed at is not a specimen of suffering but the human race's representative. The old Adam was made in a garden and lost everything; this is the new one, and the curse that fell on the first is sitting on his head in the form of thorns.

The response is the only honest thing in the scene: crucify him, crucify him. It is worth resisting the instinct to distance ourselves from it too quickly. This is what happened when God became visible and stood in front of a crowd at close range without power — not indifference, not confusion, but a demand that he be removed. Anyone who has wondered why God does not simply show himself has an answer in this verse, and it is not a comfortable one.

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has made himself the Son of God: the religious charge finally stated plainly — not political subversion but blasphemy. And Pilate was even more afraid: the Roman governor who dismissed philosophical truth (what is truth?) is unsettled by this claim. The Romans had sons of gods — Augustus was divi filius, son of the divine Julius. The claim to divine sonship was not unintelligible to a Roman; it was concerning. Pilate's fear is the beginning of the superstitious caution that will make him seek one more interview with the prisoner who unnerves him.

The real charge finally comes out, and it is not the one they have been pressing. For an hour it has been the charge of kingship. Now, cornered by Pilate's refusal, they say what the Sanhedrin had actually convicted him of: he has made himself the Son of God.

They are right that their law prescribed death for it (Lev. 24:16), and they are right that he had claimed it. Nothing in this Gospel lets a reader say they misunderstood him. The whole of chapters 5, 8 and 10 is a record of them understanding him exactly and reaching for stones.

Then the sentence that opens a window into Pilate: when Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.

More afraid — which means he was already afraid, and John has not said so until now. Something about this prisoner has been unsettling him since the first interview.

And a Roman would not hear son of God as nonsense. Augustus was officially divi filius, son of the deified Julius; the category existed and the emperors used it. Beyond that, every Roman knew stories of gods walking about in disguise and of the appalling things that happened to men who mistreated them without recognising them.

Matthew adds the detail that fixes the mood: his wife had sent word during the trial — have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream (Mt. 27:19).

So the governor is now frightened, superstitious, out of his depth, and holding a verdict he cannot enforce. It is exactly the condition in which men do the thing they know to be wrong, because the wrong thing is the one that makes the fear stop soonest.

It is worth noting how the charge has moved. Before Pilate they said we have a law — their law, which a Roman court had no business enforcing. They had spent the morning translating a religious conviction into a political one because that was the only version Rome would hear, and now, frustrated, they revert to the real one and hand Pilate a problem he has no competence to judge.

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where are you from? — the question that has been running through the gospel: 7:27, 8:14, 9:29-30. Jesus gives him no answer — not the evasion of guilt but the silence of the one who will not cast pearls before a man who has already decided. Do you not know that I have authority to release you? — Pilate's assertion of power over Jesus is the most ironic statement of the passion. The one who made all things, through whom all authority is delegated, stands before a minor provincial governor claiming jurisdiction over him. Power has never been so mistaken about itself.

Where are you from?

It is the question this Gospel has been asking since chapter 1, and it has been asked before by people who thought they knew the answer: the crowd at the feast who said they knew where he came from and therefore he could not be the Christ (7:27), the Pharisees who said we do not know where he comes from (9:29). Now a Roman asks it, frightened, in a private room, and it is the right question at last.

And he gets nothing.

But Jesus gave him no answer. After a night of speaking — to Annas about his teaching, to Pilate about kingdoms and truth and witness — the one question that goes to the centre is met with silence.

Why? Not sullenness, and not the silence of a man with nothing to say. Isaiah had described it: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter… so he opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

But there is something more specific here. Pilate had already asked the question that mattered and walked out of the room before the answer. What is truth? — and he did not wait. A man who leaves before the answer to one question does not get an answer to the next.

Now the pastoral half, because this is one of the places in Scripture where a particular reader is standing.

There are people who have asked God something real — not idly, not to score a point — and received nothing. Not a refusal. Silence. And the temptation is to conclude either that nobody is there, or that the asking was somehow disqualified.

What this verse establishes is that the silence of God is not always what it appears. Jesus' silence was not indifference; the man in front of Pilate was at that moment in the process of dying for him. The nearest thing to an answer he was ever going to get was standing there in a purple robe with his hands tied.

Which does not explain any particular silence, and it is not offered as an explanation. It establishes something narrower and worth having: that a silent Christ and an absent Christ are not the same thing, and that in the one case Scripture describes in detail, the silence was the loudest part of the answer.

Then Pilate's response to being ignored, which is the response of small authority everywhere: do you not know that I have authority? He has just been frightened. Now he reaches for rank.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You would have no authority unless it had been given you from above: the theology of human authority as derived from divine authority. Pilate's power is real but derivative; he exercises it within the limits God has set. The greater sin rests with those who delivered Jesus over — they acted with full knowledge of the law and the scriptures. From then on Pilate sought to release him: the governor is trying to do the right thing while being politically trapped. If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend: the threat to Pilate's career is the final lever the crowd uses. Personal interest overcomes legal conscience.

The word Jesus uses for where Pilate's authority came from is one this Gospel has used before, and it is not the obvious one. Unless it had been given you from above — anothen, the very word that baffled Nicodemus in chapter 3, where being born anothen could mean again or from above.

Here there is no ambiguity, and the claim is enormous. The authority by which a Roman prefect is about to have the Son of God executed is authority that was issued to him, from above, for the purpose.

Which is the answer to the question the whole trial raises: who is actually in charge? Pilate thinks he is, and says so. Jesus tells him he holds real power — the sentence concedes it — and that it is on loan.

There is a great deal of comfort in this for anyone under an authority that is behaving badly, and it needs stating carefully so as not to become a defence of tyranny. It does not say that what Pilate is about to do is right. The next clause says the opposite: somebody in this affair has the greater sin, which means sin is being committed and measured. What it says is that the power being abused is derivative, borrowed, and bounded — and that the man wielding it will answer for how he used what he was lent.

The greater sin is worth a note. It is singular — he who delivered me over to you — most probably Caiaphas, who had the Scriptures, the office, and full knowledge of what he was doing, as against a Gentile administrator out of his depth. Guilt is real in both cases and it is not equal. Scripture consistently grades culpability by light received, which is uncomfortable for the well-taught and merciful toward the ignorant.

Then the sentence that ends the trial, and it is worth knowing why it worked: if you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend.

That was not a figure of speech. Amicus Caesaris was something close to a formal designation, and Pilate's record was already poor. He had provoked riots by bringing military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem, and had been forced to remove them. He had put up votive shields in Herod's palace and been overruled by Tiberius personally, in a letter, after the Jewish leadership complained over his head. Within a few years he would be removed from office and sent to Rome to answer for a massacre in Samaria.

So the threat is precise and the men making it know his file. They are telling a governor with two black marks against him that there will be a third.

And it works immediately. Everything before this — the acquittals, the fear, the attempts to release him — collapses the moment his career is named.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of Preparation, about the sixth hour: the day on which the Passover lambs were slaughtered in the temple. The Lamb of God is condemned on the day the lambs of the old covenant are killed. Behold your king: Pilate's second presentation, this time with a throne (the judgment seat) as backdrop. The king he presents is still thorn-crowned and purple-robed — and this is exactly what the king of the new covenant looks like: enthroned in suffering, crowned with the curse, robed in the borrowed dignity of human mockery.

That clock reading needs a note, because it is one of the most frequently cited discrepancies in the Gospels. John puts Jesus still standing before Pilate at about the sixth hour. Mark says plainly that it was the third hour when they crucified him (Mark 15:25). Reckoned from sunrise in the usual Jewish way, that is noon against nine in the morning, and the trial cannot be running three hours after the crucifixion.

Two answers are offered and both are reasonable. The first is that John is counting hours the Roman civil way, from midnight, so that his sixth hour is six in the morning — early enough for everything that follows. His other time references sit comfortably enough with that scheme, and it would explain why he alone gives times that seem out of step. The second is simpler and may be truer to how anyone told the time before clocks: the day was divided into rough quarters, and a writer named the marker nearest the event. Mark reaches for the third hour, John for the sixth, and both are gesturing at a stretch of a morning that ran, by our reckoning, somewhere between the two. Notice that John writes about the sixth hour; he is not claiming precision, and it is worth remembering that nobody in that courtyard had a watch. The demand that two witnesses agree to the minute is a modern expectation laid on documents that never offered it.

But was the Last Supper a Passover meal? Matthew, Mark and Luke say it was (Mark 14:12–16), while John seems to put the Passover a day later (13:1; 18:28). Some think different groups followed different calendars that year, or that Jesus held the meal early. The more likely answer is that the day of Preparation of the Passover means the Friday of Passover week, the day of preparation for the Sabbath (cf. 19:31; Mark 15:42), and that in 18:28 the Passover means the meals of the festival week. On that reading the Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus died on the Friday of Passover.

One honest consequence follows for what was said above. If John is using Roman hours, then the neat correspondence with the midday slaughter of the lambs is not available, and the point should be held more lightly than it often is. What does not depend on the hour is the thing that matters: Jesus was condemned and killed on the day of Preparation, while the Passover lambs of that same feast were being prepared for death. John says so twice, and the symbolism he is pressing rests on the day, not on the clock.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion — times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have no king but Caesar: the most catastrophic theological statement of the passion. The descendants of Abraham, who confessed only God as king, declare their ultimate loyalty to the Roman emperor rather than receive their true king. In rejecting Jesus, they reject the kingship of God — not merely a political arrangement but the covenant relationship that defined Israel. So he delivered him over: the verb is theologically weighted — Pilate delivers over the innocent; the Father delivers over the Son (Rom. 8:32). Human justice fails; divine love triumphs through the same event.

This is the sentence to stop at, and it is easy to walk past because it sounds like ordinary political talk.

We have no king but Caesar.

It is said by the chief priests. Not the crowd, not a hothead — the men whose entire office existed to represent Israel before God.

And consider what Israel was. A nation founded on the proposition that it had no king but God. When the people first asked Samuel for a king, the LORD's verdict was they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:7). Gideon had refused a crown on exactly that ground: I will not rule over you… the LORD will rule over you (Judg. 8:23). The psalms are full of it. The LORD reigns is the shortest summary of the religion.

It is said at Passover — the feast that commemorates being brought out of servitude to a foreign power. It is said in Jerusalem, a few hundred yards from the temple. And it is said by the priesthood, about the emperor of the occupying army, in order to secure the execution of their own Messiah.

There is a Jewish prayer used at the great feasts which ends with the words besides thee we have no king. Whether it was in use in precisely that form in the AD 30s cannot be established and the point should not be pressed. What can be said without any speculation at all is that the sentence is a formal renunciation of the thing that made Israel Israel, and that the men who said it knew it.

Forty years later Caesar's soldiers burned the temple to the ground and it has never been rebuilt.

Now the guard, because this verse has been used badly. It is a sentence spoken by a handful of named officials in a particular courtyard on a particular morning, and it is not a verdict on a people — the Gospel's author, its subject, its mother and every one of its apostles were Jews, and Paul says explicitly that God has not rejected his people (Rom. 11:1). What it is, is a warning about religious leadership, and it lands nearest to those who most resemble the men who said it.

Here is the test, and it is for anybody, not for them. There is always a Caesar available — something that can be appealed to as the real authority when the true King is inconvenient. Career, safety, respectability, the approval of a group whose good opinion is load-bearing. The chief priests did not stop believing in God that morning. They simply, under pressure, named somebody else as the one whose displeasure they could not risk.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bearing his own cross: the condemned carried the crossbeam (patibulum) to the place of execution. Jesus goes willingly, bearing the instrument of the curse that will become the instrument of redemption. Golgotha — the Aramaic word for skull — is outside the city wall, the place of maximum public shame. One on either side, Jesus between them: the king flanked by condemned criminals, the scene of Isaiah 53:12 (numbered with the transgressors) enacted literally. The one who knew no sin is placed in the company of those whose sin is publicly displayed and legally condemned.

An apparent conflict has to be dealt with here, because a reader comparing the Gospels will hit it at once. John says he went out bearing his own cross. Matthew, Mark and Luke all say the soldiers seized Simon of Cyrene and made him carry it.

The resolution is not difficult and does not require anyone to be wrong. The condemned man carried the crossbeam — the patibulum, perhaps eighty or a hundred pounds — from the place of sentence to the place of execution. Jesus started out carrying his. He had been awake all night, beaten by the temple guard, flogged with a Roman flagellum and struck repeatedly by soldiers, and men in that condition frequently could not finish the walk. Luke's wording is that they laid the cross on Simon to carry it behind Jesus (Lk. 23:26), which fits a man who has collapsed part of the way.

Each writer keeps what serves his account. The Synoptics record the fact of the collapse and the stranger pressed into service. John, whose whole passion narrative insists that nothing was taken from Jesus and everything was given, records that he went out carrying it himself.

Then Golgotha, and the name is grim and plain: the place of a skull. Whether it was so called from the shape of the outcrop or from its use is not known. What is known is that it was outside the wall — the letter to the Hebrews makes a doctrine of it, that Jesus suffered outside the gate like the sin offering whose body was burned outside the camp (Heb. 13:11-12) — and that it was beside a road, because public execution was meant to be seen.

And then the shortest sentence about the most important event in history: there they crucified him.

Four words. No description. Not one of the four Gospels describes the physical process of crucifixion, and every reader in the first century knew exactly what those words covered and did not need telling. It is worth noticing the restraint, in an age that has produced a good deal of Christian art and film determined to supply what the evangelists deliberately withheld.

Two others, one on either side, and John's phrasing puts him in the middle: and Jesus between them. Isaiah had said the servant would be numbered with the transgressors (Isa. 53:12), and the arrangement of the three crosses is that sentence carried out by a Roman work detail with no idea what they were doing.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS: the placard that Pilate writes is the most accurate theological statement he has ever made — and he wrote it in mockery. In Aramaic (the language of the Jewish people), Latin (the language of Roman law and administration), and Greek (the language of culture and commerce throughout the Mediterranean world) — the three languages ensure that every literate person who passes can read the declaration. The cross is public proclamation in every tongue. What Pilate intended as ironic humiliation is the announcement of the gospel: this is who he is and why he dies.

The board was standard practice. A condemned man was preceded by, or wore, a titulus stating his offence, so that the crowd would know what the state was punishing. It was part of the deterrent.

Which makes this one remarkable. Every other titulus in the empire named a crime. This one names a person and a title, and states no offence at all — because there was none, and Pilate had said so three times.

The three languages are worth taking one at a time, because between them they cover the known world. Aramaic, which the people of that country actually spoke — the language of home, of the covenant, of the Scriptures read in the synagogue. Latin, the language of the army and the law, in which the empire issued its orders. Greek, which everybody used for trade and thought from Spain to India.

So the first public proclamation of the kingship of Jesus was trilingual, official, posted over his head beside a main road on the busiest day of the Jewish year, and paid for by the Roman government.

John adds the detail that it was well placed: the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. Golgotha was close enough to the wall and the gate that a crowd going in and out for the feast would pass it. Many read it, John says — and he means many.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What I have written, I have written: Pilate's most decisive act in the passion narrative — and it is a refusal to retract a truth. The authorities want him to change it from declaration to claim (he said he was king), removing the force of the inscription. Pilate, who has been too weak to acquit the innocent, finds unexpected resolve in maintaining an inscription. Providence uses even this small stubbornness for its purposes: the cross proclaims the truth in permanent ink. The chief priests can arrange an execution but cannot control what the placard says. God's words are not subject to editorial revision by those who oppose them.

Their objection is precise and grammatical. Not the King of the Jews — a statement — but this man said, I am King of the Jews, which converts it into a reported claim by a dead lunatic.

They are asking for the sentence to be turned into a quotation. It is the oldest manoeuvre there is for disposing of a truth without denying it outright.

And Pilate, who has spent the morning conceding everything, refuses.

What I have written, I have written. The perfect tense, twice: it stands written and it will go on standing. It is the flattest, most immovable sentence anybody speaks in the chapter, and it comes from the man who has just handed over somebody he knew to be innocent.

Why does he dig in here? Almost certainly not conscience. It reads like a man who has been pushed around all morning and finds one thing he can refuse — a small, safe, spiteful assertion of the authority he failed to use when it mattered. There is nothing noble in it.

Which is exactly what makes it worth having. God's purposes at Calvary were served by a governor's petty irritation, as they were served by soldiers gambling and by a priest's political calculation. Nobody in the chapter is trying to accomplish anything for God. Every one of them accomplishes it.

And the result is that the only official document produced by the crucifixion of Jesus Christ — the one legal text, in three languages, over his head, unretracted — says that he is the King.

And the sentence has had a long life. Quod scripsi, scripsi passed into proverb, and it is usually quoted admiringly, as the mark of a man who will not be moved.

It was said by somebody who had been moved on every question that mattered, about a notice, after the nails were in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The soldiers divide Jesus' garments, fulfilling Psalm 22. Jesus provides for his mother's care through the beloved disciple. He says 'I thirst' (fulfilling Psalm 69), then 'It is finished' — the great completion cry — and gives up his spirit. The soldiers break the others' legs but not Jesus', fulfilling two scriptures. Joseph and Nicodemus bury him in a garden tomb.

Several things here are treated at length below.

Psalm 22 and the soldiers (vv. 23-24). Four soldiers is a quaternion, the standard execution squad, and the clothes were theirs by custom. The psalm's line looks like ordinary poetic repetition saying one thing twice — they divide my garments… for my clothing they cast lots — and at Golgotha it turns out to be two separate actions, and the reason is a technical accident of weaving. Josephus describes the high priest's robe as seamless, which is a resonance worth noting and not pressing.

Who was there (v. 25). Three women or four, depending on the punctuation. The eleven are not there. The people who stayed are the ones with no power to do anything at all — and it is worth saying to anybody who has stood beside a suffering they could not fix that being present was the only thing anybody did for him that day, and John records their names. Woman is the second and last time he addresses her so; the first was at Cana, when the hour had not yet come (2:4).

The new family (vv. 26-27). He is being executed, breathing costs him a push on the nails, and he spends it on domestic administration. And he passes his mother not to his brothers — who did not believe in him (7:5) — but to a disciple. The first act of the church, performed while its Lord was still dying, is somebody taking a widow in.

Hyssop (v. 29). The detail that carries the most weight in the chapter and is the easiest to miss. Hyssop is a small herb with a weak stem, an awkward thing to use. But John wrote hyssop, and hyssop has one famous use: on the night of the first Passover, Israel was told to take a bunch of it, dip it in the blood, and daub the doorposts so the destroyer would pass over (Exod. 12:22). It is the applicator of the Passover blood, and it is lifted to the mouth of the Passover Lamb.

Tetelestai (v. 30). Perfect tense — finished, and remaining finished. And note it is not I am finished; the subject is the work. Then John's word order, which is backwards and deliberate: he bowed his head and gave up his spirit. A dying man's head falls when he dies. John has him lay it down first, and then hand over his spirit — the same man who said no one takes it from me (10:18).

Was he dead? (vv. 33-34). The swoon theory founders here. The men at the foot of the cross were a professional execution detail whose own lives answered for a mistake, and they judged him dead without bothering to break his legs. Then one made sure. Medical explanations of the blood and water vary; what is not in dispute is that this is what a corpse produces. John stops the narrative to swear to it in the manner of an affidavit — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — because by the time he wrote, teachers were already denying that Christ had really suffered (1 Jn. 4:3).

Two fulfilments (vv. 36-37). Not one of his bones will be broken is the Passover regulation (Exod. 12:46; Num. 9:12), kept by a Roman work detail hurrying to finish before sunset, who left one body intact because there was nothing to gain by damaging it. And Zechariah's wording is startling: when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced (Zech. 12:10) — the speaker is the LORD. What follows the looking in that passage is mourning, and then a fountain opened for sin (Zech. 13:1).

Two men who came late (vv. 38-40). Joseph breaks cover at the moment it costs most and profits least — a private request to a Roman governor for the body of an executed insurrectionist, made when the movement is finished. And Nicodemus brings seventy-five pounds of spices, which is a king's burial; Josephus records five hundred servants carrying spices at Herod's funeral. His arc is now complete: a night visit and a question he could not follow, one cautious procedural point in a hostile council (7:50-51), and then everything at once at the worst possible moment. Both men made themselves ritually unclean for seven days by handling the body (Num. 19:11), on the eve of the feast. They will spend Passover unfit to attend it — and they had missed nothing, because the Lamb was already dead.

The garden again (vv. 41-42). John used the word at 18:1 and is the only evangelist who uses it in either place. A garden where he was taken, a garden where he is laid — and in three days a woman will stand in this one and mistake him for the gardener (20:15). The tomb is new and unused, which forecloses any confusion about whose body was missing; Matthew adds that it was Joseph's own. And Isaiah had said something that made no sense as a prediction: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death (Isa. 53:9). Both halves came true within hours by opposite mechanisms.
verseByVerse.theology: It is finished is the single most important word of the gospel. It announces a completed action whose effects are permanent: the work of redemption is done, accomplished, complete — it does not require addition, continuation, or supplement. Every subsequent act of piety, every religious effort, every moral striving — none adds to what is finished on the cross. Salvation is received, not achieved; accepted, not earned.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross (with Mary, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the wife of Clopas) is the model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost is highest, faithful where the others fled. He sees the blood and water from the soldier's spear — the sign that Jesus is truly dead, truly human, truly sacrificed — and testifies that what he saw is true. His testimony is the foundation of the gospel that will go to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Psalm 22:18 — the same psalm that begins 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — describes the division of the garments in detail. The soldiers are unknowingly fulfilling a psalm written a thousand years earlier; their practical calculation about the seamless tunic is the exact fulfillment of a prophetic poem. The seamless tunic (perhaps echoing the high priest's garment, which was also seamless) is preserved whole even as Jesus' body is broken. God's providential oversight extends to the gambling of soldiers over a condemned man's clothes. The details of the cross are as pre-arranged as the creation of the world.

The number of soldiers tells you this is a routine detail recorded by somebody who was watching. Four parts, one part for each soldier — a quaternion, the standard Roman execution squad, and the clothes of the condemned were theirs by custom. It was a perquisite of the job.

So four men sit down at the foot of the cross and divide up a change of clothes: the outer cloak, the belt, the sandals, the head covering. One item is left over.

And the tunic is worth knowing about. Josephus describes the high priest's robe as woven in a single piece without a seam, and the coincidence has struck readers since the early centuries — the garment of the priest, on the body of the priest, preserved whole while everything else is divided. It should be offered as a resonance rather than an argument; John does not press it.

What John does press is the psalm. Psalm 22 was written a thousand years earlier by a man describing an ordeal of his own, and it contains a line that had no obvious application to anything: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. Two different actions — dividing and gambling. It reads like ordinary poetic repetition, saying one thing twice.

At Golgotha it turns out to be two things. They divided the garments and they cast lots for the tunic, and the reason they did both is a technical accident of weaving.

Psalm 22 is worth reading whole at this point. It opens with the cry Jesus quotes from the cross. It has men mocking and wagging their heads; it has they have pierced my hands and feet; it has bones out of joint and a tongue sticking to the jaw; and it ends, unaccountably, in worldwide praise. It is either the most extraordinary coincidence in literature or it is what it appears to be.

And the soldiers noticed none of it. They were solving a practical problem about a garment that would be ruined if cut, and John says: so the soldiers did these things. Four men gambling on a hillside, entirely at liberty, fulfilling to the letter a poem they had never read.
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three or four women at the cross, and the beloved disciple: the faithful remnant who did not scatter. They could not stop the crucifixion; they could be present for it. Mary the mother stands at the cross that Simeon predicted would pierce her soul (Luke 2:35). Jesus, in the midst of his death agony, attends to his mother's future care — the Son providing for the mother, the Lord providing for the human need of the one through whom he became flesh. The word from the cross is pastoral: his love extends even to the particular arrangements of his mother's household.

Count the women, and notice who is missing.

John lists his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene — either three women or four, depending on whether the second and third are the same person, and the Greek permits both readings. What is not in doubt is that the group at the cross is mostly women, plus one disciple.

The rest of the eleven are not there. Peter is somewhere in the city. The men who had sworn to die with him a few hours earlier are absent to a man except this one, and the people who stayed are the ones with no power to do anything at all.

Which is worth saying to anybody who has ever stood beside a suffering they could not fix. These women could not stop it. They had no standing, no legal voice, no ability to intervene, and if they had tried they would have been moved on by soldiers. What they could do was be there, in full view, close enough for him to see them and speak.

It was not nothing. It is, in fact, the only thing anybody did for him that day, and John records their names.

Then the address, and it is the second time in this Gospel: Woman. He said it to her once before, at a wedding in Cana, when she wanted him to do something about the wine and he told her his hour had not yet come (2:4). It sounds cold in English and was not — it is a respectful form — but it is a striking word for a son to use, and John has bracketed the ministry with it. Cana, where the hour had not come; Golgotha, where it has.

Does this make Mary the spiritual mother of all believers, as Roman Catholic teaching holds? The text shows a son providing for his widowed mother, and the disciple taking her to his own home (v. 27). Nothing gives her a role in the church’s salvation or prayers. Mary is honoured as the mother of the Lord and a believer among believers (Acts 1:14), but Christ alone is our mediator.

Luke records that Simeon had told her, when the baby was forty days old, that a sword will pierce through your own soul also (Lk. 2:35). She has had some thirty years to wonder what he meant, and she is finding out.

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that hour the disciple took her to his own home: the immediate obedience of the beloved disciple to Jesus' dying word. The new family of the resurrection (mother and son, not by blood but by the word of Jesus) is established at the cross. Knowing that all was now finished, Jesus says I thirst, fulfilling Psalm 69:21. He who is the Living Water, who gives springs of water welling up to eternal life, is thirsty on the cross. The incarnation is real: the eternal Son in a body that needs water, experiencing the physical extremity of death by crucifixion.

Two things about the arrangement he makes, and both take some getting used to.

The first is the timing. He is in the process of being executed. Breathing requires pushing up on the nails. And what he does with that breath is domestic administration — settling who will look after his mother.

The second is who he gives her to. He had brothers; John has told us that not even his brothers believed in him (7:5). Under any ordinary reckoning the eldest son's responsibility passes to the next son. He passes it instead to a disciple.

That is not a slight on the family — James will be leading the Jerusalem church within a few years, and Jude will write a letter. It is a statement about what the new family is founded on. The tie that binds this household together is not blood. From that hour the disciple took her to his own home — the first act of the church, performed while its Lord was still dying, and it consists of somebody taking a widow in.

Then I thirst, and the note John attaches to it: he said it to fulfil the Scripture, and knowing that all was now finished.

A reader may stumble there, as though the thirst were staged for the sake of a quotation. It was not. The man had been flogged, had lost blood for hours, and had been hanging in the sun since morning; dehydration is one of the mechanisms by which crucifixion kills. The thirst is as real as thirst gets.

What John means is that he knew what he was doing when he said it aloud. There is a psalm — for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink (Ps. 69:21) — and there is a line in Psalm 22 about a tongue sticking to the jaws. He is not manufacturing a fulfilment; he is naming, in the last minutes, the one thing left on the list.

And it is worth holding on to the plain fact underneath the theology. The one who told a woman at a well that he could give her water so that she would never thirst again (4:14), and who stood up at the feast and shouted about rivers of living water (7:37), died of thirst.

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is finished: the cry of completed redemption. Not 'I am finished' (I am dying) but 'it is finished' (the work is done). The entire mission of the incarnation — the bearing of sin, the satisfaction of justice, the demonstration of love, the defeat of death — is accomplished in this moment. He bowed his head and gave up his spirit: the voluntary self-giving to the end. The language is not 'died' but 'gave up his spirit' — an act of willing surrender, not the passive failure of a biological system. The Shepherd lays down his life; he gives it; it is not taken.

Before the great word, one detail that is easy to miss and is not decoration.

They lifted the sponge to his mouth on a stalk of hyssop.

Hyssop is a small bushy herb with a weak stem. Commentators have long noted the practical difficulty — it is not an obvious thing to hold a soaked sponge up with, But John wrote hyssop, and the reason is almost certainly that he knew what hyssop was for.

On the night of the first Passover, Israel was told to take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood in the basin, and daub it on the doorposts and the lintel, so that the destroyer would pass over the house (Exod. 12:22).

Hyssop is the applicator of the Passover blood. And at the moment the true Passover Lamb is dying, a stalk of it is lifted to his mouth. John has recorded it and said nothing, which is his habit.

Then the word.

It is finished. Not it ended but it is finished and remains finished — a thing completed with results that stand.

Note what it is not. It is not I am finished, which is what a dying man says. The subject is the work, not the man.

And notice the guard this word puts on everything afterwards. If the work is finished, nothing can be added to it — not by penance, not by devotion, not by a lifetime of good behaviour, not by anything a person does on their worst day or their best. The commonest form of Christian misery is the suspicion that something is still outstanding. This word was shouted from a cross to settle it.

Then the last thing, and John's word order is deliberate: he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

That is backwards. A dying man's head falls when he dies. John has him bow it first, deliberately, and then hand over his spirit — the verb is one of transmission, of giving something into someone's keeping.

Two thousand years of art has him hanging with his head fallen. John says he laid it down. The same man had said, in the shepherd discourse, no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (10:18), and this is the sentence where he does it.

Nothing was taken from him that afternoon. The clothes were taken, and the freedom, and the reputation, and the blood. His life he handed over, at a moment of his choosing, having first said that the account was settled.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The breaking of legs (crurifragium) accelerated death by preventing the victim from pushing up to breathe — death by asphyxiation within minutes. The Sabbath begins at sunset; Jewish law required that bodies not remain on the cross (Deut. 21:23). The authorities who arranged the crucifixion are now concerned about ritual propriety — the same irony as not entering the praetorium to avoid defilement (18:28). The legs of the two criminals are broken; Jesus' are not. The soldiers verify his death without breaking anything — fulfilling in precision the detail of the Passover lamb (Ex. 12:46; Num. 9:12).

The request is a mercy in the most brutal possible form, and it is worth understanding the mechanics because it explains why Jesus' death is so hard to explain away.

Crucifixion killed slowly, by exhaustion and asphyxiation. A man could keep breathing only by pushing himself up on the nail through his feet, and every breath cost him that. It could take two days. Breaking the legs removed the ability to push up at all, and death followed within minutes.

So the authorities are asking Pilate to hurry the process along — not out of pity but because of the calendar. Sunset was coming, the Sabbath with it, and this one was a high day, the Sabbath falling within Passover week. And there was a law: his body shall not remain all night on the tree… you shall bury him the same day (Deut. 21:23).

Which is the same irony as the praetorium doorstep, and it should be noted without being laboured. Men who would not enter a Gentile house in case it barred them from a meal are, that afternoon, arranging for the legs of three living men to be shattered so that the evening's observance is not spoiled.

The soldiers work along the row. The first man's legs are broken. The other one's. And then they come to the middle cross.

One further note on that Sabbath was a high day. John is flagging that this was no ordinary week's end — the weekly Sabbath coinciding with the festival — which is why the pressure to have the bodies down was unusually strong, and why the burial that follows is done at such speed.

Note also who does the asking. The Jews asked Pilate — the same officials, going back to the same governor, a second time in one day. The first request was for a death. The second is to have it hurried up so as not to spoil the evening.
verseByVerse.note: The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight; the coming Sabbath made it more urgent. Breaking the legs stopped a crucified man pushing up to breathe and hastened death.

parallels.desc: his body shall not remain all night on the tree

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blood and water: the physical evidence of true death — the separation of blood and serum (or pericardial fluid) is a sign of actual biological death. John is insisting against early docetism (which denied the reality of Jesus' suffering) that Jesus truly died in a truly human body. The blood and water also carry sacramental resonance: blood of the covenant, water of the Spirit — the two great gifts of the passion flowing from the wounded side of the crucified Lord. The church's tradition has seen here the origin of baptism and the Eucharist: water and blood, the signs of the new covenant life.

Take the historical question first, because it is the one on which everything else rests: was he actually dead?

The suggestion that he merely fainted and revived in the cool of the tomb has been made repeatedly since the eighteenth century, and it founders on this verse. The men at the foot of the cross were a professional execution detail. Killing people was their trade, and a soldier who let a condemned man off a cross alive would have answered for it with his own life. They looked at him and did not bother breaking his legs, which is the judgement of experts.

Then one of them made sure. The spear-thrust was standard practice, and what came out settled it.

Blood and water. Medical explanations have been offered — the separation of clot and serum after death, or fluid accumulated in the pericardium or the chest cavity following the flogging and the strain — and no single account commands agreement. What is not in dispute is that this is what a corpse produces and a living man does not.

Which is why John, alone of the four, stops the narrative to swear to it in the next verse. He is not making a devotional point. He is a witness giving evidence about a body.

And there is a reason he was so anxious to establish it. By the time this Gospel was written, teachers were already circulating who held that the Christ could not really have suffered — that the divine had departed before the death, or that the body was an appearance. John's letters go after exactly that error: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God… every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God (1 Jn. 4:2-3). The blood and water are his answer, and he saw them come out.

The older reading, that the two fluids signify the two sacraments, is not to be dismissed — the church has seen baptism and the Supper flowing from the wounded side since very early, and John does write on more than one level. But the primary meaning is the plainer and harder one. It is the evidence of death, offered by a man standing close enough to see it.

parallels.desc: the water and the blood
a fountain opened for sin

verseByVerse.quote: He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true: the beloved disciple's personal eyewitness attestation, placed at the heart of the passion narrative. That you also may believe: the entire gospel is written for this purpose (20:31), and the passion narrative is its center. Not one of his bones will be broken: the Passover lamb's bones were not to be broken (Ex. 12:46); the same requirement applies to the true Passover Lamb. The physical details of the crucifixion are not accidents but fulfillments — every particular of the death serves the purposes of the God who announced it through the prophets and accomplished it through the Son.

This verse is the author breaking cover, and it is worth noticing how unusual that is. John has written eighteen chapters without once stopping to vouch for himself. Here he stops the story and gives testimony, in the manner of a man swearing an affidavit: he who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth.

The doubling is deliberate and it is legal language: this is what I saw, I am telling the truth, and I know that I am. That is not the diction of piety. It is the diction of a witness statement.

And he gives the reason: that you also may believe. The same purpose he will state for the whole book at 20:31. He is not recording the spear-thrust because it is moving. He is recording it because the reader's faith depends on the man having actually died, and he was there.

Then the first of two fulfilments, and it is the one the whole Gospel has been building toward since John the Baptist pointed at him in chapter 1.

Not one of his bones will be broken.

The regulation is from Exodus 12, the instructions for the Passover lamb: it is to be roasted whole, eaten within the house, and you shall not break any of its bones (Exod. 12:46; repeated at Num. 9:12). Every Passover for fourteen centuries, in every Jewish household, the lamb was handled under that rule.

The soldiers had a routine and a schedule. They came along the row breaking legs, and at the middle cross they stopped — for the entirely practical reason that the man was already dead and there was no point.

Which is how the rule was kept. Not by anyone's intention. A Roman work detail, hurrying to finish before sunset on the day of Preparation, left one body intact because there was nothing to be gained by damaging it, and in doing so handled the Lamb of God exactly as the law required.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken.

parallels.desc: he keeps all his bones

verseByVerse.quote: And again another Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced." After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will look on him whom they have pierced: Zechariah 12:10, which speaks of the mourning of those who look on the pierced one — a prophecy that points forward to the repentance that will follow recognition of what was done at Calvary. The Zechariah prophecy will ultimately be fulfilled at the parousia (Rev. 1:7), but the soldier's spear begins the fulfillment. Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, comes out of hiding at the moment of maximum risk — when Jesus is dead and to associate with him is most dangerous. The cross, which scattered the living disciples, draws the hidden ones into the open.

The second fulfilment comes from Zechariah, and the wording is startling once it is looked at: when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced (Zech. 12:10). The speaker in that passage is the LORD. It is one of the strangest sentences in the prophets, and John quotes it over a corpse with a spear-wound in its side.

The Zechariah passage is not about condemnation. What follows the looking is mourning — a whole nation weeping, family by family — and then, in the next verse, a fountain opened… to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness (Zech. 13:1). The looking leads to grief and the grief to a fountain.

Then Joseph, and his timing is the point.

John says he was a disciple secretly, for fear of the Jews — the same phrase used of the parents of the blind man and of the authorities who believed and would not say so (9:22; 12:42). Mark adds that he was a respected member of the council, and Luke that he had not consented to their decision (Lk. 23:50-51).

And he comes forward now. Not during the trial, when a voice might have helped. Not while there was anything to gain. He goes to Pilate — a private request to a Roman governor for the body of an executed insurrectionist, which is not a small thing to be seen doing — at the exact moment when the movement is finished, the leader is dead, and there is no possible advantage in being associated with any of it.

Which is worth sitting with, because it cuts against the way we usually rank courage. Joseph's years of silence were real and this Gospel does not excuse them. But the moment he chose to break cover was the moment it cost most and profited least, and no one else in Jerusalem did it.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: they look on me, on him whom they have pierced

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who came by night: the arc of Nicodemus's faith — nighttime inquiry (ch. 3), procedural advocacy (7:50-51), and now public action — is completed at the cross. He brings seventy-five pounds of spices — an extravagant quantity fit for a king — the same extravagance as Mary's ointment but now in burial rather than anointing. The man who came asking about new birth now prepares for burial the one who promised it. The preparation is tender, careful, and complete: linen cloths, spices, Jewish burial custom. Jesus is not discarded; he is buried with honor by those who loved him.

Weigh the quantity, because it is not incidental. Seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes is an enormous amount — a load a man would struggle to carry, and worth a great deal of money.

Ordinary burials used a fraction of it. Josephus records that five hundred servants carried spices at Herod the Great's funeral, which is the register this belongs to. Nicodemus has brought a king's burial to a criminal's execution.

And notice how John introduces him: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night. He will not let the man be seen apart from that first visit, and the whole arc is now visible.

He came in the dark, cautiously, with a compliment and a question, and was told he must be born again and could not follow it. He turned up again in chapter 7, in a council meeting, making a careful procedural point — does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? — and was slapped down for it (7:50-51). And now he is here in daylight, in public, with seventy-five pounds of spices and his hands on a dead body.

Which is a slow conversion, and it is worth saying so for the reader who has been waiting a long time for somebody. It took Nicodemus years, and the visible steps were: a private conversation, one cautious question in a hostile room, and then everything at once at the worst possible moment.

Handling a corpse made a Jew ritually unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11). Both these men, on the eve of the greatest feast of the year, disqualified themselves from all of it in order to bury him. They will spend Passover unclean.

They had missed nothing. The Lamb was already dead.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds — a quantity fit for a royal burial. Myrrh and aloes were aromatic spices laid with the linen wrappings.

parallels.desc: King Asa laid on a bier filled with spices
myrrh at his birth

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A garden: the crucifixion happened near a garden, and the burial is in a garden. The Garden of Eden where sin entered; the garden of Gethsemane where surrender was offered; the garden of the tomb where resurrection will break out. New creation always begins in a garden. A new tomb in which no one had yet been laid: an unoccupied tomb ensures that the resurrection cannot be confused with any other burial. The specificity of the location, the newness of the tomb, the haste of Preparation-day burial — all of it is historically particular and theologically freighted. The story of redemption unfolds in real places, with real bodies, in real time.

John has told us there was a garden once already in this passion, in the first verse of chapter 18, and he is the only evangelist who uses the word in either place. Now he closes the bracket.

A garden at the beginning, where he was taken. A garden at the end, where he is laid. And in three days a woman will stand in this one, weeping, and mistake him for the gardener (20:15) — which is either John's finest touch or nobody's, and he does not explain it.

The story began in a garden that went wrong. It is being put right in one.

Two details in the tomb matter and both are evidential. It was new, and no one had yet been laid in it — which forecloses the suggestion that the wrong body was found missing, or that some other occupant was confused with him. Matthew adds that it belonged to Joseph himself, which means a wealthy man gave away the grave he had cut for his own family.

And Isaiah, describing the servant, had said something that made no sense as a prediction: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death (Isa. 53:9). Both halves came true within hours, and by opposite mechanisms — the state put him between two criminals, and a private citizen put him in a rich man's tomb.

Then the last clause, and it is very flat: because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.

They chose it because it was near and the light was going. There is no ceremony in the sentence, no reflection, no farewell. Two men who had been afraid of being seen with him work quickly against a deadline, put a body in a borrowed grave, and go home to keep a feast they are no longer fit to attend.

And that is where the chapter stops. John does not close it with a promise or a hint. He leaves the reader at a sealed tomb on a Friday evening, which is exactly where everybody who loved him was left.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death
