20.title: The Resurrection

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Empty Tomb and Mary's Encounter with the Risen Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb before dawn, finds the stone rolled away, reports to Peter and the beloved disciple. They run to the tomb; the beloved disciple sees and believes. Mary remains weeping, sees two angels, then turns to find Jesus — whom she mistakes for the gardener until he calls her by name.

The physical evidence itself is the heart of the passage. All of it is treated below.

A pronoun that confirms the other Gospels (vv. 1-2). John names only Mary Magdalene, where Matthew, Mark and Luke have several women — and then he leaves standing, in her own speech, the words we do not know where they have laid him. He is telling the story through Mary because she matters for what follows, and has not troubled to remove the evidence that she was not alone. That is not the mark of a fabricator. And the first day of the week: after a Friday of finishing and a Sabbath of rest, the reason Christians gather on Sundays is in that phrase.

The seeing (vv. 5-8). A glance through the entrance, a study from inside, and then understanding — he saw and believed — over perhaps a minute, described by a man who was there. And the cloths are lying — not thrown or scattered. Grave robbers do not undress a body; the wrappings and spices were worth more than the corpse.

A guard on the folded cloth (v. 7). A popular sermon holds that a Jewish servant left a napkin folded to signal I am coming back. There is no evidence for any such custom in any ancient source, and the word is not table linen but a burial face-cloth. The story appears to be a modern invention and the verse does not need it. What the text says is stranger: the face cloth was folded up in a place by itself, apart from the linen cloths.

What "he believed" rested on (v. 8). No angel had spoken to him. He had not seen the risen Lord and would not for twelve hours. Nobody had explained anything, and the next verse says he still did not understand the Scripture. He had an empty tomb and the way the linen was lying, and it was enough.

The candour of v. 9. Not they had forgotten — they had never grasped it, though Jesus had told them plainly and repeatedly. The Scriptures were there: Psalm 16 (which Peter preaches at Pentecost, Acts 2:25-31), the third day of Hosea 6:2, Jonah, and the servant of Isaiah 53 who is cut off and then prolongs his days. It had been there for centuries and none of them had assembled it — and one of them writes this sentence about himself decades later without any attempt to look better.

Then they went home (v. 10). The flattest verse in the resurrection narrative. Two men look at the most important physical evidence in history, and one of them believes, and neither says anything to anybody, and they walk back to where they are staying. Which means the first person to meet the risen Christ is the one who stayed.

Mary at the tomb (vv. 11-14). There is nothing constructive in what she is doing; she has no plan, and even the last service she could have rendered has been taken from her. She is simply unable to leave — and she is the one the risen Christ appears to first. Note also that she is not frightened by two angels and does not remark on them: her grief is large enough that they do not register. And her wording has shifted since verse 2 — they have taken away my Lord.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection appearances in John are structured around recognition: the beloved disciple sees and believes from the evidence of the linen cloths; Mary recognizes Jesus when he calls her name (the Good Shepherd and the sheep who knows his voice, 10:3); Thomas recognizes Jesus when invited to touch the wounds. Each recognition is different, calibrated to each person's need and capacity. This is the risen Lord — the same person, now transformed, who meets each disciple where they are.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the resurrection, commissioned by the risen Lord to tell the disciples: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. The announcement is simultaneously personal (my Father) and covenantal (your Father) — the resurrection makes the disciples' relationship to the Father the same as Jesus' own. The first gospel proclamation after the resurrection is spoken by a woman who was weeping at a tomb and heard her name called by the one she thought was dead. This is how the gospel always comes: to those who have not ceased to love the crucified Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first day of the week — the new creation's first day, corresponding to the first day of the original creation. Mary comes while it was still dark: she is still in the night of grief, not yet in the light of resurrection. The stone removed is not the beginning but the announcement of what has already happened — the stone was rolled away not to let Jesus out but to let the disciples in, to let the testimony begin. They have taken the Lord: her first interpretation is theft or relocation, not resurrection. The human mind moves toward the ordinary explanation before the extraordinary one.

There is a detail in Mary's own sentence that quietly confirms the other Gospels, and it is one of the most satisfying things in the chapter.

John names only Mary Magdalene. Matthew has her with the other Mary; Mark adds Salome; Luke speaks of the women who had come from Galilee. A sceptical reader would call that a discrepancy.

And then Mary opens her mouth: we do not know where they have laid him.

We. John has written the whole scene around one woman and left the plural pronoun standing in her speech, which is exactly what happens when somebody reports a conversation accurately without tidying it. He is telling the story through Mary because she is the one who matters for what follows; he has not troubled to remove the evidence that she was not alone.

That is not the mark of a fabricator. It is the mark of a man writing down what he remembers being said.

Two smaller notes. While it was still dark sits beside Mark's when the sun had risen (Mk. 16:2) — and anyone who has set out early knows both are true of the same walk. She left in the dark and arrived as it was getting light.

And the first day of the week is literally one of the week in Greek, the ordinary idiom, but with an echo worth hearing. John opened this Gospel with in the beginning, deliberately echoing Genesis. Now, after a Friday of finishing and a Sabbath of rest, comes the first day — and the whole reason Christians gather on Sundays rather than Saturdays is in that phrase.

And her report has one more thing worth registering. She runs to Peter — the man who denied him, whom the others might reasonably have written off — and to the beloved disciple, and she treats them as the people to be told. Nobody in the account has excluded Peter from anything.

Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? The day of resurrection became the church’s day of gathering (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2), and John calls it the Lord’s day (Rev 1:10). Many Reformed Christians regard it as the Christian Sabbath. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17), and that Christians gather on Sunday as a glad privilege, not under law.

Her interpretation is wrong, and it is the sensible one. A tomb that was sealed on Friday is open on Sunday, and the obvious inference is that somebody has moved the body. It takes nothing away from her that she reached for the ordinary explanation; every one of us would have.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both of them were running: the resurrection produces urgency — the news that could change everything is worth running toward. The beloved disciple outruns Peter: in every other confrontation of the passion, Peter's impetuosity has put him first. Now the one whose love kept him at the cross and in the high priest's courtyard outruns the denier. The beloved disciple arrives first but waits; Peter arrives and enters first. Both details are significant: love arrives first; courage enters first. Both are needed for the full witness of the empty tomb.

John's note that he got there first has amused readers for centuries, and it is worth noticing that he mentions it twice — here and again at verse 8. Whether it is the pride of a younger man remembering that he could outrun Peter, or simply the accuracy of somebody reporting the order in which people arrived, cannot be settled and does not matter much.

What does matter is that he stopped at the entrance and did not go in, and Peter — who had denied his Lord three times a few days earlier and had every reason to hang back — walked straight past him into a grave.

The detail is worth having for what it says about how these men functioned together. One arrives first and hesitates; the other arrives second and goes in. Neither is criticised, and John records the hesitation as his own.

And there is a small point of evidence in it. A man inventing a resurrection narrative in the first century would not have built it around the testimony of women and then had two male disciples arrive, look, and go home. The story does nothing to make its witnesses impressive.

Then the running itself, which is the only note of energy in the passage. Two grown men sprinting through Jerusalem at first light on the strength of a report neither of them believed — because Mary's message was that the body had been stolen, and that is what they were running to investigate.

Whatever they expected to find, it was not what they found.

One further thing about the pair. These two men appear together again and again in these chapters — at the supper (13:23-24), in the courtyard (18:15-16), at the tomb, and on the shore in the next chapter. John and Peter are consistently placed side by side, the one who sees and the one who acts, and the church's earliest chapters in Acts have them still together, going up to the temple at the hour of prayer.

parallels.desc: Peter runs to the tomb

verseByVerse.quote: And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The linen cloths lying there: the burial wrappings are not scattered as if the body was removed hastily but lying there — in their place, as if the body had simply passed through them. A resurrected body does not need to unwrap itself; the linen cloths lie where the body was. The eyewitness observation of the cloths' position is a detail that argues for historical memory: a story fabricated for theological purposes would not include the specific observation of where the burial cloths were. The particular details of the empty tomb are the details of those who were there and saw.

John describes the seeing in stages. At verse 5 the beloved disciple stoops and catches sight of the cloths. At verse 6 Peter goes in and takes stock. And at verse 8 the other disciple goes in, and saw and believed.

A glance, then a study, then an understanding. John is describing what happened in that small space over the course of perhaps a minute, because he was there.

And the position of the cloths is the thing they were looking at. The verb is simply lying — not thrown, not scattered, not gathered up. Grave robbers do not undress a body; the wrappings and the spices were worth more than the corpse, and anybody stealing it would have carried the whole bundle out. What these men are staring at is a set of grave clothes still lying where a body had been.

Also worth noting: the tomb is low. The beloved disciple has to stoop to look in — which fits the rock-cut tombs of the period, with an opening a man had to bend double to enter.

Two Greek words are used for the burial wrappings in these verses, and they are not the same thing. The othonia are the linen strips that bound the body; the soudarion of the next verse is the cloth that covered the face and was tied round the head.

John distinguishes them because their positions were different, and their positions are the whole point of what he is describing.

verseByVerse.quote: and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folded up in a place by itself: the face cloth is not merely dropped but separately placed — a detail that argues against hasty theft (who folds napkins while removing bodies?) and for something deliberate. He saw and believed: the beloved disciple, standing in the empty tomb, sees the arrangement of the burial cloths and believes — before seeing the risen Lord, before hearing the resurrection announced, before the Scripture of resurrection is opened to his understanding. Faith that comes from the evidence of the empty tomb is real faith; Thomas's faith that requires the visible wounds is also real. The Spirit meets each where they are.

A guard is needed here, because a sermon about this verse circulates widely and it is not true.

The story goes that a Jewish servant, clearing a master's table, would leave the napkin crumpled if the meal was over and fold it neatly if he intended to return — so the folded face cloth is Jesus saying I am coming back. It is a lovely idea with one defect: there is no evidence for any such custom, in any ancient source, and the word here is not about table linen at all. A face cloth is exactly that, used at burials. The story appears to be a modern invention, and the verse is strong enough not to need it.

What the text does say is precise and stranger. The face cloth was not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself.

So the picture the two men are looking at is not an empty tomb with linen scattered about. It is a set of grave clothes that has kept its arrangement, with nothing in it.

And then the sentence John writes about himself, in the third person, with no elaboration whatsoever: he saw and believed.

Notice what he had at that moment. No angel had spoken to him. He had not seen the risen Lord and would not for another twelve hours. Nobody had explained anything, and the next verse says outright that he still did not understand the Scripture about the resurrection.

What he had was an empty tomb and the way the linen was lying. That was enough.
verseByVerse.note: Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the cloths neatly behind.

verseByVerse.quote: for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not yet understand the Scripture: the resurrection was not what they expected even though it was what was promised. Psalm 16:10 (you will not abandon my soul to Sheol or let your holy one see corruption) and Isaiah 53's implicit restoration — these pointed to resurrection, but the disciples had not assembled the pieces. The resurrection creates the hermeneutical moment: now the Scripture opens, now the pieces fit. The disciples return home still processing; the one who believed is still gathering understanding. The Spirit will finish what the empty tomb began.

The admission in verse 9 is remarkable for its candour and it is worth asking why a writer would include it.

As yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Not they had forgotten. They had never grasped it — and Jesus had told them plainly and repeatedly that he would be killed and rise on the third day.

Which passages of Scripture? The apostles later point to Psalm 16 — you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption — and Peter builds his Pentecost sermon on it (Acts 2:25-31). Paul says Christ was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Cor. 15:4). Hosea has a third day (Hos. 6:2), Jonah has three days, and Isaiah 53 has a servant who is cut off and then shall see his offspring and shall prolong his days (Isa. 53:10).

It was all there. It had been there for centuries, and none of them had put it together, and one of them is writing this sentence about himself decades later without any attempt to look better.

Then the flattest verse in the resurrection narrative: then the disciples went back to their homes.

They went home. One of them has just believed something, and neither of them says anything to anybody, and there is no announcement and no gathering and no prayer meeting. Two men look at the most important physical evidence in human history and then walk back to where they are staying.

Which is worth having, because it is so unlike how the story would be written by anyone constructing a legend, and because it is so exactly like people. And it means the first person to actually meet the risen Christ is the one who stayed.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary stood weeping: while the disciples process and return home, Mary remains — grief rooting her to the place of loss. Those who love most intensely are sometimes last to leave the place of grief. The two angels at the head and feet of where the body had lain mirror the two cherubim on the ark of the covenant, over the mercy seat — the place where God meets humanity in grace. The empty space between the angels is the mercy seat now emptied because the sacrifice has been accepted. The tomb is the new Most Holy Place.

But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb.

The but is doing all the work. The men have gone home; she has not. She had walked there in the dark, run to fetch them, presumably walked back, and now stands outside a tomb that everyone else has finished with.

And there is nothing constructive in what she is doing. She has no plan. She is not waiting for anything, because as far as she knows the body has been stolen and the last available service — anointing it properly — has been taken from her too. She is simply unable to leave.

Which is worth saying plainly for anyone whose grief has outlasted everybody else's patience with it. This is the person the risen Christ appears to first. Not the one who reasoned correctly from the evidence, and not the one who went in first, and not the eleven. The one who could not go home.

Then she stoops and looks in — the same verb used of the beloved disciple in verse 5, and it is a second look at a space two men have already searched. Grief does that too: checks again.

And this time there is something there. Two angels, seated, one where the head had been and one at the feet.

They are sitting. Not standing guard, not blazing, not announcing. The most extraordinary beings in the account are described as sitting quietly in an empty grave, and Mary — this is the astonishing part — is not frightened by them and does not remark on them at all. She answers their question as though they were attendants, and then turns away from them. Her grief is large enough that two angels do not register.

The seating deserves one more note. One at the head and one at the feet, with an empty space between them where a body had lain — and anyone who knows the furniture of the tabernacle may be reminded of that arrangement, though John does not say so. Two figures at either end of a slab, facing inward across an empty place, is the mercy seat: two cherubim of gold, one at each end, overshadowing the lid of the ark, with the space between them the place where God said he would meet his people (Exod. 25:18-22).

The Most Holy Place had been behind a curtain, entered once a year, with blood. This one has a woman crying at the entrance and, as the other Gospels record, the curtain torn (Mt. 27:51).

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?" She said to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him." Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She turned around and saw Jesus standing: the risen Lord is present while she weeps at his absence. The one she seeks is already there; the grief that roots her to the tomb is the very thing that keeps her present to receive the first resurrection appearance. She did not know that it was Jesus: the resurrection body is recognizable but not instantly. Mary's grief has become a kind of blindness — not culpable but understandable. The Lord accommodates the blindness with a question and then a name, because he is the Good Shepherd who knows his sheep and calls them by name.

Her answer to the angels has one word in it that was not there before, and it is the saddest word in the chapter.

At verse 2 she said they have taken the Lord. Here she says they have taken away my Lord.

The public title has become a personal one. She is not making a christological statement; she is a woman explaining, to somebody who has asked, why she cannot stop crying.

Then: she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

He was behind her. He had been there — for how long, John does not say — while she was bent over an empty grave describing his disappearance to two angels.

And she does not recognise him. This happens repeatedly in the resurrection accounts: the two on the Emmaus road walk and talk with him for hours (Lk. 24:16), and the disciples on the beach in the next chapter do not know him either. Something about the risen body is not immediately familiar, and the Gospels report the fact without explaining it.

But there is a simpler thing operating here too, and it does not require any theory about resurrection bodies. She was not looking for a living man. Grief had already settled the range of possibilities, and a person standing in a garden at dawn could be one of several things, none of which was the man she had watched die.

Which is worth knowing about ourselves. She was three feet from the answer to her weeping and could not see it, and there was nothing culpable in that at all.

Note also that the angels ask her the same question Jesus will ask a verse later — woman, why are you weeping? — and it is not an accusation in either mouth. It is the question that gets somebody to say aloud what is wrong.

Nobody in this scene tells her to stop crying. Two angels and the risen Son of God, and not one of them says she should not be upset. They ask her why.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?" Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Aramaic, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Supposing him to be the gardener: the risen Lord in the garden, mistaken for the gardener — and perhaps he is, in a sense. The second Adam, Lord of the new creation, tending the garden of the new covenant. Mary — the name he speaks in a way that only he can speak it, with the intimacy of the one who calls his own by name. Rabboni: the same word she has been using but now invested with a recognition that surpasses all her previous understanding. One word from Jesus, one name spoken, and all of grief is converted in an instant. The Good Shepherd calls his sheep by name, and they know his voice.

His first words to her are a question, and it is the same question he has asked twice already in this book at moments that matter.

Whom are you seeking? He asked it of the first two disciples who followed him in chapter 1 — what are you seeking? — and he asked it of the arresting party in the garden, twice (18:4, 7). Now, in another garden, at the end, he asks it of a weeping woman.

The whole Gospel is bracketed by that question, and it has always been aimed past the person answering it.

And her reply is one of the most touching sentences in Scripture, because of what it takes for granted. Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.

She thinks he is the gardener. She is proposing to collect a corpse — a grown man's body, dead thirty-six hours — and carry it off herself. She has no plan for where to put it and no means of moving it. Love has produced an offer that makes no practical sense whatever, and she makes it to a stranger without embarrassment.

Then one word.

Mary.

Not an explanation. Not it is I. Not a rebuke for failing to recognise him, and no reference to the resurrection at all. He says her name, and she is turned round in an instant.

He had said, in a temple colonnade in winter, that the shepherd calls his own sheep by name and that they know his voice (10:3-4). This is that sentence happening.

And her reply is Aramaic, which John keeps rather than translating away — Rabboni, my teacher, my master. It is what she had always called him. She reaches for the old word because the man in front of her is the same man, and there is not yet a vocabulary for what has happened.

Consider what it cost to reach that moment. The one who says her name has been dead. He has come out of it, walked into a garden at first light, and stood behind a woman who was crying for him — and the first thing he does with a resurrected voice, before any announcement, before the eleven, before anything, is say the name of one grieving person.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful address.

parallels.desc: he calls his own sheep by name

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" — and that he had said these things to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not cling to me: Mary's instinct is to hold on to the one she thought she had lost — the natural response of love recovered. But the ascension is the destination; the resurrection is the passage. I am ascending to my Father and your Father: the resurrection makes the disciples' relationship to God the Father the same as Jesus' own — a relationship of sonship and covenant fidelity. Go to my brothers: Jesus' first post-resurrection commission is to a woman, and the content is the gospel. Mary Magdalene is the apostle to the apostles. I have seen the Lord: the simplest, fullest resurrection proclamation — personal, direct, present-tense, certain.

The old Latin rendering of the first clause has misled readers for centuries. Noli me tangere — do not touch me — has produced a great many paintings of a recoiling Christ and a rebuked woman, and it is a mistranslation.

The Greek is a present imperative, and with this verb it means: stop doing what you are already doing. She is not being kept at a distance. She has hold of him — Matthew records the other women taking hold of his feet (Mt. 28:9) — and the instruction is to let go.

Which is a completely different sentence. Not do not come near me but you cannot keep me here.

And the reason given is odd until it is thought about: for I have not yet ascended to the Father. The sense seems to be that this is not the arrangement she is hoping for. She has him back and wants things as they were — the old company, the old journeys, the old Rabboni. He is telling her that what is beginning is not a restoration of the past but a departure into something else, and that clinging to the interim is the one thing that will not work.

Then the word that ought to stop the reader: go to my brothers.

He has not called them that before in this Gospel. At supper, five chapters ago, he had promoted them from servants to friends (15:15), and that was already extraordinary. Now, after every one of them has run away, and one has denied him three times to strangers, he calls them his brothers.

The first thing he does with a resurrected body is upgrade the relationship of the men who abandoned him.

And a week later Jesus invites Thomas, Put your finger here (v. 27), so this is no ban on touching. I have not yet ascended means that Mary should not hold on as if the old way of being with him had simply returned. He is going to the Father, and from there he will be with them in a new way, by the Spirit (16:7).

And then the careful, deliberate distinction in the message itself, which should not be flattened: to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. Not our. He does not once, anywhere in the Gospels, include himself with the disciples in a single our Father — even when teaching them to pray it, he gives it to them to say. His sonship and theirs are now joined in one sentence and are not the same thing: he is Son by nature, they by gift. The two halves of the phrase preserve both.
verseByVerse.note: “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume; he is going to the Father.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — Appearances to the Disciples and to Thomas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The risen Jesus appears to the disciples on the evening of the first day, speaks peace, shows his wounds, and commissions them. Thomas is absent and refuses to believe without seeing; eight days later Jesus appears again and invites Thomas to touch. Thomas confesses 'My Lord and my God.' John closes by stating the purpose of the signs recorded in the gospel.

Two things are the largest in the section; both are treated at length below.

He breathed on them (v. 22). It is the act of two moments that matter: Genesis 2:7, where God breathed into the man's nostrils the breath of life, and Ezekiel 37:9, where the prophet is told to breathe on the slain that they may live. Creation, and re-creation from a field of corpses. The relation to Pentecost is genuinely disputed — a promise enacted in advance, a real but partial gift for the interim, or (probably best) the ordination to a commission for which nobody is sent without the Spirit, with Pentecost as the equipping. What no reading should do is make it a mere symbol. John recorded the creation act.

Forgiving and withholding sins (v. 23). The chapter's largest doctrinal crux. The verse-by-verse gives it in full, including the Roman reading — that this institutes the sacrament of penance, cited directly by the Council of Trent — and the three things that answer it: the parallel with the binding-and-loosing of Matt. 16:19 and 18:18, where the ESV margin gives shall have been bound, so the disciple announces what heaven has already settled; the complete absence of any such practice in the rest of the New Testament, where Peter sends Simon Magus to God rather than absolving him (Acts 8:22) and John's own letter directs the sinner to confess to God (1 Jn. 1:9); and what the verse does mean, which is not nothing — the church really does announce where people stand, and the minister is a herald carrying a message rather than a judge holding a power.

In defence of Thomas (vv. 24-25). He has been badly served by the church. Look at what he demands — to see the nail-marks and the side — and then look at verse 20, where Jesus showed them his hands and his side, and only then were the other ten glad. They had not believed Mary either (Lk. 24:11). Thomas is asking for exactly what his colleagues were given; the only difference is that he was out of the room that night. And this is the man who said let us also go, that we may die with him (11:16). Note too that he stayed with the group through eight days of misery and turned up the following Sunday, which is the practical counsel the passage offers: he did not reason his way out — he was in the room when Jesus came back.

The confession, and the architecture (vv. 27-28). Jesus quotes Thomas's own words back to him, though he was not there when they were spoken, and offers exactly what was asked without a word of rebuke. John never says whether Thomas touched him. Then a first-century Jew, raised on the LORD our God, the LORD is one, calls a man he watched die my Lord and my God — and is not corrected. And it closes the finest piece of architecture in the book: the Gospel opened with the Word was God (1:1) and arrives here, three verses from its original ending. If John wrote in the nineties, there is a further edge: Domitian is reported to have required the style dominus et deus noster, and Christians in Asia were being pressed on exactly that point.

The purpose (vv. 30-31). Verse 30 is the mark of an honest writer — the account is selective, seven signs out of many, and he says so. Then the book tells the reader what it is for, which almost no ancient book does. It is written to bring readers to believe and to keep them believing, and it plainly does both.
verseByVerse.theology: Peace be with you (vv. 19, 21, 26): three times in this section Jesus speaks this word. The resurrection peace is not the absence of the disciples' fear but the presence of the risen Lord. He shows them his hands and his side — the wounds are still present, the marks of the passion carried into the resurrection body. The resurrection does not erase the cross; it vindicates it, glorifies it, makes it permanently the ground of peace. The scars of Jesus in his resurrection body are the permanent declaration that the atonement is real and its benefits are everlasting.
verseByVerse.examples: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (v. 29): the beatitude of all post-apostolic faith. Every Christian since the first generation believes on the basis of testimony rather than sight — on the word of those who were there, preserved in the Scripture the Spirit inspired, applied by the Spirit who illuminates. Thomas's faith required the visible wounds; blessed are those who trust the testimony about the wounds. This is where the fourth gospel places us: in the company of the blessed who believe without seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, "Peace be with you." When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Doors being locked: the disciples are hiding in fear — the contrast with the boldness of the coming chapters is the measure of what Pentecost will accomplish. Jesus came and stood among them: the resurrection body is not limited by locked doors. Peace be with you — the Shalom of the covenant, now speaking in the voice of the one who purchased it at the cross. He showed them his hands and his side: identification and authentication — these are the wounds of Calvary, preserved in the risen body. Then the disciples were glad: the grief of crucifixion is converted into the joy Jesus promised (16:20-22). The sorrow is now joy.

Everything in this verse is worth slowing down for, because it is the reunion and John reports it in two verses.

The doors being locked… for fear of the Jews. That is where the church is on the evening of Easter Sunday: a room with the door bolted, containing men who have heard from Mary that she has seen the Lord and have made no discernible use of the information. Luke says plainly that they did not believe her (Lk. 24:11).

Then Jesus came and stood among them. John does not explain it and neither should anyone else. There is no suggestion of a door opening.

And the first word out of his mouth to the men who ran away is shalom — the ordinary Jewish greeting, the thing anyone said on entering a house. He does not begin with a rebuke, or an explanation, or I told you so, all three of which were available and deserved. He says hello.

Then he shows them his hands and his side, and it is worth asking why he had them to show.

Nothing required a resurrection body to be marked. This is a body that can enter a locked room; it is not subject to the ordinary limits. And yet the wounds are there, and he displays them deliberately, and in eight days he will invite a man to put his hand into one.

Which means the marks were kept on purpose. The one thing carried out of the grave into the new creation, the one piece of the old world that was not left behind, is the evidence of what it cost.

And then: the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord. It is a plain word — they were happy. He had promised it three nights earlier, in almost these words: you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy… I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you (16:20-22).

Seventy-two hours. The sorrow arrived exactly as described and so did the joy, and the man who predicted both was standing in the room.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom — now full of meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them again, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you." And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you: the missional commission rooted in the Trinitarian pattern. The disciples' mission is derived from and modeled on the Son's mission: sent by the one who has authority, for the purpose the one who sends has determined, in the power the one who sends provides. He breathed on them: the action echoes God breathing life into Adam (Gen. 2:7) — this is the new creation breath, the breath of the Spirit that animates the new humanity. The giving of the Spirit here is either an anticipatory sign of Pentecost or the beginning of the Spirit's indwelling that Pentecost will complete.

The verb in verse 22 occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and it is one of the most deliberate word-choices in the Gospel.

Enephysesen — he breathed into, or breathed on. It appears in the Greek Old Testament at two moments that matter enormously.

The first is Genesis 2:7: the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature. The second is Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where the prophet is told to prophesy to the wind: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live (Ezek. 37:9).

Creation, and re-creation from a field of corpses. John has reached for the verb that carries both, in a locked room, on the first day of the week.

And the word for spirit is the word for breath in both Hebrew and Greek, which is why the pun works and why it cannot be reproduced in English. He breathes, and says: receive breath.

Now the difficulty, and it should be stated honestly rather than smoothed over. If the Spirit is given here, what happens at Pentecost fifty days later? Three answers have been offered and each has serious defenders.

The first is that this is a promise enacted in advance — a sign of what Pentecost will deliver, in the way a man might hand over a key before the house is ready. The second is that this is a real but partial gift for the interim, with Pentecost supplying the public outpouring and the power for mission. The third, and probably the best, notes what the commission in the previous verse is for: they are being sent, and no one is sent on that errand without the Spirit. On this reading the breathing is the ordination and Pentecost is the equipping, and both are real.

What no reading should do is make this a mere symbol. John has just described the creation act. Something was given.

Then the sending itself, in verse 21, and the comparison is the largest ever made about the church's work: as the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.

Not in the same general spirit. As. The pattern for how Christians are sent into the world is how the Son was sent into it — which meant coming all the way in, at their level, at his own cost, and remaining available to be handled by people who did not want him.

And he says it while showing them the marks.
verseByVerse.note: Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam.

parallels.desc: the breath of life
come, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld." Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you forgive the sins: the authority to declare forgiveness — the same authority Jesus exercised in his ministry — is given to the apostolic community. This is not authority to forgive apart from Christ or independently of the gospel, but authority to declare (and withhold) forgiveness in the name of the crucified and risen Lord. The church that proclaims the gospel proclaims forgiveness to those who receive it; the church that rightly warns of judgment does so with the same authority. Thomas was not with them: his absence is providentially arranged to produce the encounter that will generate the gospel's climactic confession.

The reading being set aside there should be named, since it is held by most of the Christians in the world. Rome takes this verse as the institution of the sacrament of penance: the apostles, and the bishops and priests who succeed them, are given the power to absolve sins, exercised in the confessional, where the priest says I absolve you. The Council of Trent cited this text for it directly. It is not a frivolous reading — the words do plainly commit something about sins to these men — so it deserves an answer rather than a dismissal.

Three things answer it. The first is in the grammar, and it is decisive. The words rendered they are forgiven stand in the Greek perfect tense: they have been forgiven, and stand forgiven. The forgiveness is not created by the disciple's word; it is already in force, and the disciple announces it. It is the same construction Jesus used about binding and loosing (Matt. 16:19; 18:18), where the sense is what shall have been bound in heaven. Heaven does not ratify the church's verdict. The church announces heaven's.

The second is the plain absence of any such practice in the rest of the New Testament. Not once does an apostle hear a private confession and pronounce a man absolved. When Simon Magus needs forgiveness, Peter — who if anyone had this power, had it — does not absolve him but sends him to God: repent of this wickedness, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you (Acts 8:22). And John, who wrote this verse down, tells us in his own letter where a sinner is to take his sins: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Confession there is to God, and the promise rests on his faithfulness, not on a mediator's word.

The third is what the verse does mean, which is not nothing. Christ has entrusted his church with the announcement that decides where people stand — the keys, as Matthew calls them. When the gospel is preached, forgiveness is really offered and really withheld: to the man who repents and believes, the church may say with full authority, your sins are forgiven; to the one who will not, it must say with equal authority that they are not. The Reformers kept the substance of this and were right to. They kept the declaration of pardon in public worship, and Luther valued private confession to a pastor for a conscience too troubled to believe a general promise. What they refused was the idea that the forgiveness waits on the minister. He is a herald carrying a message, not a judge holding a power, and the best thing he can do for a frightened soul is tell him what God has already said.

verseByVerse.quote: So the other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord." But he said to them, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe." Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless I see — the condition Thomas sets is specific: not merely the risen Lord but the wounded Lord. He will not accept a resurrection that glosses over the death; he requires the continuity of wounds with the person. Eight days later: the disciples are still together, still behind locked doors, and now Thomas is with them. Jesus comes again — the risen Lord who does not abandon the doubter but returns specifically for him. Peace be with you: the same greeting, the same gift, offered to Thomas who has refused to believe the testimony of those who received it the first time.

Thomas has been badly served by the church, and it is worth putting the record straight, because doubting Thomas has become a byword and the text does not support the caricature.

Look at what he actually demands: to see the nail-marks and put his hand into the side.

Now look at verse 20. When Jesus appeared to the other ten, he showed them his hands and his side — and only then, John says, were they glad. They did not believe Mary's word either (Lk. 24:11). They believed when they were shown the wounds.

Thomas is asking for exactly what the other ten were given. He is not demanding more evidence than his colleagues had; he is refusing to accept less. The only difference between him and them is that he was out of the room on the night the evidence was handed round.

And this is the man who, when the others were arguing against going back to Judea because of the stoning, said let us also go, that we may die with him (11:16). Whatever his faults, cowardice and half-heartedness were not among them.

What he says is also stronger in Greek than in English — a double negative, I will certainly not believe — and it is spoken out of a week of misery. Consider the eight days he then spent. Ten men he had lived with for three years, all telling him the same impossible thing, all glad, and he alone outside it, unable to make himself believe them and unwilling to pretend.

He stayed, which is the thing to notice. He did not leave the group. He turned up on the following Sunday and was in the room.

Which is the practical counsel this passage offers to anyone in a stretch of unbelief, and it is not try harder to believe. It is: stay where the others are, and keep turning up. Thomas did not reason his way out. He was in the room when Jesus came back.
verseByVerse.note: Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet.

parallels.desc: they have pierced my hands and feet

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe." Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not disbelieve, but believe: the command is addressed to the whole condition of Thomas's heart, not merely to the moment's decision. The invitation to touch the wounds — Jesus offers exactly what Thomas demanded — is an act of extraordinary grace: the risen Lord accommodating himself to the doubt of Thomas. My Lord and my God: the highest Christological confession in the fourth gospel, spoken by the one who doubted most intensely. Thomas's confession is the gospel's climax: not 'a great teacher' or 'the Messiah' but Lord (covenant faithfulness) and God (divine identity). The one who was most reluctant speaks the most complete confession.

Notice first that Jesus quotes him.

Put your finger here… put out your hand, and place it in my side — those are Thomas's own words from eight days earlier, given back to him almost exactly. He was not in the room when Thomas said them. He had heard.

And there is no rebuke in the offer. He does not say you should not have needed this. He gives him precisely what he asked for, which is what he had already given the other ten without being asked.

John never tells us whether Thomas touched him. The account moves straight from the invitation to the confession, and most readers have concluded that he did not — that the offer itself was enough.

Then the sentence that closes the Gospel's argument.

My Lord and my God.

Stop and consider what has just been said, and by whom. A first-century Jew, raised on hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one, is standing in front of a man he watched die, and calls him God. Nothing in his upbringing permitted that sentence. He says it anyway, and Jesus does not correct him — which is the point, because he had corrected people about far less.

And the two possessives are the whole of Christianity in two words: my Lord and my God. Not the Lord. It is not a doctrinal formula; it is a man handing himself over.

There is one more thing, and it is the finest piece of architecture in the book. The Gospel opened: in the beginning was the Word… and the Word was God (1:1). It now arrives, twenty chapters later, at my Lord and my God — and the original ending of the book is three verses away.

John has bracketed the entire account between two statements of the deity of Christ. The first is his own, made about a Word nobody had yet seen. The last is spoken by the most reluctant man in the group, to a face, in a locked room, with the wounds visible.

If this Gospel was written in the nineties, as most think, there is a further edge to it. The emperor Domitian is reported to have required the style dominus et deus noster — our lord and god. Christians in Asia Minor were being pressed on exactly that point, and John hands them a sentence in which those words are addressed to somebody else.

parallels.desc: my God and my Lord

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed: the beatitude for all subsequent generations. The apostolic witness — the eyewitness testimony preserved in the gospel — becomes the ground for faith that does not require seeing the risen Lord directly. This beatitude places every reader of the gospel in a privileged position: our faith is not inferior to Thomas's because it comes through testimony rather than sight; it is the faith Jesus specifically blesses. The many other signs not written here: the gospel is selective, not exhaustive. John has chosen these signs for one specific purpose.

The beatitude is aimed forward, out of the room, at everybody who would ever read the book.

Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.

And it needs saying clearly that this is not a rebuke of Thomas dressed as a blessing of somebody else. Thomas is not cursed; he is standing there having just made the highest confession in the Gospel. What the sentence does is close a door that was about to shut anyway. There were, at that moment, a few hundred people alive who would ever see the risen Christ. Everybody else, for the next two thousand years, was going to have to work from testimony — and Jesus, in one of his last appearances, pronounces them blessed for it.

Which answers a suspicion most Christians have had at some point: that faith would be easier and better if only one could have been there. This verse says the opposite. Not that seeing would be worse, but that not-seeing is no disadvantage and carries a blessing of its own.

Then the admission in verse 30, which is the mark of an honest writer: Jesus did many other signs… which are not written in this book.

He is telling us the account is selective. Seven signs, out of many; a handful of days, out of three years. He is not claiming to have written everything and he does not want the reader thinking he has.

Which is worth having when somebody objects that the Gospels omit things, or differ in what they include. Of course they do. The author says so in the second-to-last verse of his book, and then explains exactly what his selection was for.

And there is a quiet generosity in how the beatitude is worded. Not blessed are those who believe without evidence — John has just spent twenty chapters supplying evidence, and will say in the next verse that he selected it deliberately. The blessing is on those who have not seen, which is a different thing. They have the testimony of people who did.

parallels.desc: though you do not now see him, you believe in him

verseByVerse.quote: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are written so that you may believe: the evangelistic purpose of the entire gospel stated with perfect clarity. Every pericope, every sign, every discourse, every confrontation — all of it is written for this outcome: believing that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. And by believing you may have life in his name: the life that the Prologue announced (in him was life, 1:4), that the Bread of Life discourse promised (whoever believes has eternal life, 6:47), that the High-Priestly Prayer defined (that they know you, 17:3) — this life is received through believing, and believing is produced by the testimony of the gospel. The book is itself the means of the life it announces.

This is the last sentence of the Gospel as John first ended it — chapter 21 reads as an addition, and its own closing verse says something different — and it does what almost no ancient book does. It tells the reader what it is for.

These are written so that you may believe.

Not so that the record would be preserved, though it is. Not so that the church would have a history, though it does. He selected seven signs out of many and arranged twenty chapters around them with one outcome in view, and he states it in a single sentence and then stops.

An honest note on the Greek. There is a well-known variant in the verb: one reading is aorist, that you may come to believe, which makes the book evangelistic, addressed to outsiders; the other is present, that you may go on believing, which makes it a book for the church. The manuscripts are genuinely divided and the argument has never been settled.

It is a happy dispute, because the book plainly does both. It has brought people to Christ who began it as sceptics, and it has held Christians steady for twenty centuries, and nothing in the sentence has to be given up.

Then the content of the faith, stated with precision: that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. Two titles, and both have been fought over in this book. The Christ — the promised one of Israel, which is what the crowds argued about at the feast. The Son of God — which is what they picked up stones over, and what the council convicted him for, and what Pilate was afraid of.

And then the purpose beyond the purpose: that by believing you may have life in his name.

Which is where the book started. In him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4). Everything between — the water made wine, the bread on the hillside, the man who could see, the voice at the tomb of Lazarus, the towel and the basin, the cross, the empty grave, the name spoken in a garden — has been in service of that one word, and it is offered, at the end, to whoever is holding the book.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.”
