21.title: The Restoration of Peter and the Beloved Disciple

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Breakfast on the Shore: Restoration and Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Seven disciples return to fishing on the Sea of Tiberias and catch nothing all night. The risen Jesus stands on the shore and directs a miraculous catch of 153 fish; the beloved disciple recognizes him; Peter leaps into the water. Jesus has prepared breakfast — bread and fish — and feeds them. He then restores Peter with three questions matching the three denials, commissions him to feed his sheep, and predicts his martyrdom. The gospel closes with testimony to the beloved disciple and a statement about the unwritten works of Jesus.

A guard on "I am going fishing" (v. 3). It is regularly preached as apostasy — Peter throwing in the towel — and the text will not carry it. The risen Jesus had told the women to send word that the disciples were to go to Galilee, and there they will see me (Mt. 28:10; Mk. 16:7). Galilee is where these men are: they have obeyed an instruction and are waiting in the place they were told to wait, with no date given, and men who are waiting have to eat. What is true, and sadder, is the flatness of it — I am going fishing is what people say when they do not know what else to do with themselves.

The scene has happened before (vv. 5-6). The words he calls across the water are ordinary and that is the point — the question a buyer shouts from the beach at dawn. And behind the whole scene is Luke 5:1-11, where Jesus first called these men after a night in which they caught nothing, told Peter to let down the nets, and filled them until they tore — and Peter fell down and said depart from me, for I am a sinful man. Here it is again, at the end, and this time Peter does not ask him to go away. He goes into the water to get to him. And the net was not torn, where Luke says the nets were breaking.

Peter dressed to swim (v. 7). The likeliest explanation is that a Jew did not greet a person of standing improperly clothed. He was a hundred yards out and could have waited three minutes for the boat. Nothing about his temperament has been corrected by his failure, and Jesus is about to give him a job without asking him to become somebody else.

Breakfast was already cooking (v. 9). Before there was a catch, and while seven men were still failing to fish, there was a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Then he asks for theirs and puts them on beside his own — which he does not need. That is very close to the whole doctrine of Christian work: nothing we bring is required, it is asked for anyway, and it goes on the fire with his.

The number (v. 11). Jerome reported 153 known species of fish; Augustine noticed it is the sum of 1 to 17 and built a structure on it. None of it commands agreement and most could be produced for almost any number. The simplest explanation is likelier and not less interesting: fishermen count the catch, and sixty years later an old man still remembered the figure. Legends do not carry inventory numbers.

Nobody dared ask (v. 12). They knew it was the Lord — and said nothing. Seven men round a fire in a silence too large to break: not doubt, and not fear exactly, but the awkwardness of standing with somebody you watched die and then abandoned. Into which: come and have breakfast.

Simon, son of John (v. 15). He is addressed by the name he had before the promise — Jesus had renamed him at their first meeting (1:42) — and it lands hard, three times. Not cruelty: the necessary honesty of a restoration that refuses to pretend. And the question is the one nobody would predict. Not are you sorry, not will you promise, not do you understand what you did. Peter is never asked to explain himself and never given the chance to make again the vow he had broken. Do you love me? — that is the entire examination for restoration to apostolic ministry.

You know everything (v. 17). His answer changes at the third question: not you know but Lord, you know everything. That is the appeal of a man who has run out of evidence about himself and can only appeal past his own record to the one who sees underneath it. Jesus accepts it, and hands over the sheep.

Follow me (v. 19). He will say them again in v. 22. He said them to Philip three years earlier (1:43) and to Peter himself beside this lake with a net in his hands (Mt. 4:19). Everything has happened in between — the confession, the sword, the courtyard, the fire, the rooster — and the instruction has not changed by a syllable. No reduced role, no probation, no adjusted terms. Note too that by what kind of death he was to glorify God is the same formula John used of Jesus at 12:33.

What is that to you? (vv. 21-22). The most practically useful sentence in the chapter. Peter has just been restored, commissioned and told how he will die — and within about one sentence he turns round, spots John, and asks what he is getting. It is not malice; it is the instinct that arrives the moment anyone is handed something hard. And the answer offers no explanation at all, then repeats the command with the pronoun brought forward for emphasis: you follow me. The call is not comparative. By early tradition Peter's road ended on a cross in Rome and John's in extreme old age in Ephesus, and neither was owed the other's.

The rumour corrected (v. 23). A hypothetical was repeated, the if fell off in transmission, and within a generation people were treating it as a promise. The response is not indignation but a quotation: the sentence given back exactly as it was said, with the if restored. It is what the church has had to do ever since, and the first recorded instance is here.
verseByVerse.theology: The threefold restoration of Peter — Do you love me? / Feed my sheep — is the most pastoral moment in the gospel. Three questions match three denials; three commissions match three failures. The charcoal fire (the same as 18:18) brings the smell of the denial back to Peter's senses; the same kind of fire is now the fire of restoration. Jesus does not ignore the failure or pretend it did not happen; he names it by re-enacting the scene in reverse. The gospel's answer to failure is not silence but renewed commission — the broken shepherd is restored to shepherd the flock.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple as the witness who wrote these things (v. 24): the gospel stakes its authority on eyewitness testimony. This is not mythology or legend but the account of one who was there — who saw the water turned to wine, stood at the cross, ran to the empty tomb, and watched Jesus break bread on the shore. The testimony is true because the witness is trustworthy; the witness is trustworthy because the one he testifies to is the resurrection and the life. The gospel ends not with a doctrine but with a person: if everything were written, the world itself could not contain the books. The Word is larger than any book.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this: the gospel has one more chapter after the stated purpose (20:31) — an epilogue that provides the restoration without which the story would be incomplete. The Sea of Tiberias, where the feeding of the five thousand occurred and where Jesus walked on water: the setting is thick with memory. Seven disciples: a complete number, a microcosm of the church. Simon Peter is listed first — the denier who will be restored is the protagonist of this final scene. The one who failed most publicly will be commissioned most specifically.

Two small things in the list of names are worth having, because John has arranged them.

Thomas is here, called the Twin, and it is the last we see of him — some time after he put his confession into the record, back at work on a lake with the others. Whatever the caricature has made of him, John's final image is of a man who stayed.

And Nathanael is given a home town for the only time in the Gospel: Nathanael of Cana in Galilee. We were never told it in chapter 1, when he was sitting under a fig tree being sceptical about Nazareth. Cana is where the water became wine — the first sign — and John has waited twenty chapters to mention that one of the men who watched it happen lived in the village.

The book is closing its own circles. It began by the water with men being called, and it ends by the water with the same men.

Seven of them, which is worth noting in a Gospel that has given us seven signs and seven I am sayings. And two are left unnamed, which is the sort of detail nobody invents; a writer constructing a scene supplies names.

And the phrase John uses for what happens is worth having: Jesus revealed himself — twice in one verse.

The word implies that the initiative is entirely on one side. These men did not find him and did not go looking; they went to work. He showed himself to them, on his own timing, while they were doing something else — which has been the pattern of every appearance in this Gospel from the first chapter onward.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee. Nathanael came from Cana; the sons of Zebedee are James and John.

parallels.desc: he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will go with you." They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am going fishing: Peter returns to what he knew before Jesus called him — the old life, the familiar work, perhaps because the failure of the denial has made him feel unworthy of the new commission. The return to fishing is not necessarily abandonment of the calling but the disorientation of a man who has failed catastrophically. That night they caught nothing: the futility of ministry without the Shepherd's direction. Just as day was breaking — the dawn of the new day, the risen Son about to appear on the shore. The disciples do not recognize him yet; recognition always takes a moment when Jesus appears in unexpected places.

A guard is needed on I am going fishing, because it is regularly preached as apostasy — Peter throwing in the towel, going back to his nets, abandoning the call — and the text will not carry it.

Consider where they are and why. The risen Jesus had told the women to send word: go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me (Mt. 28:10; and Mk. 16:7). Galilee is where these men are. They have obeyed an instruction and are waiting for him in the place they were told to wait, with no date given.

And men who are waiting have to eat. Peter owned a boat and knew a trade, and there is nothing in the story to suggest that using it was a betrayal of anything. Six of them go with him without a word of hesitation, including the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is not elsewhere presented as a backslider.

What is true, and sadder, is the flatness of it. A man who has seen the risen Lord twice, and denied him three times, says I am going fishing — which is what people do when they do not know what else to do with themselves. It is not rebellion. It is the ordinary, unglamorous business of filling the hours while waiting for something you cannot arrange.

Then: that night they caught nothing.

Professional fishermen, on their own lake, working the hours when the fish come up, and they take not one fish. It is the second time John has put them on that water in the dark with nothing going right (6:16-21), and both times the story ends with somebody standing where they did not expect him.

And the detail about the daybreak is exact. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore — at the moment the night's failure is confirmed and there is nothing left to do but come in empty.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night.

parallels.desc: we toiled all night and took nothing

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Children, do you have any fish?" They answered him, "No." He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children: a term of affection. Do you have any fish? — the question of the one who already knows the answer, opening the conversation of restoration. Cast on the right side: the direction from shore, from the one they do not yet recognize. The obedience produces abundance — 153 large fish that do not tear the net. The miracle repeats the pattern of Cana: the servants fill the jars and receive wine; the disciples cast the net and receive fish. Obedience to Jesus' word always produces what independent effort cannot. The mission of the church is fruitful when it operates at Jesus' direction.

The two words he calls across the water are both worth having, because they are entirely ordinary and that is the point.

Children is paidia here — not the tender little children of the upper room but the everyday word a man uses hailing a boat: lads. And what he asks is prosphagion, a rare word that does not mean fish in general but the bit of fish you eat with your bread. It is the question a buyer shouts from the beach at dawn: caught anything?

So the risen Son of God opens the conversation of Peter's restoration by pretending to want breakfast.

And their answer is one word. No. John records it bare, which is how a man says it after a whole night of nothing.

Now the thing that makes this scene what it is, and it depends on a story in another Gospel. Luke records that when Jesus first called these men, he got into Peter's boat after a night in which they had caught nothing, told him to let down the nets, and filled them so full that the nets began to tear and a second boat nearly sank. And Peter fell down and said: depart from me, for I am a sinful man (Lk. 5:1-11).

That is where Peter's discipleship began. A wasted night, a stranger's instruction, an impossible catch, and a man on his knees saying he was not fit.

Here it is again, on the same lake, at the end. The empty night, the instruction from the shore, the catch — and this time Peter does not ask him to go away. He goes into the water to get to him.

John does not mention Luke's story. He does not have to. The men in the boat had lived it, and when the nets went heavy for the second time in their lives, at least one of them worked out immediately who was on the beach.
verseByVerse.note: “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men.

parallels.desc: the first great catch

verseByVerse.quote: That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Lord! — the beloved disciple's recognition, based on the miracle. Peter throws himself into the sea: the same impulsive love that drove him to reach for the sword in the garden now drives him into the water toward Jesus. His love for Jesus has survived the denial — it is perhaps the one thing that remained intact through the failure. The other disciples come in the boat with the net; both responses are appropriate. The one who leaps into the water and the ones who carefully bring the boat and the fish are both serving. The church needs both the impetuous and the methodical.

The two men behave exactly as they have all the way through, and John clearly enjoys recording it.

It is the beloved disciple who works it out — he is the one who saw the grave clothes and believed, and he is the first here too. And it is Peter who moves. One sees; the other jumps.

And there is a small comic detail that has puzzled readers for centuries: he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.

He dressed to swim. Most people would do the opposite.

The likeliest explanation is that a Jew did not greet a person of standing improperly clothed — a greeting was something close to a religious act, and one did not perform it half-naked. Peter is about to meet his Lord, and he is not going to arrive stripped for work, and so he tucks up whatever he had discarded and goes over the side in it.

He was about a hundred yards out. He could have waited perhaps three minutes for the boat.

Which is the whole man. It is the same impulse that drew a sword in the garden and swore he would die first. Nothing about Peter's temperament has been corrected by his failure, and Jesus is about to give him a job without asking him to become somebody else.

And notice what the others do. They bring the boat in, dragging the net, doing the necessary work while one of them swims. John does not rank them. Both arrive.

There is one more detail of the sort that only a witness supplies: about a hundred yards off. Two hundred cubits, John says. Somebody looked at the distance and remembered it.

These small measurements run all through this Gospel — six stone jars holding twenty or thirty gallons, twenty-five or thirty stadia rowed on a dark lake, seventy-five pounds of spices, a hundred yards to a beach. They do nothing for the theology. They are what a man includes when he is describing something he watched.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits.

verseByVerse.quote: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish that you have just caught."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A charcoal fire: anthrakian — the same rare Greek word as 18:18, where Peter warmed himself at the fire of his denial. The resurrection Jesus has lit the same kind of fire. The smell of burning charcoal will bring the memory of denial flooding back — and Jesus has chosen this specific word, this specific scene, deliberately. The restoration is not private and abstract; it is sensory, evocative, specific. Bring some of the fish: Jesus involves the disciples in the breakfast he has already prepared. The Shepherd feeds the sheep; he also invites the sheep to bring what they have caught to the meal he provides.

Everything about this fire matters, and the essential thing is this: a charcoal fire, which occurs exactly twice in the whole New Testament. Here, and in a courtyard on the night Peter said I am not (18:18).

Nobody else in the New Testament mentions one. John used it once when Peter was warming his hands among the men who had arrested his master, and he uses it again now, and he does not explain.

Smell is the sense that reaches memory most directly, and every man who has ever cooked outdoors knows what charcoal smells like. Peter comes up the beach soaked, and the wind is off the fire.

He has been brought back to the scene of it.

And what is on the fire is the thing to notice: fish laid out on it, and bread. Before there was a catch. Before Peter had done anything at all, and while seven men were still failing to fish, breakfast was already cooking.

Then the invitation: bring some of the fish that you have just caught.

He does not need them. He has fish. But he asks for theirs and puts them on the fire beside his own, which is one of the gentlest things in the Gospels — the risen Lord, who has provided everything, arranging for the men to contribute to a meal they could not have produced.

That is very close to the whole doctrine of Christian work. Nothing we bring is required. It is asked for anyway, and it goes on the fire with his.

And notice that the fire is in place — already burning, already down to coals hot enough to cook on, which takes time. Somebody had been on that beach a while.

They had spent the night failing on the water and he had spent part of it making a fire.
verseByVerse.note: John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial.

verseByVerse.quote: So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." Now none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
153 fish, and the net was not torn: the specificity of 153 has generated enormous discussion (Jerome: the total species of fish known; Augustine: a mathematical figure for the totality of the righteous). What matters is that John remembered the number — eyewitness memory preserves the particular. Come and have breakfast: the risen Lord hosting a meal on the beach, serving bread and fish to his disciples. They knew it was the Lord — the recognition is now complete, the wondering is over. The risen Christ breaking bread with his disciples is the foretaste of the great messianic banquet, the fellowship of the age to come breaking into the present.

The number has attracted more ingenuity than any other detail in the Gospel, and the honest thing is to survey it briefly and then say what is probably true.

Jerome reported that Greek naturalists counted 153 species of fish, so that the catch would represent every kind of person gathered in. Augustine noticed that 153 is the sum of every number from 1 to 17, and built an elaborate structure on 10 (the commandments) plus 7 (the Spirit). Others have counted the numerical values of Hebrew letters and produced everything from the church of love to place-names.

None of it commands agreement, and most of it could be produced for almost any number. The simplest explanation is much more likely and is not less interesting: they counted the fish because they were fishermen, and fishermen count the catch. It was a remarkable haul and somebody sat on the beach and totted it up, and sixty years later an old man still remembered the figure.

Which is worth more than any allegory. Legends do not carry inventory numbers.

And the clause after it is the one that matters: although there were so many, the net was not torn.

The first time this happened, at the call of these men, Luke says their nets were breaking and a second boat was needed and both began to sink (Lk. 5:6-7). This time the same lake, the same men, a similar catch — and nothing tears.

Then the most awkward sentence in the chapter: none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.

They knew, and nobody said anything. It is the description of seven men standing round a fire in a silence too large to break — not doubt, and not fear exactly, but the awkwardness of being in the presence of somebody you watched die and then abandoned.

And into that silence: come and have breakfast.
verseByVerse.note: Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest point is that someone counted — a detail from an eyewitness.

parallels.desc: their nets were breaking

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Took the bread and gave it to them: the eucharistic gesture — taking, giving — repeated at the Last Supper, at the feeding of the five thousand, and now on the beach. Each time the risen Lord breaks bread, the reality of his resurrection body is confirmed and the sacramental dimension of the meal is deepened. The third time he was revealed: the first two were in the upper room (20:19-23; 20:26-29); this is the third. The appearances are specifically to the disciples, preparing them for the mission that the commission (vv. 15-19) will make explicit.

Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them.

Three verbs, and this Gospel has used them before. On a hillside above this same lake he took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them to five thousand people (6:11). The wording here is deliberately plain and deliberately familiar.

And he serves them. That is the fact to sit with. The risen Lord of glory, days out of a grave, with the marks still in his hands, is crouched over a fire on a beach handing bread to seven fishermen who have been up all night.

He had told them, in the upper room, that he was among them as the one who serves (Lk. 22:27), and he had knelt with a towel to prove it. Nothing about the resurrection has changed that. The one who washed their feet before he died is cooking their breakfast after.

Then John's count: this was now the third time. He is numbering the appearances to the disciples as a group — the locked room without Thomas (20:19-23), the locked room with him (20:26-29), and this one.

The first two were indoors, in a city, behind bolted doors, with fear in the room. This one is outdoors, at dawn, in their own country, over a meal, with the door of the world standing open.

And the meal itself is bread and fish — which is what he had multiplied on the hillside above this lake for five thousand people (6:9-11), and the only meal this Gospel records him providing twice.

The first time it was a sign, and the crowd wanted to make him king over it and then walked away when he explained what it meant. This time there is no crowd, no argument, and no discourse afterwards. Just seven men eating breakfast with him.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." He said to him a second time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Tend my sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, son of John: the name given before the new name — not Peter the Rock but Simon the son of John, the man before the calling. Do you love me more than these? — more than the other disciples, or more than the fishing equipment? Both readings are possible; the first recalls Peter's confident claim to greater loyalty (13:37). Three questions for three denials; the charcoal fire for the charcoal fire. Jesus is not torturing Peter but restoring him with the same precision that the failure exhibited. Feed my lambs, tend my sheep: the pastoral commission given to the one who has been through the fire of failure and come out the other side. One detail a study Bible will flag: in the Greek, Jesus' first two questions use one word for love (agapao) while Peter answers each time with another (phileo, the love of warm friendship); on the third question Jesus switches to Peter's own word. Some see real weight here — Jesus meeting a chastened Peter where he is, no longer pressing him to claim the higher love he had once boasted. Others note that John freely swaps synonyms throughout this very passage (two words each for feed/tend, sheep/lambs, know), so the change may be style, not substance. Either way the thrust is the same: three questions answering three denials, and a full restoration to shepherd Christ's flock.

Two things should be said, even-handedly.

The strongest argument that the change of verbs is stylistic rather than freighted is that it does not stand alone. In these three exchanges John uses two different words for love, two for feeding and tending, two for lambs and sheep, and two for knowing. Four pairs of synonyms in three verses. A writer who is varying his vocabulary that systematically is very likely doing it for the ear.

Which does not settle it, and the older reading remains available and moving. The point is that nothing in the passage's meaning depends on the outcome.

The second is the name. Simon, son of John — and it lands hard, because Jesus gave this man a different name at their very first meeting: you shall be called Cephas, which means Peter (1:42). The Rock.

Now, on a beach, after a courtyard and a fire and three denials, he is addressed by the name he had before the promise was made. Three times.

It is not cruelty. It is the necessary honesty of a restoration that refuses to pretend. A man who has failed catastrophically cannot be repaired by being told the failure did not matter, and Jesus does not tell him that. He takes him back to Simon son of John, and starts again from there.

And the question he asks is the one nobody would predict.

Not are you sorry. Not will you promise. Not do you understand what you did. Peter is never asked to explain himself, never asked to apologise, never once given the chance to make the vow he had made before and broken.

Do you love me?

That is the entire examination for restoration to apostolic ministry, put three times, and it is about affection rather than performance — which is worth knowing for anyone who has failed and assumes that what is wanted is a better record.

Does Feed my sheep make Peter the head of the church and the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching reads it so. But the threefold question answers the threefold denial: it restores a fallen apostle to his work. It speaks of no office above the other apostles and of no successors. Peter himself later tells the elders, as a fellow elder, to shepherd the flock of God that is among you (1 Pet 5:1–2). The commission is for every faithful pastor.

And more than these is probably aimed at the boast. Peter had said, on the way to the Mount of Olives, though they all fall away, I will not (Mk. 14:29) — the comparison was his own. Jesus raises it once and then drops it, and never mentions it again.
verseByVerse.note: “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me — Peter had claimed he would never fall away.

parallels.desc: shepherd the flock of God

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter was grieved: the third question opens the wound — he knows why three times. Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you: the appeal to Jesus' omniscience is the only resource Peter has left. He cannot claim a consistent track record; he can only appeal to the one who knows the heart beneath the failure. You know that I love you — imperfect, tested, failed, and real. Feed my sheep: the commission is threefold because the failure was threefold. You will stretch out your hands: the prediction of crucifixion — Peter's martyrdom, which tradition places in Rome under Nero. The restored shepherd is commissioned to the path the Good Shepherd walked.

Peter was grieved. The verb is strong — distressed, pained. And John tells us exactly what caused it: not the question, but the third one.

He knew what the third meant. Nobody had to say it.

And his answer changes. The first two times he says you know; the third time he says Lord, you know everything. That is the appeal of a man who has run out of evidence about himself. He cannot point to a record, because his record is a courtyard and a fire and a rooster. All he can do is appeal past his own performance to the one who can see what is underneath it.

Which is a real place to stand, and a great many Christians end up standing there. Not I have been faithful, which he could not say. Not I will do better, which he had said before and which had proved worthless. Just: you know everything, and you know that I love you.

Jesus accepts it. That is the extraordinary thing. He does not require any more than that, and he immediately hands over the sheep.

Then the prediction, and it is not a threat. When you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted — which is a description of Peter's whole life so far, including the impulsiveness that had just put him over the side of a boat. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.

Stretch out your hands was a recognised way of speaking about crucifixion in the early centuries, and the next verse says outright that it refers to his death.

So the restoration comes with the truth attached. Peter is not being told that everything will be well in the sense he might like. He had once said I will lay down my life for you and had not (13:37). He is now told, quietly, over breakfast, that he will — and that it will happen when he is old, and that he will not want to go.

The Lord does not pretend the road is easy, and he does not withhold the commission because the man will suffer for it.
verseByVerse.note: Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. “Stretch out your hands” was an expression used of crucifixion; early Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, "Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow me: the first call is the last call. Peter's entire discipleship — the calling, the confession, the failure, the restoration — ends where it began: Follow me. The follow-me that Jesus speaks now carries everything that has happened between the first and last word. Follow me means follow me to death, follow me to resurrection, follow me in feeding the sheep. Peter turns and sees the beloved disciple following. The community of the restored and the faithful will walk together behind the one who laid down his life and took it up again.

Notice first the formula John uses about Peter's death: this he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.

He has written that sentence once before, word for word in its essential parts, and it was about Jesus: he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). The same construction, applied to the Master and then to the disciple.

And the addition here is to glorify God. In this Gospel, glorifying God through a death has had exactly one referent for twenty chapters. Peter is being told that his end will do what his Lord's did — not atone, which is not on offer to anybody, but glorify.

Then two words, which he will say again to Peter in v. 22.

Follow me.

They are the words he had said to Philip as he set out for Galilee three years earlier (1:43), and the words Matthew records him saying to Peter himself beside this very lake, with a net in his hands: follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (Mt. 4:19).

Everything has happened in between. The confession and the rebuke, the walking on water and the sinking, the sword and the courtyard and the fire and the rooster and the weeping. And the instruction has not changed by a syllable.

Which is worth taking in. There was no new arrangement for a man who had failed — no reduced role, no probation, no adjusted terms. The same two words he was given at the beginning, given back to him at the end, as though nothing needed altering.

And it is not a single decision but a way of going on.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus said to him, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, what about this man? — Peter's attention immediately shifts from his own path to the other disciple's path. This is the distraction that self-pity and comparison always produce. What is that to you? — the sharpest redirection in the gospel. Each disciple has a different path assigned by the sovereign Lord; comparison is not only useless but disobedient. You follow me: the personal pronoun is emphatic — you, regardless of what anyone else is called to. The call to discipleship is never comparative; it is always direct, personal, and sufficient for the one to whom it is addressed.

The timing of Peter's question is what makes this so useful, and it is very human.

He has just been restored, commissioned, and told how he will die. And within about one sentence he has turned round, spotted John walking behind them, and asked what is going to happen to him.

It is not malice. It is the instinct that arrives the moment a person is given something hard: to find out what the other man is getting. Peter has just been handed a cross, and his first move is to check whether it is being handed out evenly.

And the answer is one of the bluntest things Jesus ever says: what is that to you?

There is no explanation offered. He does not tell Peter what John's road will be, or justify the difference, or soften it. He declines the question entirely — and then repeats the command with the pronoun brought forward for emphasis: you follow me.

Which is the most practically useful sentence in the chapter, and it applies far past martyrdom. Every Christian eventually notices that the terms are not identical: another believer's marriage, health, children, work, or capacity for prayer looks easier, and the comparison is corrosive in both directions — it breeds resentment when we come off worse and complacency when we come off better.

Here is the test, and it is simple to run. Notice the last time a comparison with another Christian occupied more than a moment of your thinking. Then ask what Jesus said about that exact activity to the man he had just restored: what is that to you?

The call is not comparative. It never was. By early tradition Peter's road ended on a cross in Rome and John's ended in extreme old age in Ephesus, and neither of them was owed the other's.

verseByVerse.quote: So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying spread abroad: the misunderstanding of Jesus' hypothetical about the beloved disciple generated a tradition that he would not die. John (through the community's editorial voice) corrects the misreading: Jesus said if, not that he would remain. The correction of a theological misunderstanding within the text itself is itself evidence of the text's historical integrity. This is the disciple who is bearing witness: the gospel's authorial claim, presented in the community's voice. We know that his testimony is true — the community vouches for the eyewitness. The chain of testimony — eyewitness, community, text, reader — is the chain by which the gospel travels across generations.

That shift to we know is worth stopping on, since it sounds like the community's voice and a reader may fairly wonder what that implies. Some scholars argue that this whole chapter was added after John's death by the church that preserved his teaching. The case is not silly: 20:30-31 reads exactly like the end of a book, this chapter opens after that ending, and here at the close someone other than the author appears to be vouching for him.

Two things weigh heavily the other way. The first is decisive and simply stated: no manuscript of this Gospel lacks chapter 21. Not one, anywhere, in any language. That is a completely different situation from the passage about the woman caught in adultery, or the long ending of Mark, where the copies genuinely divide and your Bible carries a footnote saying so. Whatever the history of how this book was assembled, it was never in circulation without these verses. The second is that the we needs no editor to explain it. John writes this way elsewhere of the shared apostolic witness — we have seen his glory (1:14) — and a document could carry the endorsement of the elders who published it without ceasing to be the author's own, much as a preface signed by others does not make a book someone else's.

And consider what a Gospel that stopped at 20:31 would have left. Peter's denial would still be lying there from chapter 18, three times by a charcoal fire, unhealed. This chapter puts him beside another charcoal fire and asks him three times whether he loves, and gives him back his work. A book that ended without it would have been correct and unfinished.

One last thing about how it closes. John never describes the ascension. Luke tells it twice because he is writing the sequel; John simply stops, on a beach in Galilee, with two words spoken to a man who had failed: follow me. He told us at 20:31 why he wrote — that you may believe, and that believing you may have life — and once that is done he does not need a departure scene. He leaves you not watching the sky, but standing on the sand, with a command and an open road.

One more thing about the rumour, because it is a small window into the early church and it is oddly reassuring.

The saying went round that the beloved disciple would not die. It is exactly the kind of thing that happens to a remark — a hypothetical gets repeated, the if falls off in transmission, and within a generation people are treating it as a promise. Presumably as John grew very old the story hardened, and presumably it was causing difficulty by the time this was written.

And the response is not indignation or embarrassment. Somebody simply quotes the sentence back exactly as it was said, with the if restored, and points out the difference.

That is a community handling a piece of misinformation about its own founder by returning to the words. It is what the church has had to do ever since, and the first recorded instance of it is in the second-to-last paragraph of this Gospel.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Verse 24 identifies him as the author of the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world itself could not contain the books: the hyperbole is the testimony of a man who was there and knows that what he has written is a selection from an inexhaustible abundance. The fourth gospel has given us twenty-one chapters; the actual life of the Word-made-flesh, if fully recorded, would exceed the capacity of the world. This is the appropriate ending: not exhaustion but inexhaustibility. Jesus is larger than any text about him. The gospel is complete as a testimony to who he is and what he accomplished; it is not complete as a catalogue of all he said and did. The invitation of the last verse is the invitation of the whole gospel: the one who is the way, the truth, and the life is always more than you have yet discovered.

The last verse of the Gospel is a joke — a deliberate, affectionate exaggeration, and the writer flags it himself with I suppose.

He knows the world could contain the books. He is not making a claim about library capacity. He is doing what a man does when he has finished writing about somebody he loves and looks at what he has produced and finds it absurdly inadequate.

And it is the right ending, because it corrects the impression that a finished book might otherwise leave. Twenty-one chapters can be read in an afternoon. A person could close it thinking he now has Jesus of Nazareth, complete, between two covers.

John's last act is to say: this is a selection. There were three years. I have given you seven signs and a handful of conversations and one week in detail, and I chose them for a stated purpose (20:31), and what is not here would swamp the world.

Which is worth having in front of anyone who has read the Gospel through and feels they have got to the bottom of it. The book is finished. The subject is not.

And so it ends: not with a doctrine, not with an ascension, not with a summary of what has been proved — but on a beach in Galilee, with a charcoal fire going out, and a man who had failed being told to keep walking.

He had made breakfast before they arrived. That is the thing to carry away from this book. Twenty-one chapters of signs and arguments and stones picked up and men walking away, and it ends with the Lord of glory crouched over a fire at dawn, cooking fish for seven tired men who had caught nothing and deserved nothing and had run away from him not long before.

He had every right to be somewhere else. He was days out of a grave and about to go home to his Father, and what he did with that morning was light a fire on a beach and wait for a boat.

Whatever else this Gospel has proved, it has established the character of the one it is about, and this is the last picture it gives: not a throne, and not a cloud, but a meal cooking, and a question that is not are you sorry but do you love me, and then two words that had never changed and never will.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.<sup>2</sup>Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.<sup>3</sup>Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.<sup>4</sup>Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>5</sup>Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.”<sup>6</sup>He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.<sup>7</sup>That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.<sup>8</sup>The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.<sup>9</sup>When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread.<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”<sup>11</sup>So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.<sup>12</sup>Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish.<sup>14</sup>This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.<sup>15</sup>When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”<sup>16</sup>He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”<sup>17</sup>He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.<sup>18</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”<sup>19</sup>(This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.) And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>20</sup>Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”<sup>21</sup>When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”<sup>22</sup>Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”<sup>23</sup>So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?”<sup>24</sup>This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.<sup>25</sup>Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
